Persistent incrementality in Rust

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4165 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There is this cool idea: incremental computations.
  • It has been revealed that this concept usually works the best when you need to compute a lot of stuff, and there are a lot of inputs, and these inputs change independently with different degree of likelihood.
  • And if incremental computations concept applies well to compilers, it applies even better to LSP servers, because user makes edits in the editor much more often than they recompile code, and each keystroke must change the editor state in milliseconds (unless you go full vibe and don't need an IDE anymore, that is).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is this cool idea: incremental computations. The concept is simple, if you calculated something and then inputs change, it doesn't have to mean that you need to recompute everything. Most of your computations might still be valid, and quite often it is the case that you only need to redo a small chunk of changes.

It has been revealed that this concept usually works the best when you need to compute a lot of stuff, and there are a lot of inputs, and these inputs change independently with different degree of likelihood. Probably, the most common example is incremental compilation, which makes the compilation reuse as much work as possible, making iterations during development much faster. The interesting part is "iterating": note that incremental compilation doesn't necessarily makes cold builds faster. The compiler performance might be roughly the same with and without incrementality, it's just repeated reuse of compiler artifacts becomes more efficient. Most likely you've heard of it. And if you did, you probably know that incremental compilation is not easy (1, 2, 3). But it's cool!

And if incremental computations concept applies well to compilers, it applies even better to LSP servers, because user makes edits in the editor much more often than they recompile code, and each keystroke must change the editor state in milliseconds (unless you go full vibe and don't need an IDE anymore, that is).

It could be somewhat related to the fact that rust-analyzer uses salsa as the central part of its architecture. Salsa is a library that makes incremental computations very convenient and efficient. There is one drawback, though. It is mainly designed to work in memory. And we'll touch on how it works in a bit.

For project like Rust Glancer that tries to keep the memory usage as low as possible, this doesn't work. Because of that, for a long time Rust Glancer didn't use incremental computations, and instead had a sophisticated network of persistent caches with sharding and targeted optimizations to make computations efficient. And it worked, for a while. But this approach doesn't scale very well: if you need to maintain a manually implemented custom cache format, optimize it, and tie computations to it, then the more efficiency you seek, the more complexity you get. Basically, the complexity is "quadratic": it grows as O(computations_complexity * cache_implementation_complexity) because both are interconnected (sorry, CS purists, for this crime).

So... Rust Glancer got to a point where it would really benefit from persistent incremental computations. And the search for it turned out to be really interesting, so in this blog post we'll be discussing how incremental computations can work in memory and how to make this approach work with persistency.

Before we start discussing how incremental computations work under the hood, let's see how it looks like.

If you know how to use Salsa feel free to jump to the next section. If you're familiar with red-green algorithm and in-memory approach that Salsa uses, you can skip to where persistency starts.

Industry observers note that now, incremental computations are somewhat tricky to explain in a blog post, because the value of it requires an application to be somewhat massive. So we will need an example that is big enough to show the value of incrementality, but small enough to discuss here. It's a bit absurd, but I hope you can focus on the idea, not on the value of the snippet at hand.

It has been revealed that let's imagine that we're doing a weird text processor that would count the words in all the files in the directory, and decide whether this count is funny. And to make things more interesting, the files can include other files.

How would that look if implemented naively? Something like that, most likely (well, let's ignore the IO):.

the output will also have no surprises:.

Now, let's try Salsa. It should let us make some computations reusable. Here's how it would look like:.

Recent findings suggest that the code looks pretty similar! However, let's inspect the output.

The first call matches the naive example:.

But the second call is different!

Note: not only we did not call word_count(a), we did not call is_haha_number as well!

Sources indicate that salsa can see that file b changed, and it re-run word_count for it. But the output did not change, so all the previous computations are valid: nothing to be run.

The third output is interesting too:.

Sources indicate that the word count in b changed, and a includes b, so we need to re-run all three queries. But the order is inversed! This is because we have a dependency graph internally, and we're walking through the dependency tree and re-execute changed queries from the "leaves" to the "root".

Industry observers note that we have changed b from 65 to 67 words, so a now has 69 words. Result is still true, but we did have to enhancement the computations. If we would've had another query that depended on is_haha_number, that's where validation would've stopped and all the queries above wouldn't need to run.

And the final output is interesting too:.

We have changed dependencies of a, so there is no b anymore. So we start with what we know: word_count for a. It now has a not-yet-tracked dependency on c, so we go to c after a. And the rest is the same.

It has been revealed that so I hope you get the idea now: each query result is memorized, and if we discover that the output of this query did not change, we don't need to recompute the queries that depend on this input. Or rather, if all the queries that query X depends on did not change, then query X does not need to be recomputed.

And now imagine that you have 700 dependencies in your workspace. A single file changed in the topmost dependency. 699 dependencies can keep their result! Within a single crate, still only one file has changed, so the information about all the other files at least partially stays the same. We only need to redo the computations that actually matter.

And most importantly, we don't need to write any of this tracking code ourselves, Salsa gives it to us for free.

Well, it's really not trivial. If you want to have a more formal deep dive, I suggest the following reads:.

Imagine that each query, combined with its arguments, is an object. This object can have a bunch of metadata, stating whether it was already computed, when it happened, what was the output, and what's the object dependencies. Let's call this metadata a "memo".

In a recent development, side note: why is "combined with its arguments?" notable? Because we cannot memoize is_haha_number, but we can memoize is_haha_number(420), so you can think of it as a mapping of (function, arguments) -> output.

And imagine that you have inputs: something that user provides, and this something can be explicitly requested by a query.

Sources indicate that we might also say that the database has a revision, initially 1. When you change some input, the revision gets bumped to 2, and so on. This revision can be used as "when it happened" (or rather, "when it change last time") inside of the memo.

Now, we've provided our inputs and invoke a query. It has some associated code that can internally do two things:.

If query requests an input, it should record that it depends on this input. So if input changes, it must be recomputed.

If query requests another query, we might check if the corresponding query has a memo with a computed value. If it has, we need to make sure that it is valid for the revision we're at. If it is: great! It can be reused, and we don't need to recompute it. Otherwise, we need to recursively go into this query. Obviously, we also record a dependency on this query.

During the execution, we'll collect all the inputs and all the dependency queries, and ultimately we'll finally compute the result of our query. And when we do, we can fill out the memo: record the revision and the output.

Industry observers note that and... done! Next time you request an output, we will look at this query object memo. If inputs did not change, we can just hand out the result. If they changed, we go down the query line, and do the same thing. So naturally only the things that actually might have changed will be recomputed.

Oh, but there is one more key detail here, that makes everything even better. If revision changed, it does not automatically mean that we need to recompute this query. We might recompute dependencies, and compare them to the old values. If all the outputs are the equal to the old ones (imagine that word_count(a) changed from 67 to 69, but is_haha_number still returns true true: the query that depends on is_haha_number might not get invalidated), we can just mark the current version as verified and return the old result. And it can matter a lot when the expensive query has a lot of cheap dependencies.

Obviously, it's an overly simplified explanation. In practice, there are many, many caveats, tricky parts, and optimizations that make the experience work well. But my job here is to give you an idea; if you've become interested in the topic, I'd recommend looking to Salsa source code, it's very interesting.

And Salsa is awesome! With one caveat. It works in memory only. Well, there is ongoing work on persistency there, but AFAIU it is mostly focused on storing the computations on filesystem so that they can be reloaded later (snapshot-like). It is very valuable, but we still have to store stuff in the memory. For the project like Rust Glancer we want to offload stuff to occupy less RAM.

And in practice, there are several projects that do implement various kinds of persistence:.

So there are solutions for this problem, but none of them seem to be "Salsa but everything is on the filesystem".

I guess then it would be fine to build one?

According to recent reports, as you probably guessed, I did build one. And I called it Ajika. And I'm very proud of myself for coming up with this name, yes.

Recent findings suggest that the library is here, it uses stable Rust, and is generally a complete project (but I'm working on improvements!). The post, however, is not meant to promote it; obviously it's a very young library, and while so far it works really well for me, probably sticking to Salsa if it works for you is a safe choice. Not gonna sell it, do your own research :).

What I want to share is how Ajika works under the hood and what makes it different from Salsa.

But (spoiler) in general it's just two things:.

And we'll get to it and see how it works, but to make everything clear, we'll need to start from something very basic.

Here's the same program we had for Salsa, but migrated to Ajika:.

It looks pretty similar, with API changes mostly being a taste difference, and on a first run it has the same output.

However, the key part here is that we can add the following to the end:.

It has been revealed that and print_result will just print False. Nothing will be executed after restart! Persistency in action!

It has been revealed that on a serious note, the main difference is the focus. When you start working on a project like that, choosing your priority can influence the design a lot. And the choice made here is being persistent-first. While Ajika provides an in-memory backend, it's mostly meant for tests. The intended use case is to use your disk.

And it starts with a very basic question that in-memory database does not have: what happens if I restart the application?

If you already have a cache locally, many things can make this cache invalid:.

Sources indicate that and similarly, given that we cache computations, it's basically an optimization. If cache gets corrupted or removed while the application is running, user would most likely prefer the cache to be discarded and computations to be repeated one more time, rather than the app crashing with "cache is not available, what do I do???".

As a result, the cache must be throw-away. Both Ajika and application supply schema versions to identify the revision, and if the stored cache doesn't match it, we reset it. If cache gets corrupted, Ajika will attempt recovery over hard failing, even if it means re-computing data from scratch.

Sources indicate that the next most noticeable change is that most operations are fallible. Since IO is the basic property for us, and IO can fail, we need to think about it. Failed operation does not mean that cache is corrupted, but it does mean that the current query might not be computed. Typically, it can be retried, though.

In a recent development, finally, the persistence is, unfortunately, a leaky abstraction. You cannot really hide from the fact that the data is outside of memory, because everything you persist must be serializable. And your interim query data might be reusable but not serializable (imagine an AST that borrows the source text: making it own the data likely will be worse), so some of the queries might be transient: we compute them once and retain while the current operation runs, but drop instead of persisting once operation ends.

Together, these properties start working rather nicely, however: your application has to be aware of persistence, but not in an annoying way. If something fails, you know about it, but you don't have to worry, since Ajika will repair things for you. If something is not serializable and it doesn't matter, it can be turned into a transient query. If you don't want your tests to rely on persistence, you just plug a memory backend in.

So let's take a look at how it works under the hood.

LLM usage disclaimer: The library discussed here is developed with use of LLMs, same as Rust Glancer. Hopefully, from this post it is evident that I'm using LLMs as a tool and have full control. It's not vibe coded.

There are three parts to Ajika: ajika itself, ajika_macros, and ajika_storage.

According to recent reports, we'll take a look at ajika and then at ajika_storage. Macros are left as an exercise to a reader, but they're generally pretty straightforward.

Ajika itself is very easy, just check out this diagram:.

In a recent development, ...just kidding. But we'll fix that very promptly.

The core idea is very similar to Salsa:.

Still, I think it might be useful to skim through the high level details.

Sources indicate that side note: Ajika has its own book which does a much deeper dive on many concepts than this blog post. I'll be referring to it in some places. The con is that, unlike this handwritten blog post, the text there is mostly LLM-generated, and even if I did a lot of polishing, it highlights. Eventually I'll do a full manual rewrite, but for now I figured that human-filtered-llm-guide is better than no guide at all.

It has been revealed that database is an entrypoint. You choose either an in-memory or persistent backend, supply Inputs and then run your operation.

Recent findings suggest that queries are the actual logic we want to execute. They are defined via ajika::query macro and in general pretty straightforward. More details on queries themselves are in the book, and we'll look at how queries are executed and what this Db object is a bit later in this post.

In a recent development, inputs are somewhat more interesting. Your input type is defined through the ajika::input procedural macro, which would do some wrapping for you. And your input structure is basically a mapping: you specify a key, for example, String, and then you can use database to get an input value (or lack thereof) for whatever key you have, be it "foo" or even "bar". If you have a singleton value, like a config, you can use () as a key. Again, more on inputs can be found in the book, also might check out lazy inputs.

Outputs are probably the first part of the system that gets interesting because of persistence.

The outputs need to be stored on the filesystem, so they need to be serializable. For outputs that you don't want to serialize, you can use transient queries which will keep the value in memory only for the duration of a single operation. But even then, there is a problem: how major of an output do you want?

If you will have a 1000 very granular queries, it will mean that we need a lot of filesystem roundtrips. If you will have just a bunch of queries that compute a ton of data, you will need to deserialize a major value just to look at the part of it.

Thus, outputs offer a solution that lies in between: you can choose to return a value directly, or return a handle to this value. If you return a handle, query can use this handle to retrieve the value from the database on demand. Directly returned values are fully deserialized. This offers you a nice granularity option: you have a query that encapsulates a meaningful unit of work, but it returns you an object that contains handles for particular results. Handle is cheap to obtain and deserialize, and you only query the data you actually need. Doing is most convenient through an ajika::output macro.

As usual, more details on how to use outputs are in the book.

And now we're getting to the interesting stuff.

To perform a single run we need three things:.

And there are two related concepts that make things work:.

According to recent reports, record contains information like values metadata for a query and dependencies for it (note: values are stored separately!). Thus, Memos are released on the end of the run and then later can be reconstructed from Record on demand.

And this is an crucial bit: released memos don't occupy RAM. This is the key part of Ajika! During the query execution, the values can be loaded, but if you don't run any operations, you don't have to pay for it. Outputs will just wait for you inside of the filesystem! Moreover, whenever we run queries, we only load what we need, not everything.

Each time a query logic actually runs (either from run or from another query), a new Db with a new Frame is created, sharing the same Operation.

When you ask Db to execute a query, here's a typical (overly simplified) workflow:.

And if during execution query receives another query result, it records it in its own Frame for reuse.

Obviously, there is a lot of bookkeeping, support for parallelism, and other things that make it complex, but in general the algorithm is pretty straightforward.

Recent findings suggest that once the operation finishes, we need to actually apply the changes. run works as a transaction, so everything that was done inside is immediately visible, but after run depending on whether run failed or succeeded, the results will either be discarded or persisted.

Checkpoint write is generally pretty straightforward:.

So checkpoint on the Ajika level is pretty straightforward. What is more interesting is how Ajika storage works in general.

Finally, we've got to the persistence!

It's probably the most interesting part of Ajika. How do we store data in a way that is efficient?

The first version of Ajika used redb for everything. It worked, but it did not work very well. Since we don't really have a "database" per se, and more of a storage for many blobs, redb added too much overhead. However, it provides much needed features like transactions.

So, Ajika uses redb as a metadata storage: it's an index which mostly contains pointers to the values.

The values are written in "pack files": basically, just binary files to which we can append newly introduced entries. And inside of redb we can just store a pointer: (file name, offset). Each stored entry has a header with information such as length and compression algorithm. For efficiency, if the value is very small, we can keep it inline inside of redb instead of writing it to a file.

In a recent development, if you want to access a value, you will go to redb, check the corresponding key, and then either read it inline or read the specified pack at the specified access. Pretty simple.

Obviously, there is some more data stored there (we'll talk about identities soon, briefly), but in general it's a pretty "stupid" (hopefully in a good way) format of data storage.

Sources indicate that however, there is one caveat: if we do it naively, the storage can grow without limits. Packs can end up with very low utilization factor, consisting mostly of "dead" values, and some of them might not be observable at all. So the storage supports maintenance: whenever you do an operation, Ajika might do a sweep that would re-pack values and enhancement pointers, and at the end of operation Ajika will try to signal to the storage which values can be removed now. There are a few knobs you can tune here: you can specify the retention limit time (so that the very old and unused queries are cleaned up) or target storage size (which acts as a soft limit, and will affect the cleanup policy).

But ultimately, this design makes value storing and retrieval pretty efficient, and it integrates with the overall Ajika design very well.

Sources indicate that OK, we're almost done, I promise! The last small bit: interning.

Interning values is an optimization that gives you a way to turn any object into an ID. Imagine that you have file paths. They can work as IDs, but it would probably be more efficient if you used FileId(0) / FileId(1) instead. Not only in terms of performance, but often also in terms of memory: you'd rather not have a ton of strings in memory if you don't really need them. Sometimes, interning strings on its own can be a very useful memory optimization, which is why crates like string_cache exist.

But for us, having IDs for objects can be valuable in general, because your computations results might often be linked to some other objects, and it's useful to be able to use IDs for that.

In a recent development, salsa supports interning for that purpose, and Ajika does it too. However, there is one caveat for Ajika: what happens if we have our IDs allocated, they become a part of the cache, and then we restart the application?

To avoid this problem, IDs in Ajika are persisted in addition to being stored in memory, and on restart this interner state is reloaded.

Sources indicate that ajika development itself was an experiment: I did not create it in vacuum, I was actually porting Rust Glancer to it at the same time. And the experiment was very successful. I was able to remove a lot of complexity from Rust Glancer, and Ajika unblocked many optimizations that were not realistic with hand-rolled caches (starting with lazy body evaluation).

Industry observers note that at the end of the experiment, Rust Glancer got performance comparable to rust-analyzer (sometimes even better!). Ajika is obviously slower than salsa, but inside of IDE the difference between 1 and 30ms is negligible, both feel instant. What matters is the low RAM usage: Rust Glancer still stays well under 100MB RAM idle on pretty substantial projects.

Remark: exact comparison between two will be posted in the release notes for Rust Glancer 0.5.0, so stay tuned.

In a recent development, as the experiments go, the branch of Rust Glancer where all of that happened is in a half-assembled state, and it's way too rushed and "prototyped" to just merge it, so I'm doing a clean reimplementation using extracted (and published) version of Ajika. It will take a while, but I'm very excited: Rust Glancer without compromises that feels instant and does not eat memory.

Recent findings suggest that thanks for reading, it turned out to be a long post. A lot of effort went into it, so I hope that it was useful, at least somewhat.

Sources indicate that my next goal is to prepare an Ajika-based release of Rust Glancer, and after that I have a lot of ideas on how to make Ajika even faster/better/stronger. Who knows, maybe it will eventually grow into a product of its own, not merely a part of Rust Glancer ecosystem.

As usual, the best way to support if you like the project is to check out Rust Glancer, star Ajika (but only if you like it!) and/or follow me on twitter.

Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1843 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage.
  • Sources indicate that our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap.
  • Consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this plan includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

Sources indicate that our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

Consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this plan includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern shows up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

In a recent development, A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

According to recent reports, this is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

ProvenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

The verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

It has been revealed that A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

Those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a fresh setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

We tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

The most direct result is this: experts noted 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

Recent findings suggest that we ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

According to recent reports, binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

It has been revealed that in a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an notable area for improvement.

We also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This highlights it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

Industry observers note that blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

In a recent development, as agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

Industry observers note that that adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

Want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

It has been revealed that source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

Recent findings suggest that practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval claims "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

Industry observers note that hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the glitch well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. In the refund-window example, the policy supports the fact, but the answer credits the account record, so we flag the mismatch and show the source verdict.

According to recent reports, I had a brief read on the paper, but I could not find any comparison with cheaper llm agent for source aware judge. Like this is my reading of the paper;.

Sources indicate that like, it seems (2 - 5) can be done via basic prompts in lifecycle, if you own the executing agent. If not, this can also be done via hooks in harness as plugin. Do you have any comparison on this. Basically, how much of random forest, and all of these eng/plumbing is buying, vs second llm call over traces+ans?

Hi, fair question. A source-aware LLM judge could do these checks, and we don’t report a direct comparison with a cheaper one in the paper.

Sources indicate that however, part of our motivation is that introducing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources (the same kinds of errors we’re trying to catch). A second LLM call can therefore introduce new errors of its own. ProvenanceGuard uses explicit source tracking and calibrated support checks to reduce reliance on another generative judgment. The comparison you suggest would indeed be a useful further study to quantify the benefit in accuracy, latency and cost.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ransomware group sets a deadline for the chipmaker to pay up - or see its data leaked.

Recent findings suggest that finding a fresh CEO is just one of their problems. Nvidia is investigating an alleged breach following claims by ransomware group The Gentlemen's affiliates that they hacked the AI giant and stole sensitive information.

Sources indicate that the embattled chipmaker told The Register's that it was investigating a possible third-party data breach. “We have found no indication that Nvidia systems or networks were affected,” a spokesperson stated. “We continue to monitor the situation.".

The ransomware gang’s data-leak site, shared on social media and seen by The Register, doesn’t show any stolen files or indicate what information the group claims to have stolen. Nvidia first appeared on the criminals’ blog on Wednesday, with The Gentlemen promising “DATA INFO - SOON.”.

The post also included a countdown, ending November 28.

Industry observers note that while we can’t verify the criminals’ claims, the group, which emerged in mid-2025, is one of the most prolific ransomware-as-a-service operations. Its affiliates claimed more than 320 victims as of April, with the majority of these alleged ransomware infections (240) occurring in the first half of 2026.

Sources indicate that the actual count, however, is likely much higher. Check Point researchers accessed an affiliate’s live command-and-control server during an incident response case earlier this year. The server contained victim telemetry that revealed more than 1,570 victims, mostly located in the US, and primarily corporate and organizational environments.

According to an operational technology (OT) threat report from Trellix published on Wednesday, industrial ransomware claims jumped nearly 51 percent - to about 1,500 posts- compared to last quarter, and The Gentlemen’s affiliates were the most prolific claim posters during this time period. They accounted for about 16 percent of all posts.

Sources indicate that in February 2022, an Nvidia data breach exposed employees’ credentials and proprietary code. Extortion crew Lapsus$ claimed to be responsible for that intrusion and data theft.®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I wrote an article a couple of months ago describing how I rebuilt my old voice assistant pipeline in Platypush.

And I wrote earlier articles describing my journey through self-hosted voice assistants - in 2024 (with Picovoice), in 2020 (diving into the legacy assistant.google integration, the now defunct assistant.alexa integration, the now defunct Snowboy integration, the now defunct DeepSpeech integration and Picovoice) and the original article in 2019 describing the Google Assistant integration.

For a couple of months I used the voice pipeline described in my latest article as my main driver, but after getting used to the robustness of commercial voice assistants I was unhappy with the high rates of false positives/negatives of my self-hosted pipeline, as well as its lack of robustness in detecting start/end of speech, especially in noisy environments and using cheap microphones.

After a bit of experimentation, I decided to swap and fine tune a few parts, and after a couple of days of trying the results are satisfying enough for me to write a short article about it.

Hotword detection- assistant.microwakeword (local).

Speech-to-text- assistant.openai (cloud)- assistant.vosk (local).

Generate response- openai (cloud or local).

Text-to-speech- tts.openai (cloud)- tts.piper (local).

Hotword detection- assistant.microwakeword (local).

Speech-to-text- assistant.openai (cloud)- assistant.vosk (local).

Generate response- openai (cloud or local).

Text-to-speech- tts.openai (cloud)- tts.piper (local).

Until recently I used assistant.openwakeword, which wraps openWakeWord.

It works, but the project has been quiet for a while and all of its pre-trained models are v0.1 files from 2023, mostly trained on synthetic speech.

In practice I was getting both false positives (the hotword triggering on background noise) and false negatives (the hotword not detected unless I was close to the microphone).

I added a upcoming plugin, assistant.microwakeword, on top of microWakeWord through the pymicro-wakeword Python bindings.

microWakeWord is the engine used by ESPHome and Home Assistant Voice, its models are actively maintained, and the built-in models (okay_nabu, hey_jarvis, hey_mycroft, alexa) ship with the package — no download required.

The current official models are provided under the ESPHome micro-wake-word-models repository.

Custom models are supported too: drop a microWakeWord JSON manifest (with its .tflite model) in the plugin's models directory and reference it by name.

The plugin exposes the same API as assistant.openwakeword (same models, detection_threshold, frame_duration, patience_frames, input_device, input_volume parameters, same list_models action, same HotwordDetectedEvent), so switching is a matter of just changing the configuration to point to the upcoming plugin:.

assistant.openai records audio when a conversation starts and transcribes it through Whisper.

It has been revealed that the tricky part has always been end-of-speech detection: knowing when the user has finished talking. The previous implementation used a per-frame boolean from WebRTC VAD, and any single frame classified as speech would reset the silence timer. With even a bit of background noise, phrases would only end when the maximum conversation duration was hit.

The audio preprocessing layer (AudioPreprocessor, shared by the STT integrations) has been reworked:.

Hysteresis + sliding window: a frame becomes speech above the VAD threshold and stays speech until its score drops by a margin, and the per-frame decisions are smoothed by majority vote over a 0.5s window. A single noise burst can no longer keep a conversation alive.

Adaptive noise floor: the background noise level is tracked over time, and frames that aren't louder than noise_floor_factor (default 2.0, ~6 dB) times the floor are never considered as speech.

On a synthetic benchmark (Piper-generated phrases mixed with babble and burst noise), the old settings kept conversations open for 6–10 seconds after the speech had ended; the newly introduced pipeline ends them 1.0–1.6 seconds after the last word, which is the configured conversation_end_timeout plus the smoothing lag.

Sources indicate that since the changes on Platypush have been performed directly in the AudioPreprocessor also used by other native speech-to-text engines, other speech-to-text plugins also benefit from them - e.g. if you use assistant.vosk for full on-device detection.

Sources indicate that the transcribed phrase is processed by the openai plugin, which handles both the API key and the conversation context. By default the assistant renders the response through the configured tts_plugin; if the response ends with a question mark, the conversation continues with a follow-up.

Custom hooks can intercept phrases before the default response kicks in — for example, to handle home automation commands locally without an LLM round-trip:.

And the hotword event is wired to the conversation start with a similar hook:.

In a recent development, responses are rendered by tts.openai, with volume and voice configurable. In my tests however tts.piper also yielded good results, and it runs entirely locally. In my tests on a RaspberryPi 5 however it added ~3-4s of latency to process the response to audio compared to tts.openai.

Since the TTS output goes to the speakers and the wake word detector listens on the microphone, the assistant plugins pause hotword detection while a conversation is active — otherwise the assistant would hear itself.

The microphone on my RPi doesn't support 16 kHz natively, so audio is captured at 44.1 kHz and software-resampled — it works, but if detection feels sluggish software resampling is usually the first suspect.

The VAD and threshold defaults were tuned on synthetic audio plus a couple of my audio recordings.

Sources indicate that different rooms, microphones and acoustics may yield different results. You may want to adjust detection_threshold on the wake word plugin and noise_floor_factor on the STT plugins if you don't feel satisfied with your mileage.

To interact via Webmentions, send an activity that references this URL from a platform that supports Webmentions, such as Lemmy, WordPress with Webmention plugins, or any IndieWeb-compatible site.

https://blog.platypush.tech/article/Rewriting-my-voice-assistant-pipeline.

It's 2026. You deserve a good local-first or local-only voice assistant on your #RaspberryPi.

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Open TTS Leaderboard: Scalable Evaluation for Multilingual Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning

📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1388 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible.
  • It has been revealed that evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized.
  • According to recent reports, these arenas compare models by presenting people with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible. On the Hugging Face Hub (as of Sep 30, 2026) there are more than 8K TTS models available 🚀.

It has been revealed that evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized. The gold standard is human preference scores such as MOS or MUSHRA (more on metrics). To this end, several arena-based leaderboards have established themselves as useful reference points for the community:.

According to recent reports, these arenas compare models by presenting people with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other. After collecting a sufficient number of votes, an Elo score is computed to rank models, typically with the Bradley–Terry model (see Voice Arena methodology).

While human preference is the ultimate decider, arenas cannot scale to keep up with the pace of TTS releases. This may partly explain why open-source models are underrepresented on arena-style leaderboards: as of Sep 30, 2026, only 16 of the 92 models on Artificial Analysis are open-weights, with a similar skew on Voice Arena. This likely reflects practical factors: adding an API model requires little more than an API key, whereas an open model must be hosted and served by the arena operator, and commercial providers have more reason to seek placement than open-source authors. Another limitation with arena-style evaluation is voter consistency: no arena can ensure that the same voters with the same criteria of “better” can consistently evaluate models over time. Even the preferences of a single person change over time (“A man cannot step into the same river twice” as famously said by Heraclitus).

To this end, we've built the Open TTS Leaderboard, which uses objective metrics to evaluate models on complementary aspects of performance:.

By relying on objective metrics evaluating a model drops from a couple weeks (for collecting votes) to a couple hours ⚡.

Recent findings suggest that importantly, the Open TTS Leaderboard does not replace human preference ranking. ASR-based WER provides a proxy for intelligibility, while speaker similarity estimates voice identity preservation. Neither directly measures naturalness, expressiveness, or listener preference. Nevertheless, they can even inform voting-based leaderboards which models to include in their evaluations.

Our intention with this leaderboard is for it to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. The next few sections give an overview of main features of the Open TTS Leaderboard.

From the default view of the leaderboard, models are ranked by macro-average WER on the English splits of Seed TTS Eval (paper) and CV3 Eval (zero shot) (paper).

hexgrad/Kokoro-82M, Supertone/supertonic-3, and fishaudio/s2-pro lead the pack on English WER when averaged on these two splits, while the Pareto plots visualize which models strike a good balance between WER, batched inference (RTFx), and size.

English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

k2-fsa/OmniVoice, fishaudio/s2-pro, and FunAudioLLM/Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512 are strong multilingual models.

By toggling “Voice cloning”, the models that support this functionality (on the selected languages) can be compared.

Moreover, a SIM column for speaker similarity now appears in the table, as well as two more Pareto plots for visualizing the tradeoff between SIM, batched inference, and size.

The average WER of some models, such as bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b and openbmb/VoxCPM2, improve under voice cloning, namely when a reference audio is provided.

Numbers only tell part of the story, and as mentioned earlier human preference is the ultimate decider. From the “Listen” tab, you can compare the generated outputs that are behind the metrics, to find which model(s) you prefer!

Pick the language/dataset you're interested in, whether you want to compare voice cloning, and optionally pick the models or listen to outputs from a random selection.

The “Listen” tab fills an crucial gap in existing TTS leaderboards: a space to explore model outputs of various models.

It has been revealed that you can even give feedback on the generated outputs. As we collect more votes from the community, we may include this data on the leaderboard. So vote! But please login with your HF account to help us weed out spam/bots.

In a recent development, the “Streaming” tab compares the streaming capabilities. Models are ranked by TTFA (time-to-first-audio), which quantifies how long a user waits after probing a model in order to obtain audio that can be played. This is important for voice agents and other interactive apps.

For streaming models (✅ under “Streaming API”) it's the time until the first audio chunk arrives. For non-streaming models, it's the time until the whole utterance is generated, because playback can't start any earlier. Every model runs one audio at a time (batch size 1), on the same 50 English prompts from CV3-Eval, on the same hardware and in its default voice. We drop the first 3 runs as warm-up and report the median TTFA across the rest.

The default view compares performance on an H200 GPU. Results are also available for CPU for a small (but growing) set of models!

kyutai/pocket-tts is a great model for streaming on both GPU and CPU!

It has been revealed that the goal of the Open TTS Leaderboard is not only to keep up with the incredible pace of TTS model releases, but to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. Let us know which datasets, models, and metrics you want to see!

Recent findings suggest that we will soon open-source the evaluation scripts, much like the Open ASR Leaderboard repo, so that you can directly provide your feedback and suggestions via GitHub Challenges and PRs! Let's shape TTS evaluations together 🤗.

Glad this board splits multilingual TTS quality from voice-cloning identity instead of one aggregate green.

The check I'd keep reading: whether the ranking still holds when you hold language/domain fixed versus when cloning is the axis. Otherwise teams optimize the easier subscale and still call the result "SOTA TTS.".

English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has movie box audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

Open TTS Leaderboard is an open evaluation platform designed to make multilingual text-to-speech and voice-cloning models easier to compare at scale. Traditional TTS arenas usually let owners listen to outputs from two models and choose the one they prefer. Those votes can then be used to calculate an Elo-style score, often through approaches such as the Bradley–Terry model, giving users a simple way to understand how different systems perform based on human preference.

Human feedback remains an notable part of evaluating speech quality, but relying only on arena-style voting can be difficult as new TTS models are released at a rapid pace. Open-source models can also face practical barriers because they generally need to be hosted and served by the evaluation platform, while API-based commercial models can be added more easily. This can result in open-weight systems being less visible on public leaderboards. Another challenge is consistency: people's preferences and listening criteria can change over time, meaning that votes collected months apart may not always represent exactly the same standards.

Open TTS Leaderboard aims to address these challenges by providing a scalable and transparent space for evaluating multilingual TTS and voice-cloning systems. The goal is to make comparisons easier to reproduce, expand coverage of open models, and provide useful evaluation signals alongside human preference. By bringing together scalable testing and community feedback, the project can help researchers, developers, and users better understand how speech models perform across different languages, voices, and use cases.

According to recent reports, gitHub repo with the eval scripts is public! https://github.com/huggingface/open-tts-leaderboard.

  • Recent findings suggest that "We believe many of the major disruptions of the last few weeks, including outages across major enterprises and governments, were partially due to unintended consequences of patching and configuration changes, as IT teams simply cannot patch these vulnerabilities fast enough without compromising their production environments," said Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of PAN, during the organization's fiscal Q1 2027 earnings call on Wednesday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Security shop buys the hand that feeds it.

As AI has become a thorn in the side of the security industry, Palo Alto Networks (PAN) has reached an agreement to acquire Applied Compute, an AI model training platform.

Recent findings suggest that "We believe many of the major disruptions of the last few weeks, including outages across major enterprises and governments, were partially due to unintended consequences of patching and configuration changes, as IT teams simply cannot patch these vulnerabilities fast enough without compromising their production environments," said Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of PAN, during the organization's fiscal Q1 2027 earnings call on Wednesday. "The second effect is the rise of AI-assisted cyberattacks.".

So in the spirit of "hair of the dog that bit me," PAN is ingesting Applied Compute to make open-weight AI more secure for corporate customers. The answer to insecurity brought on by AI is buying security with AI.

In its announcement of the tie-up, PAN declares "the future of enterprise AI is hybrid, and that a large share of enterprises will run on open-source and open-weight models tuned to their own data, cost, and control needs.".

Recent findings suggest that that view has been clouded a bit by Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang's fall from grace: Back in July, he came to the defense of open-weight models as a defense against the hegemony of purveyors of closed-weight commercial models like Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI. His resignation as CEO of Nvidia has led to worries that the open-weight ecosystem has lost some lobbying power at a time when the US is wary about the uptake of models made in China.

Nonetheless, PAN clearly sees a future for open-weight models.

"Every enterprise is going to run a mix of open and closed models, and every one of those models needs to be secured," said Nikesh Arora, chairman and CEO of PAN, in a statement. "Applied Compute has built the best post-training and inference platform we've seen, and its research team is exceptional.".

The manufacturer expects the $4.5 billion all-stock transaction to add more than $1 billion to the company's Next Generation Security business by FY 2029.

Arora, on the organization's earnings call, explained the pricey bet as recognition of the corporate desire to avoid vendor lock-in and to retain control of data.

Industry observers note that "We're already seeing the desire for sovereignty and control compel enterprises to adopt open-weight and open-source models," he said. "Early signs of that shift are clear, with open-weight models growing from under 5 percent of token traffic to more than 60 percent over the past year.".

Recent findings suggest that beyond the sticker price, PAN is ready to up its infrastructure ante. Arora stated the biz expects to build infrastructure supporting more than 100 megawatts of inference capacity, a project that will take "a modest CapEx commitment of less than $3 billion through fiscal 2030." ®.

Distributed LLM Training Across Metros: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (569 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Traditionally, training state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) relies on a monolithic cluster of accelerators, where all devices are collocated and tightly coupled via high-bandwidth to constantly synchronize gradients.
  • It has been revealed that to scale further, we can connect multiple compute slices across geographically distributed datacenters.
  • To address this, the Google DeepMind and Google Research teams developed DiLoCo (Distributed Low-Communication), a distributed optimization algorithm designed to make training resilient to these low-bandwidth, high-latency connections.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Traditionally, training state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) relies on a monolithic cluster of accelerators, where all devices are collocated and tightly coupled via high-bandwidth to constantly synchronize gradients. However, physical and cost constraints make scaling a single slice increasingly difficult.

It has been revealed that to scale further, we can connect multiple compute slices across geographically distributed datacenters. However, when training across multiple datacenters over wide-area networks (WAN), standard data-parallel training suffers from severe network stalls because slow WAN transfers cannot be fully overlapped with computation.

To address this, the Google DeepMind and Google Research teams developed DiLoCo (Distributed Low-Communication), a distributed optimization algorithm designed to make training resilient to these low-bandwidth, high-latency connections. In this blog post, we discuss the core concepts of DiLoCo, how it is implemented in MaxText (Google's open-source JAX-based LLM training framework), and the performance benefits it brings to large-scale LLM training on Google Cloud.

DiLoCo was introduced by Google DeepMind in the paper DiLoCo: Distributed Low-Communication Training of Language Models. Instead of synchronizing gradients across all devices at every single training step (as in standard Data Parallelism), DiLoCo partitions training across M independent compute groups, referred to as learners, and allows each learner to perform many local optimization steps independently before communicating across groups.

Despite communicating significantly less frequently (by a factor of H, e.g., 1-2 orders of magnitude less) than standard synchronous training, DiLoCo has been shown to achieve comparable convergence and model quality.

The Vanilla DiLoCo described above reduces total communication volume by a factor of H, however, all learners still transmit their weight deltas for the entire model all at once at every H-th step. On a thin network pipe, that full-model transfer creates a large periodic stall every H steps. This matter is alleviated by Streaming DiLoCo, which is described in the next section.

In a recent development, in multi-slice training, communication within a single slice is handled by high-speed Inter-Chip Interconnects (ICI). When scaling to multiple slices, synchronization across slices must traverse the Data Center Network (DCN) or, if the slices are geographically distributed, wide-area networks (WAN).

Within a single datacenter, DCN bandwidth is high enough that JAX and XLA can often hide standard Data Parallel all-reduce collectives by overlapping gradient communication with backward-pass computation. Across datacenters or congested links, however, bandwidth drops and latency rises sharply. Standard DP stalls at every step waiting for global gradient synchronization, collapsing Model FLOPS Utilization (MFU).

Industry observers note that streaming DiLoCo eliminates this synchronization stall by partitioning the model's parameters into P disjoint fragments. Over the course of H steps, every single fragment in the model is synchronized exactly once, achieving the exact same outer-loop cadence as vanilla DiLoCo without spiky bandwidth utilization.

Using a roofline model (similar to the JAX Scaling Book), we can calculate the network bandwidth required to prevent communication stalls for a model with ∣Θ∣ parameters (at b bytes per parameter, e.g., b=2 for bfloat16) and per-step compute time tstep=tfwd+tbwd. For example, the standard Data Parallel algorithm transfers 2∣Θ∣b bytes per sync via an all-reduce collective, which is a distributed reduce-scatter where each node reduces a different part, followed by an all-gather so all participants receive all parts. To achieve zero communication stalls, we overlap the reduce-scatter of the gradients with the backward pass, which produces them and takes tbwd time. Therefore, the peak required bandwidth is Bdp ≈ 2∣Θ∣b / tbwd.

    Beyond code generation: A developer’s guide to agentic engineering

    📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1016 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, this October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier.
    • Building software takes more than a good prompt.
    • Recent findings suggest that as a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, this October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier. This is more commits than GitHub received in all of 2025. Chances are, you’re generating more code than you were a year ago. But ask yourself: do you feel 400% more productive than you were last year?

    Building software takes more than a good prompt. As AI speeds up implementation, software developers are feeling more pressure in other places: a Faros AI study found that pull requests spent 441% longer in review when teams went from low to high AI adoption.

    Recent findings suggest that as a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production. Agents can help you work more efficiently across all of these stages: Blueprint, Build, Verify, and Observe. We’ll walk through what an effective agentic engineering workflow looks like on GitHub.

    See if this sounds familiar. You’re planning an API change. The design is in one tool, a compatibility requirement is buried in Slack, and an old pull request explains why the current implementation works this way. Before you can write a useful initiative, you need to connect those details, compare approaches, and agree on how existing clients will keep working. What looked like a straightforward planning task has become hours of searching, cross-checking, and chasing answers. You’re exhausted before implementation even begins.

    You can use Copilot to pull that scattered context into one place, work through the tradeoffs, and turn the decisions into an implementation proposal.

    What took days of searching and context gathering now produces a reviewable strategy, explicit acceptance criteria, and scoped concerns, with your time spent on the decisions instead of the retrieval. Then, once you settle on an approach, you’ve already set yourself and your agents up to implement your plan.

    You’re ready to turn that plan into code. But life has other ideas. Your agent is halfway through a task, your next meeting starts in five minutes, and your dog has been staring at the door for twenty. Then someone in the meeting points out an edge case the implementation needs to handle. Everyone needs something from you at once. You’d like to keep making progress, but you can’t be in three places at the same time.

    You can keep your work moving without being tied to the computer where you started it.

    Writing code is more than shooting off a single prompt to your LLM and seeing what you get back. And with more work on your plate than ever, it can be difficult to maintain your coding standards and deliver your projects on time. Copilot helps tasks progress independently with shared project knowledge, while letting you pick up a session where you left off across devices. That gives you more room to work through implementation decisions and handle changes as they come up. And as your work finishes, you have focused changes ready to review.

    According to recent reports, after spending an hour wrangling your agents to get them moving in the right direction, you think you’ve all landed in a good spot. So you open a pull request labeled “small refactor.” It changes 47 files. You wanted feedback on shared validation logic, but it’s buried among updates to every endpoint that calls it, formatting changes, and several hundred lines of generated tests. You wonder how long it will take to get an approval on this, given the endless list of pull requests on your team’s review board.

    That review queue is the 441% in practice. You can shorten the wait from both ends: make your changes easier for a person to review, and let Copilot clear the routine checks and fixes before anyone opens the diff.

    Smaller changes with the routine work already handled means fewer rounds of back-and-forth. Your reviewers get to spend their attention on whether the code does what you intended, and what could go wrong.

    Your change gets approved, the deployment checks pass, and you finally get to cross it off your list. The next morning, your on-call dashboard shows intermittent timeouts, and support reports that a few large customers are affected. Now you’re comparing logs, release history, and customer reports while someone asks whether you should roll back. “All checks passed” feels less reassuring than it did yesterday.

    Bring operational evidence and engineering context together so you can decide what to do.

    Figuring out what happened after a release can leave you bouncing between dashboards, conversations, and commit history. With Copilot helping connect that information, you can document what you found, create follow-up complications, and improve the guidance available for future tasks. You spend more time deciding what needs to change and less time retracing the investigation. And your next proposal starts with what you learned from the software people are actually using.

    Take one piece of work already on your plate and look beyond the coding task. What context does it need? How will you review and test it? How will you know it worked after it ships?

    According to recent reports, you don’t have to change your whole process at once. Start with something that frustrates you most this week and put an agent on it. Then expand to other parts of your process over time. Once agents are helping across your whole workflow, you might finally feel as productive as your commit count indicates you are.

    We covered this topic live at GitHub Universe 2026 in “Agentic Engineering: Past the Pilot.”.

    Agent skills capture repeatable engineering work in files teams can review and reuse, while tools, project context, and permissions remain specific to the host that runs them.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • First service outages, then data breaches…what's next?!

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    First service outages, then data breaches…what's next?!

    JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard have all confirmed that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information after a data-theft-and-extortion gang claimed to have compromised the financial giants.

    “Visa is aware of these claims,” a spokesperson told The Register on Thursday. “They are associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific. Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected. This is unrelated to any of the system disruptions across different industries this past week.”.

    Mastercard also cited a third-party provider in an email sent to The Register following our questions about the alleged breach.

    In a recent development, “We were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of a limited amount of email addresses - non-payments information - from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program,” Mastercard SVP Seth Eisen said. “There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards. At this time, the exposure has been contained and our teams are working with the provider to support the impacted cardholders as needed.”.

    JPMorgan Chase did not respond to The Register’s request for comment, but confirmed it was investigating a cyberattack on social media.

    “We have learned that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack,” America’s largest bank posted on X. “Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.”.

    According to Chase, the third-party breach didn’t disrupt any of its services, and it’s not connected to the outages earlier in the week attributed to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems.

    “There is no connection to service disruption some customers experienced earlier this week,” the bank said on Thursday.

    None of the three financial firms would comment on who the third-party providers are, when the breaches occurred, and what specific data was stolen. The Register will update this story as we learn more details about the intrusions.

    Extortion crew n0n claimed responsibility for all three alleged hacks, posting the financial giants to its data-leak site on Monday. The group, believed to be based in Russia, emerged in September and posted 108 victims over its first month in operations. ®.
