    Industry News: AutoSynthData: Generating Training Data for Enterprise Agents

    📅 02 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2026 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments.
    • The difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data.
    • It has been revealed that at ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments. The work they ask these agents to do is shaped by the systems they use, the rules they follow, and the state of their data. A model may be broadly capable and still struggle with a particular environment: a workflow it handles poorly, a combination of tools it misuses, or a constraint it fails to respect. Those are the weaknesses an enterprise needs to improve.

    The difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data. An individual failure tells us something, but training a model requires many newly introduced tasks that exercise the same capability in different situations. Those tasks must also be possible to complete in the environment, resemble work someone would actually request, and have a reliable way to check whether the agent succeeded.

    It has been revealed that at ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data. It uses a target model’s failures and a stronger teacher’s successes to decide what the model should learn next, then generates and validates upcoming tasks that exercise those capabilities. As the model improves, the curriculum shifts toward what it still finds difficult. We illustrate the pipeline with EnterpriseOps Gym (Malay et al., 2026), using the released dataset. We begin by describing the environment an agent operates in and what makes a task useful for training.

    An agentic environment defines the world in which an agent operates: the state it can observe and modify, the tools and APIs it can invoke, and the state transitions produced by its actions.

    Industry observers note that A task is instantiated within this environment. We use the following abstraction:.

    The system specification defines the constraints under which the agent operates, including system instructions, environment policies, and, when applicable, task-specific initialization such as a seeded database state or a set of knowledge articles.

    According to recent reports, the specification must be compatible with the environment’s tools, state, and supported actions. Its instructions should be clear and avoid arbitrary constraints introduced solely to manufacture difficulty.

    The user prompt specifies what the user wants the agent to accomplish, together with any user-level constraints. A generated task should satisfy three properties.

    In a recent development, feasibility. There should exist at least one trajectory in the current environment that satisfies the user prompt while respecting the system specification. This rules out tasks that depend on unavailable tools, inaccessible knowledge, impossible state transitions, or actions prohibited by policy.

    Realism. The user prompt should resemble something a user would plausibly ask in the target environment. The space of executable behaviors is usually much larger than the space of realistic workflows.

    Sources indicate that difficulty. For training, the task should expose a weakness of the current agent. Tasks that are already solved reliably provide little fresh training signal. The useful region is therefore tasks that are feasible and realistic, but not yet consistently solved.

    The verifier determines whether the resulting trajectory successfully completes the task. It should satisfy three properties.

    Consistency. It should agree with the user prompt, the system specification, and the task-specific environment state.

    Soundness. It should reject trajectories that fail to satisfy the task or violate relevant constraints.

    According to recent reports, completeness. It should accept valid solutions rather than encode one particular reference trajectory.

    Industry observers note that these properties matter directly during training. A lax verifier can reward incorrect behavior, while an overly restrictive verifier can penalize valid solutions.

    Industry observers note that given an environment and a target model, AutoSynthData generates training tasks consisting of a system specification, user prompt, and verifier. The generated tasks are grounded in the environment and selected to provide useful training signal for the current model.

    Industry observers note that autoSynthData first evaluates the target model in the environment using diagnostic tasks and identifies patterns in the tasks it struggles to complete. A stronger teacher helps characterize which of those tasks are solvable and what successful behavior looks like. AutoSynthData turns the resulting capability gaps into fresh executable tasks, checks each task in the environment, and uses accepted samples for post-training. Evaluating the updated model reveals which gaps remain and can guide the next round of generation.

    According to recent reports, autoSynthData uses evaluation runs in the target environment to identify what the model needs to learn next. In our EnterpriseOps Gym experiment, we run both the target model and a stronger teacher on the evaluation tasks. We examine those runs to identify:.

    Industry observers note that we distill these findings into sanitized capability specification cards. The evaluation tasks guide what the model should learn, but the generator does not receive their original prompts, entities, trajectories, or verifier details. It receives the cards and uses them to create new tasks with different prompts, states, and solution paths.

    In a recent development, identifying a capability gap tells us what to teach, but training requires many varied tasks that exercise it. AutoSynthData uses the specification card to generate those tasks.

    Suppose the target model struggles with tasks that require the following workflow:.

    The generator creates fresh tasks that exercise this workflow, varying the entities, initial environment state, workflow composition, tool combinations, wording, and difficulty. The stronger teacher then demonstrates a successful trajectory for each task. For supervised fine-tuning (SFT), these demonstrations teach the target model how to apply the capability in new situations.

    AutoSynthData builds the dataset in two phases: first generating and validating core samples, then expanding them into novel variants.

    The target phase creates the core set of training samples from the capability specifications. Workers generate independent tasks in parallel, picking up a new target when they finish. Each candidate goes through validation, execution, solver evaluation, and repair before acceptance. The result is a batch of vetted examples built around what the target model needs to learn.

    The multiply phase expands the dataset by creating novel variants of accepted target samples. Each variant has its own user request, environment state, entity configuration, reference trajectory, and verifier, and must pass the same validation and execution checks. A multiplied sample cannot seed another multiplied sample. This anchors expansion to the vetted target set and limits drift across generations.

    According to recent reports, to support both phases, AutoSynthData separates generation control from environment-specific execution. A shared controller coordinates generation, quality control, coverage, and dataset construction, while an adapter handles environment execution, task and state management, reference replay, deterministic verification, solver execution, and task profiling.

    Sources indicate that together, parallel target generation and multiplication provide a path to training-scale datasets. Their usefulness depends on the checks applied to every candidate: the task must be executable, the solution must work, and the verifier must distinguish success from failure.

    Generating a plausible request is not enough to produce useful training data. A task may be impossible in the target environment, its reference solution may fail when executed, or its verifier may reward the wrong final state. AutoSynthData checks these properties before accepting a task for training.

    AutoSynthData reviews quality at two levels: individual candidates must pass verification, and batches must provide useful coverage and diversity.

    Recent findings suggest that each candidate must clear a quality-control loop before entering the training dataset. We begin with solver evaluation to measure difficulty. In the configuration used here, we favor tasks the target model solves on no more than one of three trials and the stronger solver solves on at least two of three trials. Candidates also undergo positive and negative verification and a bounded repair process.

    The positive gate asks: Does the intended solution solve the generated task?

    The pipeline executes the reference trajectory in the target environment and checks the resulting state against the candidate’s verifier. This reveals mismatches among the prompt, initial state, solution, and success criteria.

    The negative gate asks: Do relevant incorrect outcomes fail?

    Industry observers note that for example, it can mutate parts of the expected outcome and confirm that those states no longer pass verification. This catches weak verifiers that award success without requiring the intended behavior.

    Sources indicate that failed candidates go to a critic before being discarded. The critic examines the sample and its failure, looking for inconsistent state, impossible workflows, incorrect task construction, bad reference trajectories, weak verifier logic, or a mismatch with the intended capability. The critic’s findings guide repairs, with a fixed limit on retries:.

    A repaired task must pass the relevant checks again. The diagnosis guides repairs to the existing candidate rather than requiring generation to start over.

    According to recent reports, passing these checks makes a sample eligible for training, but individually valid samples can still form a repetitive or unbalanced dataset. AutoSynthData therefore also reviews generation at the batch level.

    A batch may overrepresent a few easy task families, miss a capability, or reflect too much generation effort spent on a low-yield pattern.

    A meta-review examines accepted samples, rejected samples, and generation behavior across each batch. It asks:.

    The controller tracks coverage in the accepted dataset, reduces generation in overrepresented regions, and directs more work toward gaps. When a region repeatedly produces poor candidates, critiques and meta-review guide changes to the generation strategy. These adjustments balance useful learning signal, task quality, coverage, diversity, and low redundancy within the available generation budget and dataset size requirements.

    Together, these feedback loops improve both individual tasks and the dataset they form: sample-level checks guide candidate repair, while batch-level review guides future generation.

    It has been revealed that the useful training distribution changes as the model improves. AutoSynthData treats synthetic data generation as a search for tasks near the target model's capability boundary: difficult enough to expose weaknesses, but solvable enough for the teacher to provide reliable demonstrations.

    After post-training, we evaluate the updated model in the same environment. Tasks it now solves reliably are less useful for the next training round; persistent failures point to capabilities that still need attention. Those results can guide the next generation round.

    According to recent reports, our experiments focus on SFT, but the same mechanism could support reinforcement learning (RL): generate tasks that challenge the current policy and provide reliable learning signal, train, then move the generation target with the updated policy. We plan to test this moving, difficulty-calibrated frontier beyond SFT.

    We use EnterpriseOps Gym to test whether this approach improves a model on tasks in a stateful enterprise environment. We generate training tasks in the Gym’s Hybrid and ITSM environments, fine-tune the target model on accepted samples, and evaluate the resulting checkpoints.

    We tested the pipeline on the Hybrid domain of EnterpriseOps Gym using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and Qwen3.8-27B as the teacher.

    AutoSynthData generated 2,000 synthetic training samples in about 18 hours. We fine-tuned Gemma on this dataset and evaluated the resulting checkpoints on the benchmark. The best checkpoint was epoch 5.

    The synthetic SFT checkpoint improves mean Pass@1 by 7.2 percentage points, a 35% relative improvement, and raises verifier success from 63.01% to 68.55%. It closes 59% of the original Pass@1 gap between Gemma and the reference model.

    The training tasks were newly generated from capability specifications; the generator did not receive the original evaluation tasks. The result demonstrates improvement in EnterpriseOps Gym Hybrid, the environment used for this experiment.

    In a recent development, we also applied AutoSynthData to the ITSM domain of EnterpriseOps Gym, using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as the teacher. AutoSynthData generated 1,994 synthetic training samples in 66 hours. Generation took longer than in the subsequent Hybrid run described above, primarily because the ITSM run used a larger teacher model and preceded pipeline optimizations that improved throughput.

    On ITSM, synthetic SFT raises mean Pass@1 from 18.77% to 27.18%, showing that the approach also improves performance in a second domain.

    The tasks most useful for training depend on both the environment and the model working in it. AutoSynthData uses the model’s failures to choose what to generate, validates new tasks against the environment, and makes those tasks available for post-training. Our EnterpriseOps Gym results show the value of that approach in a controlled setting. As the model changes, the same process can focus on the gaps that remain.

    Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Tunix and Gemma 4 on Google TPUs

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (217 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Googleblog

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In our previous posts - Easy FunctionGemma finetuning with Tunix on Google TPUs and Autonomous LLM post-training with Tunix on TPUs - we revealed how Google Tunix streamlines Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and single-turn Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on Cloud TPUs.
    • We will revisit the Plane Strike board game from an earlier TensorFlow/JAX reinforcement learning blog, replacing the custom MLP policy with Gemma 4 E2B in thinking mode on a single Cloud TPU v6e-8 host.

    In our previous posts - Easy FunctionGemma finetuning with Tunix on Google TPUs and Autonomous LLM post-training with Tunix on TPUs - we revealed how Google Tunix streamlines Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and single-turn Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on Cloud TPUs. Real-world AI agents, however, rarely finish their job in a single turn. They have to reason over partial observations, invoke tools, observe environment feedback, and adapt their strategy across multiple steps. So in this post, we will walk through how to train a multi-turn, tool-using LLM agent using Tunix's agentic reinforcement learning pipeline on Cloud TPU v6e-8. You can find the complete code in this GitHub repository.

    We will revisit the Plane Strike board game from an earlier TensorFlow/JAX reinforcement learning blog, replacing the custom MLP policy with Gemma 4 E2B in thinking mode on a single Cloud TPU v6e-8 host. Plane Strike is played on a 6x6 grid (A1 to F6) where one 8-cell plane is hidden in one of 4 orientations. Each turn, the agent sees the result of its previous strike and the raw visible board (. untried, X hit, O miss), thinks through candidate placements, and calls the strike(cell="...") tool to strike one cell. The game ends when all 8 plane cells are hit, or after 23 strikes.

    #11395. Germ Network infects Android, but in a good way

    Germ Network infects Android, but in a good way

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (789 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Bluesky's preferred encrypted messaging app allows multiple identities without tying you to a phone number.
    • The Germ Network encrypted messaging client, known as Germ DM, became available for Android on Wednesday, and made a bigger splash than its iOS touchdown back in 2023.
    • "Our usage took a 20x jump yesterday from our Android launch," co-founder Tessa Brown, a communications scholar and former Stanford lecturer, told The Register in an interview.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Bluesky's preferred encrypted messaging app allows multiple identities without tying you to a phone number.

    The Germ Network encrypted messaging client, known as Germ DM, became available for Android on Wednesday, and made a bigger splash than its iOS touchdown back in 2023.

    "Our usage took a 20x jump yesterday from our Android launch," co-founder Tessa Brown, a communications scholar and former Stanford lecturer, told The Register in an interview. "Android has been really exciting for us because not only is it 70 percent of the global mobile market, but we rolled out on iOS first. People were so excited to use Germ for their end-to-end encrypted Bluesky DMs, but half of their friends couldn't talk to them.".

    Industry observers note that building a upcoming messaging platform isn't easy, much less one with credible end-to-end encryption. Co-founder Mark Xue hails from Apple, where he worked as a privacy engineer on systems like iMessage and FaceTime.

    "At the core level, the end-to-end encryption is built on a standardized encryption and Messaging Layer Security," Xue noted. "The premise of Messaging Layer Security was to be as good as Signal and deployable by many, many different parties in different applications, which we're taking advantage of to extend the reach of that encryption.".

    Xue stated the app is built with its own transport protocol to minimize the amount of message metadata, adding that while the team hasn't gotten around to a formal security audit, it's a step they're considering.

    It has been revealed that germ Network's goal, remarked Brown, is to give people more confidence when they communicate. "We do that by giving you more tools to protect your identity, to control what you're sharing with whom," she explained.

    Instead of using a person's phone number as an identity key, Germ allows users to create cards which represent distinct identities on the network.

    "Instead of sharing your number, you share a card," Brown explained. "You can build multiple cards; they're not mutually discoverable. And our vision for the product that will continue shipping over the coming years is that these cards become a more intelligent way to manage your social life, even your work life.".

    At some point, AI might play a role in that, but both Xue and Brown expressed reservations about the current state of play.

    Recent findings suggest that citing concerns Signal has raised about the integration of AI and messaging, Xue remarked, "The products today that I might characterize as technology demos, they're most powerful when they run on someone else's computer. So you end up with these systems where you upload all your messages or you give another entity the power to observe your computing, and that's extremely dangerous for what we protect as private content.".

    Xue noted rapid progress toward addressing information exposure concerns and therefore plans to explore the kinds of smart tooling that people want while also meeting security and privacy requirements.

    Recent findings suggest that "I think a lot of the AI conversation sometimes is a hammer in search of a nail," remarked Brown. "But people do want more tools to make sense of their busy lives and following our consumers, our people, and what they want, we do want to give them smart tooling that will help them organize threads, stay in touch, find the right people to talk to in groups, in a private way that's using a lot of the intelligence that's already on their device.".

    If Germ DM were simply trying to win people away from widely adopted services like Instagram or respected encryption apps like Signal, it would be difficult to see a path to success.

    But Germ DM may be able to reach a point of sustainability by standing on the shoulders of Bluesky.

    It has been revealed that bluesky debuted Direct Messages in 2024 but chose to focus its development resources elsewhere and left E2E DMs to Germ Network. Germ DM, which supports Bluesky's AT Protocol (ATproto), fills that gap and even has Bluesky promoting the app for that purpose.

    Sources indicate that "On a business strategic level, it's been a really wonderful move for us," said Brown. "So we're natively a multi-identity messenger. And you can say that ATproto is the first external identity that we brought into the app, after we first shipped local identities that you just build in our app.

    Bluesky assists further with marketing by allowing Germ DM customers to add a Germ messaging button to their Bluesky profiles. So anyone interested in encrypted DMs in Bluesky may end up seeing that option.

    According to recent reports, at some point, expect paid, premium features but at the moment, Germ Network is focused on spreading the encrypted word. ®.

    #11394. The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

    📅 03 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2628 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.

    📅 03 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2628 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row.
    • Industry observers note that figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind.
    • Recent findings suggest that A customer writes in.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row. It is now available through Hugging Face.

    Industry observers note that figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper.

    Recent findings suggest that A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date.

    Recent findings suggest that the AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation.

    Then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ”.

    Two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold, pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked.

    According to recent reports, an AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees.

    That gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv.

    You can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006, and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper.

    Want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself.

    Final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question.

    The gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap.

    A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test.

    Industry observers note that an agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times, each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things:.

    Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers.

    It has been revealed that we use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing.

    Sources indicate that starting with the familiar view. The table below reports pass@1, the single-attempt score estimate, broken out by domain. This is the number most leaderboards publish, and on its own it reads like an ordinary capability ranking.

    Industry observers note that table 2: ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain. Each model is evaluated on every task for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the group leader; underline marks the runner-up. The standard errors for the single attempt score estimates are provided in Table 4 in our ThinkingBox paper.

    Recent findings suggest that claude Opus 5.5 leads overall at 67.16%, two-thirds of a point above Claude Opus 5. Kimi-K3 is the strongest open-weights model, within a point of GPT-6-Astra. Domain matters just as much: Claude Opus 4.6 scores 68.62% on retail but 8.30% on auto insurance.

    Industry observers note that one good run tells you a model can do the work. It does not tell you whether it will do it again. So run every task 20 times and ask how much of that score survives.

    Figure 2: How much of each model's single-attempt score survives 20 repeats.

    In a recent development, only three hold on to most of their pass@1 scores: GPT-6 Astra retains 78% of its single-attempt rate, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 each retain 71%. At the other end, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro each keep about 8%.

    The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story.

    It has been revealed that figure 3: Breadth and consistency pull apart. Twelve of the eighteen models are shown; six below 33% pass@1 are omitted for legibility.

    Kimi-K3 has the broadest coverage of any model we tested. It solves 93.89% of the benchmark at least once: 476 of 507 tasks. Only 31 tasks defeat it entirely, the lowest count in the field. On retail workflows it leads outright at 82.24% pass@1, ahead of every proprietary model.

    Kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts.

    In a recent development, claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt.

    Sources indicate that A newer model does not fix this. Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than Claude Opus 5 on every-attempt average, 67.16% against 66.50%, and solves more tasks at least once. It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all.

    If you are choosing a model for work that touches real records, pass@20 is the wrong column to look at.

    Sources indicate that capability comparisons usually stop at the score. For anyone deploying, the relevant question is what a successful unit of work costs. We measure that as cost per successful task attempt. We say task attempt because every benchmark task is run repeatedly and cost is incurred per attempt, so pass@1 is the matching quality denominator.

    We took each model's recorded token usage from its full 507 × 20 campaign and priced it at undiscounted list rates available on OpenRouter+, reversing promotional discounts and excluding endpoints that declare quantization. Input, output and cache rates all come from one provider endpoint per model.

    Then we divided one run's cost by the number of attempts that succeeded:.

    Cost per successful task attempt = estimated cost for 507 attempts, one per task ÷ (507 × pass@1).

    Recent findings suggest that this is a comparative efficiency index, not an invoice, and not the price of serving one production request. It also prices single successes, not consistency. We price consistency next.

    Example: GPT-5.4 costs $43.49 for 507 attempts (one attempt per task) and has 65.36% pass@1, so $43.49 ÷ (507 × 0.6536) = $0.131 per successful task attempt.

    Industry observers note that A model is on the frontier if no other model is both no more expensive and at least as accurate. Three models qualify; every other model is dominated on at least one axis.

    Sources indicate that figure 4: Cost per successful task attempt against pass@1. Ringed dots are pareto cost frontier models.

    In a recent development, the frontier has three steps. GPT-5.6 Sol has the lowest cost per success at $0.127; GPT-5.4 raises pass@1 by 3.45 percentage points for $0.004 more per success; Claude Opus 5.5 adds another 1.80 points at $0.276 per success. Each of the three remains on the cost frontier line because no cheaper model matches its pass@1.

    Claude Opus 5 is the clearest case: at $0.475 per successful attempt and 66.50% pass@1, it is both more expensive and less accurate than Claude Opus 5.5 at $0.276 and 67.16%.

    Cost per success rewards a model that is cheap and often right. It does not reward a model that is right every time. So we also compute cost per dependable task: the cost of the full 20-run campaign divided by the number of tasks the model passed on all 20 attempts.

    Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of 20 runs of 507 attempts ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

    Example: GPT-6-Astra costs 20 × $86.03 = $1,720.60 for the campaign and passes 231 tasks on every attempt, so $1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $7.45 per dependable task.

    In a recent development, table 3: The nine lowest costs per dependable task among models with at least one observed 20/20 task, sorted low to high. Estimated $, not actual cloud bills.

    Recent findings suggest that now rank by consistency. GPT-5.4 is the cheapest at $6.80, though only 128 tasks meet the bar. GPT-6 Astra reaches 231 at $7.45, and Claude Opus 5.5 the joint-highest 241 at $7.80.

    None of the three dominates the others: each additional dependable task costs more. Claude Opus 5 also passes 241, but at $13.30, so Opus 5.5 dominates it outright. GPT-5.6 Sol, the cheapest per single success at $0.127, costs $9.76 per dependable task. The cheapest way to get a right answer is not the cheapest way to get a dependable one.

    In a recent development, we assign each failed trace one deterministic diagnostic signature, and the headline is actionable: roughly four in five failures are tool handling, not reasoning. Across an ablation study in Table 5 of our paper:.

    These are unweighted averages of per-model shares and observable labels, not unique causal explanations.

    It has been revealed that the practical pattern is simple: agents usually get far enough to attempt the workflow, then fail to recover from tool errors, failed preconditions, or empty lookups. That is a retry and error-recovery problem before it is a model problem.

    Difficulty also changes by domain: across the models listed in Table 2 above, retail averages 59.52% pass@1 while auto insurance averages 33.83%.

    Sources indicate that what to do about it. Treat the 20/20 rate as a design input, not a verdict. The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it.

    Classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. We have not measured the lift from any of these on this benchmark, which is exactly the kind of thing the environment now makes testable.

    Recent findings suggest that thinkingBox is the agent sandbox, while ThinkingBox-Bench is a dataset benchmark to evaluate agents. The diagram at the top of this post shows the loop; here is what each part does.

    Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges.

    Each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked.

    Every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful.

    In a recent development, at the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects. For requirements with no clean database value ("did the agent disclose this is not guaranteed?"), a narrow binary rubric question handles the semantics. 477 of the 507 tasks are graded on state alone; 30 add response rubrics.

    In a recent development, the trust boundary: the model sees tasks, dialogue and tool schemas. Golden state, assertions, grading internals and credentials stay on the evaluator side.

    ThinkingBox is now on Hugging Face, both the harness and the dataset. ThinkingBox-Bench now sits behind the OpenEnv interface, and each finished episode returns a binary pass/fail reward. The released adapter is designed for evaluation; separate, non-benchmark scenarios can use the same interface in training workflows.

    According to recent reports, tested on Linux and WSL, with Python 3.11+, uv and Docker. You also need a thinkingbox-data checkout at the pinned release and model endpoints for the agent, simulated user and judge. One endpoint can serve all three roles, which is the simplest way to start. The OpenEnv image starts only the OpenEnv API; everything else you run yourself.

    In a second terminal, start Typesense 30.1 and wait for its health check:.

    In a third terminal, start the Session Proxy and MCP servers.

    Back in the first terminal, start the OpenEnv server against a ThinkingBox YAML config naming your three models (config guide):.

    Gate on readiness before running anything. It returns 503 until its observable data, configuration and Session Proxy checks pass. It cannot observe Typesense or live-probe every model endpoint, so confirm those separately:.

    Recent findings suggest that now score a real episode. example_usage.py only resets and lists tools; for agent actions, effects and assertions use the packaged evaluator:.

    Sources indicate that the OpenEnv adapter writes operational failures to an errors sidecar so they can be rerun rather than silently mixed with model outcomes. A canonical result must resolve or explicitly account for those attempts; we counted system errors as unsuccessful trials.

    Runs are gated on a pinned framework commit, a pinned data release and a bundle hash, so a canonical result is verifiable rather than asserted.

    In a recent development, the useful part of this work is not our pass@1 leaderboard. It is the environment.

    If you are evaluating an agent that touches real records:.

    Further details can be found in the following links:.

    ThinkingBox code is MIT-licensed; the benchmark data is CDLA-Permissive-2.0; the OpenEnv environment ships under OpenEnv's BSD-3-Clause.

    In a recent development, disclaimer: every task in the public benchmark is a synthetic reconstruction. The workflows and policies are modeled on real AI agentic enterprise patterns; the customers are not real.

    Sources indicate that thinkingBox and ThinkingBox-Bench is built by the Microsoft Copilot Studio team in partnership with Toloka with collaborators from the University of Pittsburgh, Northwestern University, Columbia University and UC Irvine who interned at Microsoft. Questions are welcome in the comments section below or on github or by email at firstnamelastname@microsoft.com.

    + OpenRouter cost snapshot taken on Sept 20th 2026; Opus 5.5 pricing as per the Anthropic site.

    According to recent reports, ST003_006 delegates its pass check to validate_database. Unequal result and golden database hashes fail even when diff is empty. The diff explains a failure; it does not decide the pass.

    This small replay exercises the released function with four authored effect inputs. Run python3 reproduce.py. It verifies the source pin and tests supplied hashes; it does not calculate a database hash, run an agent, or reproduce the full environment.

    AI-assisted source reading and example by CyberNative AI LLC.

    The useful cut is agent-reported "done" versus backend terminal state.

    According to recent reports, A green success from the same process that acted is a claim, not a grade. I'd want the eval to score durable side effects (ticket status, refund state, policy-cited fields) against a frozen oracle — and fail when the narrative is green while the database disagrees.

    Practical check: can a run be marked done when the terminal-state fixture is red?

    #11392. GitHub availability report: October 2026

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2075 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Github ↗ Open Full Page

    GitHub availability report: October 2026

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2075 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Github

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.
    • In a recent development, the short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate.
    • It has been revealed that as of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.

    In a recent development, the short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery.

    It has been revealed that as of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity.

    That capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range.

    Recent findings suggest that we also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm.

    According to recent reports, we removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%.

    Reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in users. More details on these and other incidents follow.

    Sources indicate that the East US 3 buildout is about one week behind plan. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery.

    The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features.

    Duration: approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes.

    It has been revealed that customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to revision, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features.

    Actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted.

    Jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs.

    How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

    Duration: approximately 6 minutes of failed or slow requests across github.com, followed by approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes during which enterprise migrations were paused.

    Industry observers note that customers may have seen server errors or slow responses when signing in, working with repositories and pull requests, calling the API, or using GitHub Codespaces. Retrying a short time later would have succeeded, and delayed webhook deliveries caught up soon after. At the peak, about 1.3% of all requests failed or timed out, and about 6.4K organizations saw at least one failed or slow request.

    Migrations were paused for customers using GitHub Enterprise Importer, and were resumed once a fix was deployed.

    In a recent development, A surge in migration activity caused GitHub Enterprise Importer to send a burst of very large queries to a shared database. These queries took much longer than usual and, together with normal traffic, used all of the database’s available connections, preventing other github.com features relying on the same database from completing their requests.

    It has been revealed that the importer did not reduce its load when the database became overloaded. The impact ended within minutes, once the importer finished its queued queries and the database’s connections were released.

    To prevent a recurrence, we paused migrations until we deployed a mitigation that runs these queries in smaller batches.

    How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

    According to recent reports, duration: two separate write outages lasted approximately 10 minutes and 9 minutes, totaling about 19 minutes. The second was a recurrence of the first, with the same cause.

    Industry observers note that customers may have seen errors when pushing code, signing in, updating pull requests or problems, or making changes through the API. Webhooks, GitHub Apps and OAuth, actions, code scanning, codespaces, and Copilot were also affected. Viewing content was largely unaffected. Data that was already saved was not lost, and actions that failed during the outages succeeded when retried after recovery.

    In a recent development, web and API request failures peaked at 8.9% in the first outage and 9.3% in the second, affecting more than 12,000 and more than 11,000 organizations, respectively. Some organizations may have been affected by both outages.

    During regular maintenance, we replaced machines that manage where database writes are sent. One newly introduced machine started with outdated records that still listed retired database servers. Once it was automatically elected leader, it published routing settings that sent writes for several core databases to those retired servers. Incorrect settings passed our existing validation and took effect immediately. Later, an automated maintenance task did not honor a pause on maintenance and triggered another election, and because the new machine had not yet been removed, it became leader again.

    How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

    Duration: approximately 1 hour and 28 minutes.

    It has been revealed that customers may have seen delays in GitHub Actions workflow status updates, logs, and checks. About 5% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners experienced delayed starts, a very small share of workflow runs failed, and some requests to the actions jobs REST API returned errors. GitHub Pages deployments and workflow and check webhook events generated by actions runs were also delayed. For part of this time, live updates on github.com and code search were degraded.

    An internal actions service that stores workflow logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region. Every server running that service then retried those connections at the same time. Together, those retries saturated the network connections between GitHub’s data center and that region, disrupting other services that use the same link.

    How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

    Duration: approximately 6 hours and 46 minutes.

    In a recent development, customers may have seen delays in pull request updates, GitHub Actions workflow status updates, and webhook deliveries. After a push, new commits were slow to appear on pull requests. Workflows triggered by the push started late. Status checks from actions workflows could look stuck on pull requests, which held up merges that require those checks to pass. These features recovered within about 2 to 3.5 hours.

    Industry observers note that audit log events were affected the longest. Recent activity took longer to appear when customers searched their audit logs, with delays of up to 1 hour and 50 minutes. Audit log events were fully caught up after about 6 hours and 46 minutes.

    Some webhook deliveries from this period may be missing from webhook delivery history, though the webhooks themselves were delivered.

    In a recent development, some servers in our event streaming platform were close to their memory limits, and memory use on these servers grows with the number of client connections. When requests to these servers failed, latest connections were opened immediately, which increased the number of connections and the memory they used. The increase in memory use slowed down and overloaded the servers.

    We took the overloaded servers out of service, and their traffic moved to other servers. Those servers then became overloaded too, and the problem spread to more servers over the following hour. We began rebalancing overloaded partitions onto brokers that had available capacity and this mitigated the problem.

    In a recent development, audit logs took the longest to recover. The service that writes audit log events kept restarting on errors from the platform for more than two hours and fell further behind. Once stabilized, it could only write events at a limited rate, so the backlog took several more hours to clear.

    How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

    Duration: approximately 1 hour and 32 minutes.

    Customers may have seen errors when using several GPT-family models in Copilot. Requests using these models in Copilot Chat in IDEs and on github.com, the Copilot CLI, Copilot code review, and the Copilot coding agent returned errors or did not complete. About one in 10 requests to the affected models failed. Other models continued to work, and choosing another model avoided the errors. Auto model selection reduced the errors by sending some requests to an unaffected model.

    Code scanning autofix and code quality, which are built on one specific model without an alternative model to switch to, were affected more heavily.

    According to recent reports, copilot reaches these models through an upstream model provider and uses a credential to authenticate with that provider. That credential became invalid, the provider began rejecting our requests as unauthenticated, and our service returned those rejections to clients as authentication errors. Copilot features that use these models send their requests through that provider, so they began failing at the same time.

    How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

    Duration: approximately 9 minutes.

    Customers may have seen some requests to github.com hang for up to about 10 seconds and then fail with a server error. Pull request merges and Git operations over SSH and Git LFS were hit hardest. At the worst point, about 43% of merge attempts failed, compared with about 3.5% of API calls. Issues, GitHub Pages, notifications, and sign-in for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps also saw intermittent errors.

    In a recent development, A database connection pool used by many github.com services reached its limit, and for several minutes no connections were available. Latest requests that needed a connection waited until the connection timeout expired and then failed.

    Recent findings suggest that the pool was already running near capacity when some revision requests started holding their connections far longer than expected. Each one began writing a change, then ran a separate lookup that could take several seconds, keeping its connection reserved but unused the whole time. With little headroom, those held connections helped tip the pool over.

    How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

    Industry observers note that follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog.

    #11391. Breaking: Flaws in VMware and KVM need attention, if you have time while fixing Java, PHP, and everything else

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (592 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theregister ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: Flaws in VMware and KVM need attention, if you have time while fixing Java, PHP, and everything else

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (592 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Critical Virtzilla bugs allow authentication bypass, as a nested virtualization matter got Digital Ocean ducking.
    • If you’ve got a moment to spare in between sorting out emergency patches for PHP, Java, and PostgreSQL, VMware has just bid for any remaining space on your schedule by publishing two critical-rated security advisories.
    • According to recent reports, VMSA-2026-0009 addresses CVE-2026-123890, a 9.8-rated flaw that VMware states means a malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this concern to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Critical Virtzilla bugs allow authentication bypass, as a nested virtualization matter got Digital Ocean ducking.

    If you’ve got a moment to spare in between sorting out emergency patches for PHP, Java, and PostgreSQL, VMware has just bid for any remaining space on your schedule by publishing two critical-rated security advisories.

    According to recent reports, VMSA-2026-0009 addresses CVE-2026-123890, a 9.8-rated flaw that VMware states means a malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this concern to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. vCenter is the tool admins use to manage fleets of virtual machines. The flaw is present in VMware’s flagship Cloud Foundation suite.

    VMware also wants its consumers to address CVE-2026-123891, which allows attackers to read and write the database used by SDDC Manager, the tool for managing entire software-defined datacenters. Attackers can execute arbitrary commands and elevate privileges to root.

    The prospect of an unknown party getting access to vCenter or SDDC manager is not pleasant. At least VMware has fixed its software.

    The virty giant hasn't done the same to address a second advisory, VMSA-2026-0010, which warns that Cloud Foundation, Aria Operations, and VCF Operations HCX products all use Apache – which has a 9.8-rated remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618).

    VMware prepares to ship new versions of its products with a patched version of Apache, but for now only has workarounds that disable the http2 protocol.

    Admins who oversee virtual infrastructure also need to pay attention to Linux KVM, the subject of a curious incident over the last 24 hours.

    This mess started with the November 18 disclosure of CVE-2026-99312, a bug which allows an attacker to use a guest virtual machine to inflict Denial of Service (DoS) or memory corruption attacks on the host.

    It’s bad news whenever someone with access to a guest VM can attack the host, because it means gaining access to a single tenant can potentially harm all the other guest VMs or peer into the memory a guest uses.

    This flaw, however, isn’t a worst-case scenario guest-host escape, because it only impacts users of AMD processors who employ nested virtualization – the practice of running a hypervisor inside a virtual machine. Nested virtualization isn’t commonly used in the enterprise, but clouds employ it to do things like powering OS emulators. The bug’s CVSSv3 score is therefore a modest 5.5.

    Security researcher Oren Tomtov of Accomplish.ai claims the flaw meant he could access 127 GB of host RAM on a Digital Ocean “Droplet” – the junior cloud’s name for its cloudy VMs.

    Yomtov states he told Digital Ocean and the Linux kernel security team about the flaw in October. Maintainers got busy and delivered a fix to the mainline kernel on November 2, full fixes landed on the 17th. The CVE then appeared on November 18.

    Yomtov and Terra Security swiftly posted their analysis of the flaw – but then took the posts down within hours.

    Sources indicate that the Register understands that Digital Ocean asked for the posts to come down because it needed more time to update its Linux implementations. The company has not responded to multiple requests for comment.

    In a recent development, terra’s analysis of the flaw asserts that it was introduced to KVM in 2022, when developers wrote a fix for CVE-2022-3344. The company believes 3.2 percent of CVEs in the Linux kernel were introduced by the fix for another CVE.

    The good news about CVE-2026-99312 is it’s easy to defeat without an enhancement, by disabling nested virtualization in KVM. ®.

    Introducing Falcon ASR

    📅 07 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1280 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%.
    • We’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect.
    • Sources indicate that in our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%.

    We’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect. Developed at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi, it also supports English, French, Spanish and Portuguese.

    Sources indicate that in our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used. On our internal Emirati evaluation, it recorded the lowest word and character error rates among the systems we compared.

    We also support word-level timestamps for transcriptions, linking each transcribed word to its position in the audio.

    Sources indicate that arabic speech varies by region, speaker and setting. A model that handles a formal news broadcast may still struggle with a conversation in Emirati or with speech recorded over a phone line. Dialectal Arabic also has fewer transcribed resources than Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), which makes training and evaluation harder.

    It has been revealed that we trained Falcon-ASR on Emirati, MSA, other Gulf and Arabic dialects, and English. Our aim is to transcribe the words people use in everyday speech, including dialectal forms and changes between languages.

    The Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard, maintained by the ELM Research Center, ranks systems by the equal-weight average WER across six test sets. It also reports character error rate (CER). Lower values are better for both metrics. Our Falcon-ASR evaluation follows this protocol.

    According to recent reports, WER = Word Error Rate; CER = Character Error Rate. A lower value indicates better performance.

    It has been revealed that we evaluated Falcon-ASR on the same six benchmarks using the leaderboard’s pinned manifests. Competitor figures are the published leaderboard averages checked on 30 September 2026. Falcon-ASR’s average WER is 2.25 percentage points better than the best published result in that snapshot.

    Public evaluation data already includes Emirati: Casablanca has a UAE subset. We complement that coverage with an internal evaluation of additional Emirati and Gulf speech, using held-out recordings and human-validated transcripts to assess transcription accuracy beyond the public UAE subset.

    In our internal Emirati evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved 22.73% WER and 10.19% CER:.

    According to recent reports, falcon-ASR has the lowest WER and CER among the systems compared here. Its WER is 4.07 percentage points below Qwen3-Omni, the next best result. The results show improved transcription accuracy at both the word and character level on this evaluation.

    We included background noise, overlapping speech, music, room reverberation and telephony effects, as well as variations in speed and pitch. We applied the same treatment to Emirati recordings, exposing the model to a range of conditions it may encounter in meetings, calls and other everyday recordings.

    Falcon-ASR also transcribes English with the same model weights. In our evaluation on the seven public English test sets used by the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, it achieved a mean WER of 5.74%.

    According to recent reports, the model also supports French, Spanish and Portuguese. All five languages use the same weights, without requiring a language flag. The output is a transcript in the language spoken.

    According to recent reports, falcon-ASR builds on our Falcon3-Audio work. The architecture and training approach for Falcon3-Audio are described in Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data.

    It has been revealed that our Hugging Face Demo Space lets you try Falcon-ASR and explore its transcription capabilities. API access and native applications are planned. We invite you to try the Demo with your own recordings.

    We thank the team behind the Falcon-Emirati model for their support with Arabic foundation models. Read about their latest work in the Falcon-Emirati blog post.

    We also extend our sincere thanks to Mikhail Lubinets for continued support with the compute infrastructure.

    نقدّم Falcon-ASR، نموذجنا للتعرف على الكلام العربي بحجم 1.6 مليار معلمة، مع اهتمام خاص باللهجة الإماراتية. طوّرنا النموذج في معهد الابتكار التكنولوجي (TII) في أبوظبي، وهو يدعم أيضًا اللغات الإنجليزية والفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية.

    Industry observers note that في تقييمنا، حقق Falcon-ASR متوسط معدل خطأ في الكلمات بلغ 20.92% عبر ست مجموعات اختبار باللغة العربية، مقارنةً بأفضل نتيجة منشورة بلغت 23.17% في نسخة لوحة المتصدرين التي استخدمناها. وفي تقييمنا الداخلي للهجة الإماراتية، سجّل النموذج أدنى معدلات خطأ في الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة التي قارناها.

    ندعم أيضاً الطوابع الزمنية على مستوى الكلمات في عمليات التفريغ النصي، بحيث ترتبط كل كلمة بموضعها في التسجيل الصوتي.

    Recent findings suggest that يختلف الكلام العربي باختلاف المنطقة والمتحدث وظروف التسجيل. فقد ينجح نموذج في تفريغ نشرة إخبارية رسمية، ثم يجد صعوبة في تفريغ محادثة باللهجة الإماراتية أو تسجيل عبر الهاتف. كما أن الموارد الصوتية المفرّغة نصيًا للهجات العربية أقل من تلك المتاحة للعربية الفصحى، مما يزيد صعوبة التدريب والتقييم.

    Sources indicate that درّبنا Falcon-ASR على اللهجة الإماراتية والعربية الفصحى ولهجات خليجية وعربية أخرى، إلى جانب الإنجليزية. وهدفنا هو تفريغ الكلمات التي يستخدمها الناس في حديثهم اليومي، بما في ذلك الصيغ اللهجية والانتقال بين اللغات.

    Sources indicate that ترتّب لوحة المتصدرين المفتوحة الشاملة للتعرف على الكلام العربي، التي يديرها مركز ELM للأبحاث، الأنظمة وفق متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات عبر ست مجموعات اختبار، بوزن متساوٍ لكل مجموعة. وتعرض أيضًا معدل خطأ الأحرف (CER). وكلما انخفضت قيمة أي من المقياسين، كان الأداء أفضل. ويتبع تقييمنا للنموذج هذا البروتوكول.

    Sources indicate that WER هو معدل خطأ الكلمات؛ وCER هو معدل خطأ الأحرف. تشير القيمة الأقل إلى أداء أفضل.

    Recent findings suggest that قيّمنا Falcon-ASR على مجموعات الاختبار الست نفسها، باستخدام قوائم العينات المثبّتة في لوحة المتصدرين. وأرقام النماذج المنافسة هي المتوسطات المنشورة في اللوحة، والتي جرى التحقق منها في 30 سبتمبر 2026. وكان متوسط خطأ الكلمات للنموذج أفضل بمقدار 2.25 نقطة مئوية من أفضل نتيجة منشورة في تلك النسخة.

    تتوافر بالفعل بيانات عامة لتقييم اللهجة الإماراتية، إذ تضم مجموعة Casablanca قسمًا خاصًا بالإمارات. ونكمّل هذه التغطية بتقييم داخلي لتسجيلات إضافية من الكلام الإماراتي والخليجي، باستخدام تسجيلات مخصّصة للاختبار ونصوص مرجعية خضعت لمراجعة بشرية، لتقييم دقة التفريغ على مواد إضافية إلى جانب البيانات الإماراتية العامة.

    حقق Falcon-ASR في تقييمنا الإماراتي الداخلي معدل خطأ كلمات قدره 22.73٪ ومعدل خطأ أحرف قدره 10.19٪:.

    سجّل Falcon-ASR أقل معدل لخطأ الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة المقارَنة هنا. وكان معدل خطأ الكلمات أقل بمقدار 4.07 نقطة مئوية من Qwen3-Omni، صاحب النتيجة التالية. وتُظهر النتائج تحسنًا في دقة التفريغ على مستوى الكلمات والأحرف في هذا التقييم.

    Industry observers note that ضمّنا بيانات التدريب ضوضاء خلفية وكلامًا متداخلًا وموسيقى وصدى الصوت وتأثيرات الاتصالات الهاتفية، إلى جانب تغيّرات في سرعة الكلام وحدّة الصوت. وطبّقنا المعالجة نفسها على التسجيلات الإماراتية، لتهيئة النموذج للتعامل مع ظروف مختلفة قد يواجهها في الاجتماعات والمكالمات والتسجيلات اليومية الأخرى.

    It has been revealed that يفرّغ Falcon-ASR الكلام الإنجليزي باستخدام أوزان النموذج نفسها. وفي تقييمنا على مجموعات الاختبار الإنجليزية العامة السبع المستخدمة في لوحة Hugging Face المفتوحة للتعرف على الكلام، بلغ متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات 5.74٪.

    According to recent reports, يدعم النموذج أيضًا الفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية. وتستخدم اللغات الخمس أوزانًا واحدة، دون الحاجة إلى تحديد اللغة مسبقًا. ويكون الناتج تفريغًا نصيًا باللغة المنطوقة.

    Industry observers note that يستند Falcon-ASR إلى أعمالنا في Falcon3-Audio. وتعرض ورقة Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data بنية Falcon3-Audio ونهج تدريبه.

    It has been revealed that يتيح عرضنا التجريبي على Hugging Face تجربة Falcon-ASR واستكشاف قدراته في تفريغ الكلام. أما الوصول عبر واجهة API والتطبيقات الأصلية فهو مخطّط له. ندعوكم إلى تجربة النموذج باستخدام تسجيلاتكم.

    According to recent reports, نتوجّه بجزيل الشكر إلى الفريق القائم على تطوير نموذج Falcon-Emirati على دعمهم في مجال النماذج التأسيسية للغة العربية. ويمكن الاطّلاع على أحدث أعمال الفريق من خلال المقال المنشور حول Falcon-Emirati.

    كما نتقدّم بخالص الشكر والتقدير إلى Mikhail Lubinets على دعمه المستمر للبنية التحتية الحاسوبية.

    #11388. Nudeps: bundler-like imports, none of the baggage

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1568 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Verou ↗ Open Full Page

    Nudeps: bundler-like imports, none of the baggage

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1568 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Verou

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that bundlers are presently the only way to use dependencies without losing our sanity, but introduce complexity and overhead.
    • vue), you write import { createApp } from "vue", and it works — as long as there is a bundler in between.
    • According to recent reports, but bundlers add a significant tax.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that bundlers are presently the only way to use dependencies without losing our sanity, but introduce complexity and overhead. Today, I’m releasing a latest type of lightweight build tool that challenges that.

    You npm install a package (e.g. vue), you write import { createApp } from "vue", and it works — as long as there is a bundler in between. Without one, the browser has no idea what "vue" is: it only understands URLs, and node_modules/ was never meant to be deployed. So even the simplest project ends up needing a bundler, only so it can use dependencies instead of reinventing the wheel.

    According to recent reports, but bundlers add a significant tax. They process every single file, introduce several layers of abstraction between source and deployment, and these abstractions often leak: things that work fine in the browser can break in the build.

    Earlier this year, I published Web dependencies are broken: Can we fix them? that discusses this from a platform architecture perspective. Besides the architectural concerns, the complexity is an active developer pain point: in State of JS 2025, “Managing Dependencies” was the 3rd biggest pain point, and “Build tools” were 6th.

    According to recent reports, however, getting rid of build tools is not the goal. Some use cases should not be handled by the browser, so bundlers and build tools will always have a role to play. The goal is making them lighter, composable, and less essential.

    Nudeps1Which you can choose to read as either nude deps or nu (fresh) deps is a new kind of lightweight build tool that lets you continue using npm install to manage dependencies, vendor them locally, and import them via bare specifiers (package names like "vue" or @floating-ui/dom instead of URLs), without the bundler.

    According to recent reports, you set it up once, and then you can forget about it: you keep npm installing packages and importing them by name, and they work in the browser. And it only ever touches your dependencies, never your own code.

    Since my apprentice Dmitry and I prototyped the initial MVP in February, we and others have tested it on a variety of projects, and at this point I’m confident that — while not perfect — it’s ready for prime time.

    A core architectural difference between Nudeps and bundlers is that your own code remains untouched. In fact, it doesn’t even need a watcher that runs whenever you make edits! It only touches dependency files, and doesn’t rewrite anything, making it extremely lightweight in terms of complexity it adds.

    Sources indicate that this means it can complement any other tooling — or none. You write raw HTML, CSS, JS? This is for you. You use a templating engine, a CSS preprocessor, and TypeScript? This is also for you (though understandably you may have less use for it). This also makes it complement static site generators and island architectures particularly well.

    In a recent development, does it replace your build process? If all you needed it for was getting imports to work, it could. If you also compile your code (JSX, TypeScript, single-file components), you still need a tool for that, but it can be a much smaller one.

    Bundlers make complex things possible. Nudeps is hoping to occupy the space on the left of the curve and make simple things easy.

    Recent findings suggest that assuming you don’t need to customize anything (e.g. using /importmap.js for the map, client_modules/ for the dependencies, all default settings) it goes like this:.

    That’s it. You’re done. You can now npm install and npm uninstall to your heart’s content, and start using packages right away in your code. Things Just Work™.

    We have been so trained to expect friction and complexity, that some testers thought they were doing it wrong:.

    In a recent development, I ran the npx command and added the import map to my app, but I assumed that there was still a lot more work to do. I was shocked to realize I was done.

    Most of the pieces were already there, and were just waiting for someone to put the puzzle together.

    Sources indicate that import maps allow us to import bare specifiers (package names like "vue") instead of URLs in the browser and are Baseline Widely Available. JSPM is a library that traces a dependency graph and generates an import map. It focuses on CDN use cases, but its engine is exposed as a separate library that can be repurposed, which is what Nudeps uses under the hood (with a lot of tweaks).

    Import maps currently have to be inline in the HTML of every page, which would require templating, but external import maps can be easily emulated via a small script that injects the map.

    Package managers like npm already give you the file structure and let you manage versioning, that structure just can’t be deployed as-is to the web.

    Installing Nudeps via npx nudeps install does a few things, most notably:.

    In a recent development, using dependencies as a hook means there is no Nudeps watcher or command to run when you start working on a project! In that sense, Nudeps actually gets you better DX than a bundler2Of course if you need to start a server for development, that doesn’t make a ton of difference. But localhost is cheap. Your editor can start one. Your agent can start one. Heck, I even have one running at the root of all my cloned repos. .

    Then, whenever npx nudeps runs, it….

    Here’s an example of what that script may look like.

    In production, you can prune to only the specifiers actually used (via the prune option), and including them all in development means the import map only needs to change when your dependencies do, not whenever you write an import.

    In a recent development, yes! Obviously some frameworks are compile-only (e.g. Svelte), but many have runtime-only imports. Even React can be used, though without JSX the ergonomics are poor. My personal go-to is Vue.

    Most libraries also work fine, including D3, gsap, Lit, Three.js, Floating UI, interact.js, and Underscore.

    Beyond common cases, Nudeps supports quite a few edge cases too:.

    Many CJS-only packages like lodash work too, via a tiny require() shim (that Nudeps handles), and the jQuery demo even loads two different jQuery versions side by side through npm aliases.

    Yes! In fact the demos include two such dependencies: Open Props and Bootstrap Icons.

    Sources indicate that the catch is that since browsers presently have no way to include CSS stylesheets via specifiers, you need to use actual URLs (this is changing). This also means these packages cannot use other dependencies (unless they bundle them). Thankfully, that’s the case for most.

    To make this easier, Nudeps creates symlinks (or redirects, where symlinks are not supported) so you can import versionless URLs like client_modules/open-props/.

    From the very beginning of our testing (back in February), Claude understood it just fine, making only minor mistakes that were unnecessary, but ultimately harmless (Nudeps still worked fine), such as:.

    And the package now includes a SKILL.md file, which makes them go away entirely once the agent is instructed to actually use it.

    Also, since Nudeps doesn’t bundle, packages with a lot of tiny modules pulled together by ESM imports may be slower to load initially. If you’re a package author that wants to provide a Nudeps-friendly bundle, generating a bundle that consolidates them somewhat can improve performance. But there is a tradeoff to all bundling: the more files are bundled, the less granularly they can be loaded. There is typically a sweet spot, and that varies depending on the structure and usage patterns of your package. But please do not bundle your package’s dependencies in there as well — these need to remain separate, so they can be shared with other packages that use the same version of the same dependency.

    Nudeps does one job, so there are things it doesn’t do, and things it doesn’t do yet:.

    Nudeps is just the beginning, and is far from perfect. There are certainly plenty of unknown unknowns, and many things we simply haven’t gotten around to.

    Besides bugfixes and closing the gaps above, at the top of the roadmap is testing more packages to ensure compatibility and uncover edge cases.

    If you want to give Nudeps a try, the easiest way is to head to your terminal and run npx nudeps install in your project directory — or just let your agent do it.

    I’m hoping that Nudeps is the first step towards a future of lighter, composable build tools. Try it and let us know how it went!

    Sources indicate that it's only $25, I don't know why people here are all in an uproar. Seems like it could cut down on an awful lot of malware.

    I write some Android cellphone apps myself, mostly for personal use. You can register for a limited distribution account for free, it lets you install your app on up to 50 devices.

    Also you need a support phone number (again, shown on your profile in the play store). We all know that 'da kids' just love to phone all sorts of people for support /s.

    In a recent development, if you don't want your actual phone number on there (which Google recommend you don't), then you'll be paying for some other phone number as well. That's a monthly cost. You can rent a business address too, which again is monthly - all before you've even uploaded your first app. How are you going to pay for all this monthly outgoing? You weren.

    It has been revealed that the uproar is the amount of effort to bypass the requirement or the shakedown of open source developers. That's before you consider your own self-compiled apps on what was nominally supposed to be *your* device.

    Please send me $25 since you really don't seem to care who shakes you down.

    In a recent development, there may be more comments in this discussion. Without JavaScript enabled, you might want to turn on Classic Discussion System in your preferences instead.

    UNIX is many things to many people, but it's never been everything to anybody.
