    It has been revealed that weâre announcing, and honestly celebrating, the next chapter in our push for memory safety: Sovereign Tech Agency have selected us as their partner for helping critical free and open source (FOSS) projects transition to memory safe tech like Rust, as part of their Sovereign Tech Resilience Program. In this article, weâll go over the Program, why now is the right time to transition, and weâll explain the basics of how FOSS projects can benefit from this collaboration, free of charge.

    Recent findings suggest that weâre announcing, and honestly celebrating, the next chapter in our push for memory safety: Sovereign Tech Agency have selected us as their partner for helping critical free and open source (FOSS) projects transition to memory safe tech like Rust, as part of their Sovereign Tech Resilience Program. In this article, weâll go over the Program, why now is the right time to transition, and weâll explain the basics of how FOSS projects can benefit from this collaboration, free of charge.

    In a recent development, the Sovereign Tech Agency are well-known in the FOSS ecosystem for their Sovereign Tech Fund, which does âstrategic investments in the digital infrastructure of our economy and societyâ. In September 2026, they relaunched the Sovereign Tech Resilience Program, which works a little differently; STA has contracted suppliers to perform various services for FOSS projects, to strengthen the resilience of these projects. Unlike many grant programs in the industry, the Sovereign Tech Resilience Program does not give money directly to projects; instead it provides support from a paid-for engineering team.So how does this program strengthen the resilience of FOSS projects? By âimproving projectsâ underlying capacity to prevent, withstand, and respond to [bugs]â in various ways (which you can read more about here), including by offering support for transitioning code bases to Rust, Go, or Python.Transition to memory safetyThat is where we come in. Weâve been contracted to support participating projects in transitioning codebases, whole or in part, from memory-unsafe languages such as C or C++ to memory-safe alternatives where appropriate.The services we will be delivering to FOSS projects are:assessing which components are suitable for rewritesproducing prioritized migration roadmapscarrying out rewrites while maintaining functional equivalence and compatibilitytraining maintainers to keep developing the memory-safe componentsWhy nowA lot of our world depends on various critical open source projects. By now, itâs obvious that hardening these critical open source components, by investing in them and contributing to them, is important. As weâre currently seeing a surge in both (agentic) cyber attacks and AI-assisted vulnerability discoveries, this has become more pressing than ever before, and weâre not expecting this urgency to let up.There are, thankfully, different ways to go about it, and many excellent initiatives (e.g. the Alpha Omega project), but hereâs why weâre so excited to be a part of this one specifically:The Programsâs criteria ensure a risk and impact based investmentA projectâs maintainers stay in the leadThe effort is substantial enough (i.e. secured for at least 3 years) to create real and lasting impactTo us, being STAâs partner in this also presents a very tangible step in our advocacy for memory safety, which started in 2023 but has felt more pertinent each year since.How to apply for this programFor FOSS projects that are interested, the process is very straightforward:Read the participation criteriaApply to the programGet selectedMake a blueprint with STA and us, while you stay in the leadWe collaboratively execute the planYou can apply for one or multiple areas of support (aside from memory safety, think e.g. software supply chain security, security audits, and more). The resulting engagement can be large or small, long or short, depending on the services youâre interested in and that fit your projectâs needs.Questions?We are currently working on several FOSS projects that are unrelated to the Resilience Program. If youâd like to know more about our open-source work first, here are some of those projects:e-KS and Abacus, for the Dutch Electoral CouncilOpen Device Partnership for MicrosoftVarious projects at Trifecta Tech Foundation, the non-profit that we founded in 2024 to develop and maintain digital commons, open-source software and open standards for the Internet and other vital systems. Projects range from time synchronization (e.g. ntpd-rs and sectime.org), to compression (e.g. zlib-rs) and privilege boundary (e.g. sudo-rs).Any other questions? Please refer to the Programâs FAQ, or reach out to me, Hugo.Weâre thankful for the opportunity to work with various open source projects and maintainers in such a constructive way in the years to come. We look forward to working with you, to helping you get things done that were challenging before, and making a positive impact together!

    Stay up-to-date with our work and blog posts?

    Itâs July 2026, and part of the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA) is now in effect; the remainder is imminent. The new EU regulations aim to significantly improve the cybersecurity of connected products placed on the European market. If your organization develops digital products such as IoT devices or EV chargers, youâre affected.

    Earlier this month Marc and I had the opportunity to deliver a talk at ONE Conference in The Hague, The Netherlands, on a topic thatâs near to our hearts: memory safety. Below we share some context, as well as our slides.

    According to recent reports, weâve been raising awareness of the importance of using memory-safe technology to build systems that are truly secure-by-design. We do this alongside our core business, which is to help companies to use Rust successfully. With the CRA standardization process well on its way, now is the perfect time to patch you on what weâve been doing and why.

    #11384. Tech Report: The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

    📅 08 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1556 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

    📅 08 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1556 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1.
    • Recent findings suggest that over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way.
    • The first message is where I spend my effort.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

    Recent findings suggest that over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

    The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

    Sources indicate that A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub challenges made the fallback trainer risky.

    According to recent reports, two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

    Sources indicate that at the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

    You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

    According to recent reports, A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

    In a recent development, on the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

    Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App.

    Sources indicate that image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

    It has been revealed that the agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

    Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App.

    Recent findings suggest that ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

    According to recent reports, training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

    Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App.

    No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

    It has been revealed that before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

    Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

    Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App.

    It has been revealed that training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

    Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena.

    It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

    I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

    Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE.

    These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

    ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

    If you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace. We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Not many of the deals went through, but Chinese clouds no longer care about importing GPUs.
    • The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) allowed Nvidia and AMD to sell hundreds of thousands of advanced GPUs to entities that the Department of War classifies as “Chinese military companies” that help Beijing to build its military.
    • That news comes courtesy of Brian Mast, chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, who asked BIS to provide information about NVIDIA’s and AMD’s applications for the export licenses required to sell advanced AI chips to China.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Not many of the deals went through, but Chinese clouds no longer care about importing GPUs.

    The US Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) allowed Nvidia and AMD to sell hundreds of thousands of advanced GPUs to entities that the Department of War classifies as “Chinese military companies” that help Beijing to build its military.

    That news comes courtesy of Brian Mast, chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, who asked BIS to provide information about NVIDIA’s and AMD’s applications for the export licenses required to sell advanced AI chips to China.

    The congressman on Thursday revealed requests to sell 3.4 million AI chips to China, and that BIS approved the sale of 879,000 items.

    BIS refused to authorize some giant deals for Nvidia, which applied to sell 610,000 chips to Alibaba and 508,000 to TikTok owner Bytedance.

    But the agency allowed many other sales, including to Alibaba and Tencent.

    Mast points out that both of those companies are on the Department of War’s List of Chinese Military Companies, the designation it uses for entities deemed to be a “military-civil fusion contributor to the Chinese defense industrial base.” That’s a polite way of saying that Washington thinks China relies on these companies to operate and improve its military, and therefore to challenge America’s national security.

    Advanced chips are essential when designing nuclear weapons, stealthy submarines, or advanced aircraft.

    Those applications are the core reason the US bans exports of advanced GPUs to China, so that the People’s Liberation Army can’t develop advanced weapons.

    The congressman also claims that some of Nvidia’s applications were attempts to sell its wares to “chip-smuggling fronts to facilitate their sales of advanced AI chips to Chinese companies.” The Latest York Times reports that some of those front entities are linked to Megaspeed, the outfit fronted by suspected Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang, whose intimate relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a key factor in his resignation.

    Megaspeed is accused of what the US calls “diversion” – claiming to buy chips for one reason while intending to either ship them to China or rent them exclusively to Chinese companies in ways that breach the spirit of export restrictions if not the letter of the law.

    One of the documents Mast shared states “Every Nvidia and AMD application stated that the proposed transfer posed a ‘low’ risk of diversion.”.

    Mast’s point therefore appears to be that the BIS has authorized sales that go against the clear intent of established policy, and the national interest, and that Nvidia and AMD may have been a little too optimistic in their assessment of diversion risk.

    Earlier this week, Washington adopted a latest policy that outlaws allowing remote access to advanced AI chips, in the hope it would stop diversion and dent China’s AI ambitions.

    Two Chinese tech giants, Tencent and Alibaba, have signaled the policy had immediate impact.

    Chinese web giant Tencent on Wednesday noted that newly introduced ban will reduce the quantity of advanced compute capacity available to the company and mean its efforts to train models will slow.

    Alibaba offered similar sentiments on Thursday. Speaking on the company’s earnings call, CEO Eddie Wu said the latest policy “will definitely have some impact on the long-term construction of Alibaba Cloud's data centers both domestically and globally.”.

    “Based on our initial assessment, the long-term target of 20 gigawatts may be lowered, which will also lead to a reduction in our overall capital expenditure plan,” he remarked.

    But both Tencent and Alibaba don’t see the new policy as creating long-term problems, because both companies believe Chinese chipmakers will be making advanced AI hardware at scale in 2027 or 2028.

    Alibaba’s Wu predicted his manufacturer “will go through a phase of the largest investment in AI infrastructure” once Chinese chipmakers get up to speed.

    Once that happens, Nvidia and AMD may not even be able to sell chips to China through backdoors.

    And for what it’s worth, even after the two sultans of silicon went through the front door by asking BIS for permission, many of the approved orders never resulted in shipments.

    Industry observers note that that’s likely because Beijing needs to approve imports and chose not to do so while its own chipmakers develop improved products. ®.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device.
    • LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA.
    • It has been revealed that pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

    LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

    It has been revealed that pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:.

    In a recent development, we evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

    *All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

    For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

    These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

    LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

    Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

    According to recent reports, GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

    Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

    Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):.

    It has been revealed that serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:.

    The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

    Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:.

    We can't wait to see what you build.

    If you use this work, please cite the release blog:.

    Big Tech's compliance with EU market rules is performative, consumer group notes

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • BEUC urges Brussels to impose tougher penalties over alleged barriers to switching services and controlling personal data.
    • Massive Tech has earned a finger-wagging from the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC), which indicates the industry's compliance with the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) still leaves consumers short of meaningful choice.
    • BEUC said: "Major Tech companies Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, ByteDance, Meta and Microsoft (so-called 'gatekeepers') still likely breach the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) far too often for consumers to reap the full benefits of real choice over their digital services and products.".
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    BEUC urges Brussels to impose tougher penalties over alleged barriers to switching services and controlling personal data.

    Massive Tech has earned a finger-wagging from the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC), which indicates the industry's compliance with the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) still leaves consumers short of meaningful choice.

    BEUC said: "Major Tech companies Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, ByteDance, Meta and Microsoft (so-called 'gatekeepers') still likely breach the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) far too often for consumers to reap the full benefits of real choice over their digital services and products.".

    The European Commission designated the six companies as gatekeepers in 2023, imposing obligations on specified core platform services such as search engines, messaging services, and app stores. The DMA aims to make digital markets fairer and more open to competition.

    The devil is in the details. In the years since, the EC has lined up Amazon and Microsoft's cloud businesses for gatekeeper status. In March 2025, the Commission issued preliminary findings against Alphabet over Search and Google Play, while separately specifying measures Apple had to take to meet its interoperability obligations. In 2024, Microsoft's browser rivals argued that Edge should also be covered by the DMA's gatekeeper obligations, and so on.

    BEUC is a fan of the act – it published a report on its consumer benefits in 2025 – but is less impressed with industry's implementation. Its latest analysis draws together evidence of potential breaches submitted to the Commission between June 2025 and June 2026.

    It has been revealed that in the case of Microsoft, BEUC stated that the firm used "behavioural techniques" and "non-neutral interfaces" to elicit consent from users for data sharing across services – emphasizing benefits, while not explaining why a user might want to decline. The Windows behemoth is also accused of making it tricky to change defaults and stop behavior such as apps opening links in Edge or using Bing as a search engine.

    "Microsoft also regularly prompts owners who have selected an alternative browser or search engine to switch to Edge or Bing using increasingly subliminal techniques, such as prompts coming from the device manufacturer, which undermine effective compliance with the DMA," BEUC remarked.

    Then there's Google, which was fined €890 million in July for favoring its own services in Search and restricting developers' ability to direct Play Store customers to alternative purchasing channels. As with Microsoft, BEUC expressed concerns about the non-neutral language Google used to obtain user consent, as well as how it allegedly made it difficult to change default settings or uninstall gatekeeper applications.

    The alleged behavior of Apple, ByteDance, Amazon, and Meta was also highlighted, with examples including Apple's restrictions on alternative app distribution and Amazon using interface design techniques to nudge people into handing over their data.

    Apple unveiled new terms for developers earlier this year in response to its App Store dispute with the European Commission, but BEUC noted it was "concerned that the new terms do not resolve fundamental non-compliance complications.".

    Google did not respond to requests for comment from The Register. A Microsoft spokesperson told us: "We are continuing to engage with the Commission and industry at large to ensure Microsoft's designated platforms comply fully with the DMA.".

    It has been revealed that an Amazon spokesperson told The Register “Our consent experience is clear and gives customers informed choice about how their personal information is used across Amazon services. We see that in practice.

    “A seller that uses Amazon Stores in the EU can offer the same products on any third-party online marketplace or its own direct to customer website at any price, without affecting their eligibility to be highlighted as the Featured Offer. This is set out clearly in our DMA Compliance Report.”.

    It has been revealed that BEUC director general Agustín Reyna said: "The era of cosmetic compliance must end. It is high time the Commission holds gatekeepers to account and imposes dissuasive penalties in all cases where they bypass the DMA's rules.".

    The report has been shared with the Commission. Whether BEUC's allegations lead to further findings of non-compliance or penalties is now a matter for the regulator. ®.

    Ruby2Shell (GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5)

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (336 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Verialabs

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that the bug is reachable from the following frameworks in their default configuration.
    • These products bundle their own Ruby, so the fix has to come from the vendor.
    • Upgrade Ruby to a fixed release: 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that the bug is reachable from the following frameworks in their default configuration. Other frameworks are not exposed by default, but application code that upcases strings received in a legacy encoding may also be vulnerable.

    These products bundle their own Ruby, so the fix has to come from the vendor. Products marked Vulnerable have no fixed release yet: every current version is vulnerable.

    Updated 20 November 2026 at 15:00 UTC.

    Upgrade Ruby to a fixed release: 3.3.14, 3.4.13 or 4.0.10.

    Install the vendor's fixed release. See Self-hosted software for fixed versions of popular products.

    Most of Ruby's single-byte encodings have no capital Ã. Upcasing it writes two bytes, SS, but the loop only bounds-checks one (to < to_end).

    The output buffer is allocated as the input length plus 20 bytes. Each Ã adds one byte to the output, so an input with 21 of them overflows the buffer by one byte.

    It has been revealed that the same loop is in several ISO-8859 and Windows-125x encodings and has been there since Ruby 2.4.0. It is reached by upcase, swapcase, downcase(:fold) and casecmp?.

    UTF-8 strings take a different code path and are not affected.

    Fixed upstream in ruby/ruby@d582f8f.

    According to recent reports, A one-byte heap overflow. The byte written is S (0x53) when upcasing or s (0x73) when case-folding, and it lands directly after the output buffer. The attacker controls the size of the buffer through the input length.

    Copying the result out of the buffer then reads one byte out of bounds.

    We'll be publishing a proof of concept demonstrating remote code execution on stock Rails on 25 November 2026, or later if major vendors have not shipped a fix by then.

    Veria Labs found this vulnerability independently and was the first to demonstrate remote code execution.

    It has been revealed that the Ruby security advisory also credits Stephan Lipp (Ada Logics) and Anthropic with reporting the underlying primitive. Additional discoverers include Moritz Sanft in collaboration with OpenAI.

    Breaking: Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers

    📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1696 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one.
    • Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:.
    • You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

    Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:.

    You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

    Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):.

    Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:.

    According to recent reports, FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

    Industry observers note that pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

    In a recent development, with several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:.

    Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

    Recent findings suggest that boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

    Sources indicate that for edits, each region states where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

    This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:.

    Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

    In a recent development, black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

    For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

    FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

    Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:.

    To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:.

    --gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

    In a recent development, A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

    For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

    See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

    In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

    End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:.

    Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

    A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call.

    Recent findings suggest that let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:.

    Industry observers note that FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

    The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

    Recent findings suggest that so one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

    Industry observers note that the text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

    Industry observers note that this gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

    The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:.

    The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

    According to recent reports, in stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

    At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

    Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

    Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

    In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

    Recent findings suggest that in FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

    According to recent reports, the noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

    In a recent development, the distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

    Sources indicate that attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:.

    Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

    FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

    At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:.

    In a recent development, the fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

    If you are latest to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

    FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

    You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

    get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

    Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

    The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:.

    Built something with FLUX.3? Share your LoRAs and pipelines on the Hub. We'd love to see them! 😎.

    #11374. Farcall, a terminal-ready Rust PC+DOS emulator

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2801 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dialup ↗ Open Full Page

    Farcall, a terminal-ready Rust PC+DOS emulator

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2801 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dialup

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that I was curious what it would take to write an x86 emulator, so I wrote Farcall, presently an emulator for the original IBM PC and its 8088 CPU.
    • At the launcher, choose a disk to insert, press Enter, and type PLAY at the DOS prompt.
    • Coming back from the Vintage Computer Festival Midwest in September, I had a random thought—why not try writing my own x86 emulator?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that I was curious what it would take to write an x86 emulator, so I wrote Farcall, presently an emulator for the original IBM PC and its 8088 CPU. You can SSH into it and land in DOS, where you can experience fun programs including Zork, NetHack, GW-BASIC, Sopwith, and Digger Remastered.

    Try it for yourself in your terminal:.

    At the launcher, choose a disk to insert, press Enter, and type PLAY at the DOS prompt. Press Ctrl-] to return to the launcher.

    Coming back from the Vintage Computer Festival Midwest in September, I had a random thought—why not try writing my own x86 emulator? How hard could it be? I’d always assumed that writing an entire x86 emulator was a lot of work, but attending VCF gave me a hankering to learn more deeply how things work under the hood on computers in my vintage computing niche, but also the computers I use every day.

    According to recent reports, in 1978, Intel released the 8086 chip that introduced the x86 architecture. The 1981 IBM Personal Computer used a variant, the 8088, and is the ancestor of PCs as we know them today. I picked up my very own early-model IBM PC a few years ago. It boots into PC-DOS, and runs programs off 5¼ inch floppy disks (mine has no hard drive). The Monochrome Display Adapter and the IBM 5151 monitor display its beautiful green-on-black text. The only input device is the famously clicky Model F keyboard.

    An IBM PC, just like my own, that I saw recently at The National Museum of Computing in Bletchley Park, England.

    It has been revealed that as a concrete target, I decided to emulate the 8088, as that’s the chip in my IBM PC. I am by far not the first person to do this—there are far more capable emulators for the IBM PC, including MartyPC, DOSBox, and 86Box. This was very much meant as a personal education mission for me.[1].

    My first naive thought was that I needed to implement each of the instructions of the 8088. I knew I wanted it to boot DOS, run programs on it, and eventually boot Windows 3.1 (one of my favorite operating systems of the era). But I didn’t realize quite how much there would be to get to that point.

    I set out by trying to run COM files. COM is DOS’s simple executable format (you may recognize it from hits like COMMAND.COM, FORMAT.COM and indeed, WIN.COM if you ever typed “win” at the command line to start Windows). I started with a simple COM program that prints “Hello World” to the console as my first target.

    Sources indicate that my emulator, which I’m calling Farcall, started off very simply: a Rust command-line program running on my Mac, that reads in the bytes of a COM file from disk, and decodes and executes each instruction in a loop. Each instruction in the 8088 has an opcode byte (a number from 0x00 to 0xFF), optionally followed by more bytes.[2] (This is different from many RISC architectures like Arm64 where every instruction is the same width). For example:.

    Farcall reads in the opcode (50, B0, or 83 above), and then however many additional bytes are necessary to interpret that type of instruction.

    If there were any opcodes that my emulator didn’t recognize, it would panic, and print out the unsupported opcode. I soon got into a rhythm: I would implement one instruction, run the program, and see where it next stopped. I just needed to do this ~300 more times, for each of the instruction forms.

    To keep track of my todo list, I printed out the full list of instructions from Intel’s 8086 Family People Manual, and put a blue check mark next to each instruction as I implemented it.

    Even from my “Hello World”, I realized that it’s not enough to implement the CPU’s instructions. The x86 has an INT (interrupt) instruction that looks up an address in the interrupt vector table and calls the handler there. On the IBM PC, these handlers are typically set up by the BIOS or DOS. My “Hello World” used INT 21h to ask DOS to write a string to the screen, so in addition to implementing the CPU’s INT instruction, I had to also emulate the DOS service to write the string.

    It has been revealed that once my Hello World COM program worked, I repeated this process a few more times with some other simple programs. And then I found out that Microsoft open-sourced some versions of MS-DOS a few years ago, so I set my sights on running MS-DOS 2.0’s MORE.COM (the pager), as my first “real” program. While it was a bit of a slog with all the instructions I had to implement, it was still an incredibly rewarding cycle–with each new instruction, the program would run just a bit more, and hundreds of instructions would fly across my screen as they were executed.

    I also implemented part of INT 10h—the BIOS’s Video service, which MORE.COM uses to learn about the current screen dimensions, etc. So now I was emulating a small subset of yet another layer, the BIOS. With that, though, MORE.COM ran properly—a DOS program seemingly running in the macOS terminal.

    My eventual goal is to run Windows 3.1 on Farcall. However, one of the many steps before that is to get DOS to boot, since Windows 3.1 runs on top of it.

    It has been revealed that in order to do that, I knew that I needed to deal with boot sectors—some code at the beginning of a disk that typically loads an operating system. I own a bunch of 5¼ inch floppy disks that came with my IBM PC with software for it. I took an image of my PC-DOS 2.0 floppy, and added a “boot” mode to the emulator that would take an image and execute its boot sector, instead of a COM file.

    When a PC boots from a floppy, the BIOS reads the first sector (512 bytes) into memory and executes the instructions in it. On my PC-DOS diskette, those instructions start loading DOS. Methodically, I implemented even more of the 8088’s instructions (about 200 more), and several interrupts that a BIOS would normally listen for, including keyboard support, video handling (the simplest 80x25 text mode), and reading from a floppy disk. With some persistence, I got to the point where the boot sector transferred control to the system files (IBMBIO.COM and IBMDOS.COM), and eventually to COMMAND.COM.

    Getting DOS to boot was a bit of a relief—before this point my emulator was performing the work of the CPU, the BIOS, and DOS; now I could stop handling INT 21h myself and let the emulation run DOS’s real handler.

    It also opened up the kinds of programs I could run. Multiplan, a spreadsheet program from 1982 (Microsoft’s answer to VisiCalc, the world’s first “killer app”) was the first one I got running, by implementing a bunch more instructions, and supporting 16-color text mode to let Multiplan's beautiful magenta-on-blue palette shine through.

    So far I had been emulating a BIOS by intercepting interrupts to e.g. the Video, Keyboard, and Disk services. This was easier for me to get started, because in the emulator code I have free rein over memory and the CPU’s registers and I can talk directly to the frontend, and I can write only the specific missing pieces until things work.

    However, it was also limiting—the subset I’d built was just enough to boot DOS 2.0 and 3.3, but there are a lot more BIOS services, each with its own quirks and features, and the ones I had weren’t enough to boot FreeDOS, for instance. And around the same time, I discovered GLaBIOS, a modern and open-source BIOS implementation that runs on real IBM PCs.

    According to recent reports, while using someone else’s BIOS sounds easier than emulating one, it actually increased the scope of the emulator quite a bit: to support an actual BIOS ROM, you now need to emulate all the hardware the BIOS expects to talk to! This was where my naivety became clearer—I didn’t realize just how much peripheral hardware is inside an IBM PC. I knew there was a floppy drive, video card, and keyboard, of course, but I didn’t realize there’s also a Programmable Peripheral Interface (PPI), Programmable Interval Timer (PIT), and a Direct Memory Access (DMA) controller.

    In a recent development, there’s a lot I had to learn about how each of these peripherals work together. For instance, I didn’t know that the floppy disk controller works with the DMA controller to read data from a disk into memory. Thankfully, there are some great resources like the MartyPC PC Emulation Book, the datasheets for the Intel chips, and previous versions of MIT’s 6.828 course website.

    I eventually implemented enough of each of these devices that I got GLaBIOS to boot. Seeing the BIOS go through its POST sequence, and then deposit me at the DOS prompt, gave me a great sense of satisfaction. And now, because the devices were actually implemented, I could focus on improving the fidelity of the graphics.

    Until then, I’d only supported text output, which is all that my own IBM PC can do, since it has the Monochrome Display Adapter. But the video card can be upgraded, like to one that supports CGA, known for its iconic color palettes like magenta-cyan-white. I decided I wanted to add CGA’s graphics mode so I could run programs with color graphics.

    Sources indicate that to do this, I needed to convert the bytes that programs write to video memory into RGB pixels for the Farcall frontend. Quite naturally, I expected the horizontal lines of pixels, or scanlines, to be stored in order: 0, 1, 2, 3. Here’s what Sopwith looked like when I interpreted video memory that way:.

    Sopwith, when reading video memory lines contiguously.

    Both the monochrome and color graphics cards are built around the Motorola MC6845 chip, a Cathode Ray Tube Controller (CRTC). This controller was designed around rows of text. As it draws the screen, the CRTC outputs two numbers: a memory address that tells the card where to fetch the current character, and a scanline number to select which horizontal slice of that character to draw.

    Sources indicate that for 320x200 graphics, IBM couldn’t simply set the CRTC to output 200 rows of one scanline each, because the register that sets the number of character rows is only 7 bits wide, so it maxes out at 127. Instead, the engineers configured it to return 100 rows of 2 scanlines each, and wired the CRTC’s two outputs to build the address at which each pixel’s data could be found in video memory.

    CGA has 16 KiB of video memory, split into two 8 KiB halves. The card uses the CRTC’s memory address to select a location within one of those halves. Both scanlines in a pair use the same relative location, but the card wires the scanline number (0 or 1) to bit 13 of the final address. Because 213 = 8192, the second scanline starts 8 KiB after the first. So the first half of memory holds scanlines 0, 2, 4, and so on, and the second half holds 1, 3, 5, etc. Once the scanlines are interpreted that way, Sopwith looked correct:.

    Sopwith, reading video memory correctly with 8 KiB offset.

    I started Farcall as a terminal program that could run COM files in my macOS terminal. There was something attractive about seeing an old DOS program running in a modern terminal, as opposed to in a graphical window like a normal VM hypervisor.

    Industry observers note that this worked great for text-mode programs, but I wanted to go further to see if I could render CGA graphics-mode programs directly in the terminal too. I learned that the terminal emulator I use, Ghostty, supports the Kitty graphics protocol, which allows terminal applications to display inline images. I figured I could try using this to stream each frame from the guest’s video memory. And it turns out this works—though it feels like it’s at the edge of what the protocol and Ghostty’s implementation are meant to support. (e.g. I found I could reliably crash Ghostty when sending zlib frames, and a change in a recent version of Ghostty made frames flicker).

    Now that I could display graphics-mode programs like Sopwith in the terminal, I wanted to share this experience of “running DOS in your terminal” with others, so I decided to put an installation of my emulator on a public SSH server. An increasing number of iconic DOS programs of the era are now being made open source by their owners (including MS-DOS itself as I mentioned, but also programs like GW-BASIC, Zork, and Sopwith), so I decided to put those in the environment for anyone to try.

    As I was preparing to launch the SSH service, one issue I needed to solve was that of performance. Even though I was emulating a processor operating at 4.77 MHz on a VPS with a shared CPU supposedly running at 2.4 GHz, I was only able to fit 6 or so instances of Farcall running Sopwith per core before the emulation started dropping frames.

    There were a couple things that were contributing to unnecessary CPU usage. Firstly, before every step of the emulation, I was checking the clock to see if it was time to pause emulation and handle some input/draw the screen. In profiling the code using a sample program, I found that fetching monotonic time (Instant::now() in Rust) was actually using ~43% of CPU time. Making the loop only check every 128 steps removed this bottleneck. (Note that this didn’t change the fact that the emulator is nowhere near cycle-accurate, or properly emulating how long each instruction or hardware operation takes; I’m pretending that every instruction takes equal time, for example).

    It has been revealed that another culprit was in my Kitty graphics code. Each frame is sent down as a separate PNG image.[3] At first I was sending full-color RGB PNGs, which was contributing to a significant amount of CPU usage in preparing each frame. However, by switching to 4-bit indexed (palette) images (which works perfectly given that you can only use one of 16 colors in CGA in normal circumstances[4]), I was able to save more than 70% of CPU time in preparing the frames.

    Industry observers note that I was surprised just how much I’ve learned from this project in such a short period of time. I’ve been using computers since the 90s and am familiar with words like IRQs, DMA, and Cylinders/Heads/Sectors—but it wasn’t until I had to implement them in software that I truly appreciated them for what they are. It was also a fantastic refresher for how CPUs work at the instruction level, which feels a lot more concrete now. On the other hand, I was not ready for how rapidly “emulating a CPU” ballooned into “emulating a whole computer including all its peripherals”.

    As for what’s next: My emulator is far from complete, and I still have a goal of running Windows 3.1. Probably the biggest hurdle in the way is support for protected mode, and emulating a 286. (Windows 3.0 is easier to run in this regard, since it supports the 8088, and still supported real mode). Even before that, I need to support hard drives, as well as a newer graphics mode like EGA or VGA. There’s a lot to do—but I look forward to learning a lot more about how computers work along the way!

    You can try out Farcall yourself on a standard SSH client. You will unlock the full graphical experience on terminal emulators that support Kitty graphics like Ghostty, Kitty, iTerm2, and Konsole.

    In a recent development, at the launcher, choose a disk to insert, press Enter, and type PLAY at the DOS prompt. Press Ctrl-] to return to the launcher.

    The source code is licensed under the MIT license and is available at https://github.com/keito/farcall. Provenance of the programs on the SSH server is available here.

    It has been revealed that I wrote the code for the emulator by hand. I used Codex to help write unit tests and some test programs, and perform research. ↩.

    An opcode is optionally preceded by one or more prefixes, which can do things like repeat the instruction. ↩.

    I initially sent zlib-compressed pixels, but it kept crashing Ghostty, caused by a bug in the Zig DEFLATE library, so I switched to sending PNG images. This bug is fixed in the latest Ghostty after they switched to Wuffs. ↩.

    Recent findings suggest that this is why I care about open ISAs. I like the Arm ISA, really I do, but it's a product one company rents out. Arm tried to make Qualcomm destroy the Nuvia core designs (and lost). And look at Apple: the userspace is plain AArch64, but everything around it is undocumented Apple-only weirdness. Custom interrupt controller, custom boot chain, secret GPU. Asahi has to reverse-engineer every new chip, and M3 support only just landed this month, still with no GPU acceleration. That's the kind of lock-in an architecture license lets you build.

    RISC-V and Power are royalty-free, and there's no single company to buy, sue or headhunt. Until Arm is in that category, I'm backing RISC-V or Power ISAs and I'm staying on x86-64 ISA until one of those two open ISAs takes off. x86-64 isn't an open standard on paper, but the baseline (x86-64-v1) AMD Athlon 64 patents have expired, and x86 has 40+ years of inertia and a long line of non-Intel implementations behind it: Cyrix, Transmeta, VIA, Zhaoxin. Compaq clean-rooming the IBM BIOS is why the PC platform is open in the first place. Used x86-64 servers are a dime a dozen on eBay, and I can scrounge a working CPU pretty much anywhere on the planet, even on an island like Hawaii, without anybody's permission or a working supply chain.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    ‘I gave up at least $6,000 and I’d do it again’.

    Welcome to Friday and therefore to another edition of On Call, The Register's reader-contributed tech support column in which we share your tales of cleaning up messes made by clients and colleagues.

    This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Dennis" who told us he once ran a tech support business in a major US city.

    "I got a call from a very well-known lawyer's office," he told On Call. "Over the two decades I spent supporting his office, this attorney and I became close friends.".

    The attorney was also a good client because Dennis found himself billing a three-figure sum every month for malware removal that resulted from the lawyer’s – ahem – personal browsing habits.

    Dennis eventually tired of malware removal and told his client to expect a substantial bill for the iMac he was about to buy as a replacement for his PC.

    "I told him this would pay for itself in 18 months," Dennis wrote, because he figured it wouldn't get malware all the time.

    "He actually stated, with genuine concern: 'If you do that, you will make less money'.".

    Dennis replied that he aimed to give his clients the best advice, and that on this occasion his counsel was to pay Apple instead of himself!

    According to recent reports, "It took him about five years to stumble across anything that could harm that iMac," Dennis wrote. "When he did, I had no idea what to do: I had never seen an infected Apple product.".

    So he did what all tech support people do: reinstalled the OS and crossed his fingers.

    Dennis was rewarded when the machine came back to life, with all data and settings intact.

    Recent findings suggest that "I had given up at least $6,000 in support revenue by solving his problem and I'd do it again," he wrote, before winding up his story by letting us know "I retired five years ago. It’s still on his desk!".

    Have you done less tech support to deliver more value? If so, click here to send On Call an email and charge us with the responsibility of telling your story on a future Friday. ®.

    Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

    📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3054 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta.
    • Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.
    • Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

    Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

    Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post indicates you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

    Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

    The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

    In a recent development, muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

    In a recent development, the language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

    Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

    Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

    Recent findings suggest that A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

    In a recent development, muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

    Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

    The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

    Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

    According to recent reports, the Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

    Sources indicate that use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

    You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

    Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

    The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

    It has been revealed that video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:.

    As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

    Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

    Industry observers note that the Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

    If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:.

    The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

    You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead.

    Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/upcoming/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint.

    You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section highlights how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

    First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:.

    In the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

    According to recent reports, now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

    Recent findings suggest that the core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

    Then we can run this command across each node:.

    Recent findings suggest that we trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

    Muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

    We combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

    According to recent reports, we initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.
