    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

    📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3314 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face!
    • It has been revealed that beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases.
    • Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the fresh US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

    It has been revealed that beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

    Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post highlights you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

    Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:.

    If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

    Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

    Industry observers note that the decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

    Inside the attention block (both layer types).

    The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

    It has been revealed that attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

    In a recent development, the first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

    The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

    Industry observers note that only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

    If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

    The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

    Industry observers note that beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

    It has been revealed that every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

    Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

    These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

    Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

    According to recent reports, the most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

    A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

    Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

    Install the latest version of transformers.

    The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:.

    Sources indicate that the pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

    Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

    Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

    Recent findings suggest that pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

    In a recent development, beam's config defines an expert-parallel blueprint. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:.

    Industry observers note that launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

    Sources indicate that beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:.

    Industry observers note that for faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:.

    Recent findings suggest that both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

    Sources indicate that beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:.

    According to recent reports, on Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):.

    Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

    We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

    It has been revealed that below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

    * Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

    Industry observers note that † Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

    Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

    You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

    The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

    The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

    Industry observers note that after one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

    In a recent development, training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

    Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can patch the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the upcoming weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

    The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:.

    Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

    Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

    Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

    Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

    Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

    Sources indicate that evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

    The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

    You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

    Industry observers note that if you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

    At Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

    Industry observers note that we asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

    Sources indicate that we used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

    According to recent reports, you can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

    Recent findings suggest that we wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

    For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

    Our score-versus-latency plot indicates the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

    You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

    Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

    We wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

    Industry observers note that first, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

    For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

    If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

    In a recent development, beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

    Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

    In a recent development, that’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

    Recent findings suggest that thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

    Industry observers note that this is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

    According to recent reports, one question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

    Also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

    #11359. Latest Update: Lisp Game Jam devlog: Polydraw

    Latest Update: Lisp Game Jam devlog: Polydraw

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1955 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Spritely

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that this year's Autumn Lisp Game Jam has just wrapped up!
    • The rest of this post is a daily devlog of how we made Polydraw so you can see what the process look likes to make a game with Goblins and Hoot under a tight deadline.
    • First, we created a Git repository on Codeberg and copied the Hoot game jam template into it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that this year's Autumn Lisp Game Jam has just wrapped up! Spritely's contribution to the jam was Polydraw, a peer-to-peer party game that is easy to pick up and play with friends. In Polydraw, players take turns being the artist who draws an image based on a prompt. The catch is that the artist only has 60 seconds and can only draw using triangles. All of the other players are guessers who try to correctly guess the prompt. We're quite pleased with how the game turned out!

    The rest of this post is a daily devlog of how we made Polydraw so you can see what the process look likes to make a game with Goblins and Hoot under a tight deadline.

    It's go time! First, we created a Git repository on Codeberg and copied the Hoot game jam template into it.

    Since the core activity in Polydraw is drawing triangles, the first thing Dave implemented was an interface for doing that on a canvas. This first version was crude and didn't include a color picker.

    We took the weekend off to prepare for a busy week ahead.

    This is the day that we really got to work on the game jam.

    Industry observers note that the first version of the triangle editor stored pixel coordinates of the local canvas, but that wasn't going to be good enough to display on other machines with different sized canvases. So, Dave simply normalized triangle vertices into the [0,1] range so each peer could scale them as needed.

    Dave also implemented a basic scene system, a common game programming pattern, to encapsulate the coarse game states such as the title screen, the lobby, and the main game.

    A color palette was added along with some additional mockup UI around the canvas.

    With a good enough game engine in place, we turned our attention to the game protocol. Since we are using Goblins, all interactions are modeled using actors. Dave came up with the following actors:.

    Player: Used for player identity within the game and contains the player's self-proposed name.

    Sources indicate that lobby: The place where players gather before the game starts. The player that creates the lobby is the host and all other players are guests.

    Game: Holds all of the game state like the player list, whose turn it is, and the scoreboard.

    It has been revealed that controller: A player's virtual game controller. Used to speak to the game actor, but all actions are scoped to the individual player.

    A test script was written to simulate creating a game, joining the lobby, and playing a round. At this stage, everything was happening in a single process. Goblins makes it easy to start with a single process and then distribute the actors to multiple machines later.

    It has been revealed that now it was time to get the actors onto the network and hook them up to the game UI. For networking we used OCapN, naturally. Jessica started up an instance of our new end-to-end encrypted relay netlayer that we set as the default relay so the game would "just work" when we uploaded it to itch.io. In fact, dogfooding the relay was a large part of the motivation behind participating in the game jam in the first place!

    In a recent development, dave got the actors online with OCapN and connected the game UI to the actors, then confirmed that a three player game works. Three players is the minimum number of players needed to trigger OCapN's third-party handoff feature. Handoffs are what enable distributed networking in OCapN: Alice can give Bob a reference to Carol, which causes Bob and Carol to establish a newly introduced OCapN session with each other. This is the first application we've made that does handoffs over the relay netlayer and it was nice to see them working as intended.

    Unfortunately, we discovered an issue with how Goblins handles two peers connecting to each other concurrently, a problem known as "crossed hellos". OCapN mandates that only one connection may be open between any two peers, so we have to pick which connection wins. The bug is that any promises that were created over the losing connection never resolve. This was observed in the game as an empty lobby player list that should be populated. It didn't prevent the rest of the game from working, though, so we didn't try to fix it (yet).

    Sources indicate that on this day, Dave discovered that, despite his best efforts, he fell victim to the "identity footgun". We could write a whole blog post series about the many subtle issues of object identity (in the sense of Scheme's eq?) in object capability systems, but instead we'll refer you to the The Grant Matcher Puzzle and just mention that using object references as keys in associative data structures is error-prone. A promise that eventually resolves to a reference to Alice is not identical (again, in the eq? sense) to a reference to Alice. So, if you accidentally use a promise as a key somewhere or use eq? directly you will probably have a bad time, which is exactly what happened to us.

    To deal with this identity crisis, Dave first detected it at runtime by writing a wrapper around eq? called geq?. This fresh predicate throws an error when comparing a promise to a non-promise. Then he used the resulting backtraces to find the offending code and change it to resolve all necessary promises before doing identity comparisons.

    Christine finally cleared enough other things off her plate where she could start contributing to the game. We thought it would be nice to have the game start with a splash screen of triangle'y animations that would resemble the kinds of art players would make in the game. We decided to use the Blender add-on by Ursula Kurdali named Stop Motion since it gives a great amount of freedom to animate by creating and destroying as much geometry as you like. Christine made the first mockup of a splash screen animation of a "death" type character swinging a scythe.

    However, the animation hadn't left Blender yet. We're gonna have to figure out how to get those polygons out and into the game engine!

    This was the day to finish implementing the core game loop. We wanted the weekend to be all about fixing bugs and making it look and feel as good as we can. At last, the points awarded at the end of each round were displayed in the UI. The player list on the left side of the screen was transformed into a leaderboard that sorted players by score.

    Sources indicate that while creating the leaderboard it was discovered that Goblins was not correctly parsing pairs received over OCapN. Christine swooped in with a quick fix and Jessica folowed up with a regression test.

    According to recent reports, we also added a small set of emoji reactions underneath the leaderboard. Reactions were not critical to the core gameplay but they were planned from the very beginning of the project. It's good that we had time to add them because it was a lot of fun to spam emojis at the artist to give them an indication of how good or bad they were doing.

    With two days left and the core gameplay loop complete, the focus shifted to bug fixing and adding juice. Up until this point the HTML was mostly unstyled (as you can see in the videos above), so Dave added a little CSS to improve the look and feel.

    Sources indicate that A playtest revealed that the simple PRNG we were using was implemented incorrectly. We noticed because the artist prompt was always "bus" no matter how many rounds you played. Oops! This was fixed.

    Remember that crossed hellos bug from day 7? Dave finally implemented a workaround, which was to simply throw out the first pancake and try again, as suggested by Christine. A simple race against a timeout was all that was needed. We'll be thinking about how to fix this in Goblins so this situation cannot happen in the future.

    Christine started work on making more animations for the game's intro. The "death" animation was a good "hello world" for testing the exporter, but being all black it was too simple to make sure everything worked right; draw order, etc, didn't matter. Christine made a "square guys" animation as a kind of Acid2 test equivalent. This file had several tricky properties to it, most especially that draw order would matter, colors would be crucial, et cetera.

    Christine also made this triangle'y duck themed piece:.

    It has been revealed that christine wrote a Python script to export the animations from Blender into a custom format encoded using Syrup. The encoded data was then embedded into the Scheme program as bytevector literals using a little script. Dave then started work on a renderer for these animations, but it wasn't working quite well enough by the end of the day to commit and push it.

    According to recent reports, up until this point we only had a small number of frequently-repeated words. Morgan Lemmer-Webber curated a word list for us, starting with an existing public domain word list of 5000 words, and curated down to a 621 words, selecting for words that were more feasible to draw (ranging from easy to challenging, but all trying to be feasible).

    The game name was changed from the placeholder "Twenty Triangles" to "Polydraw".

    The code to render animations was finished. Some final minor bug fixes were made. Some CSS was tweaked. Original music and sound effects by encrypted.whispers were added. Additionally, we used a few CC0-licensed sound effects by Kenney.

    Sources indicate that A few gameplay improvements were made, such as showing guessers what the prompt was when the round ends and how many triangles the artist had remaining. Little improvements can make a significant difference and both of these changes were very helpful for players and made the game feel more polished.

    There wasn't enough time remaining to do as much work on resiliency in the face of network partitions as we would have liked, but Dave did squeeze in a commit that allowed the game to survive if a guest leaves. Unfortunately, the experience for the disconnected guest isn't very good as they don't see any message that their connection dropped.

    It has been revealed that we did a final playtest to confirm that there weren't any showstopper bugs. Christine added final splash animations.

    Finally, Christine added some code (fixed up by Dave) and animations which would overlay over the drawings indicating that drawing was starting, it was time to guess, or the results.

    In a recent development, we submitted the game two hours before the deadline! Now it was time to catch our breath and show off the game to everyone we could. Dave even played it live with a couple other people on a stream! Here's a screenshot which gives you a good look of the final result:.

    It has been revealed that the response was quite positive! The feedback we received closely matched the things we wanted to improve upon if we had more time: better disconnect handling, a way for the host to skip to the next phase instead of being forced to wait for the timer to run out, and invite URLs (rather than URIs) that auto-join the game when visited.

    Polydraw ranked 5th overall in the official game jam results.

    Try playing it over on itch.io and leave us a comment!

    Your support makes our work possible! If you like what we do, please consider becoming a Spritely supporter today!

    Industry News: Redict deprecated in favor of Valkey

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (172 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Lwn

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Drew DeVault has declared that Redict, a fork of Redis that was created in response to Redis's 2024 license change, has been deprecated.
    • According to recent reports, I had hoped to rally the Redis diaspora around a copyleft initiative, to protect ourselves from future rug-pulls, and made Redict to serve this purpose.
    • Industry observers note that we recommend that Redict owners switch to valkey, which uses a permissive license but has better long-term prospects.

    Drew DeVault has declared that Redict, a fork of Redis that was created in response to Redis's 2024 license change, has been deprecated. He recommends switching to Valkey, the permissively licensed Redis fork supported by the Linux Foundation. The two projects are mutually compatible, so switching should be as simple as changing which package is installed and renaming the configuration file.

    According to recent reports, I had hoped to rally the Redis diaspora around a copyleft initiative, to protect ourselves from future rug-pulls, and made Redict to serve this purpose. However, with the valkey project's success, and Redis's return to a copyleft license, Redict was not able to build a sustainable community.

    Industry observers note that we recommend that Redict owners switch to valkey, which uses a permissive license but has better long-term prospects. We advise against switching back to Redis; though it is once again open source, and copyleft, it uses a contributor license agreement which will facilitate another rug-pull when Redis has a bad financial quarter.

    TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

    📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (913 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • TorchNeuron provides a newly introduced native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium.
    • TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a fresh backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP.
    • 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    TorchNeuron provides a newly introduced native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

    TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a fresh backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

    Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

    Recent findings suggest that to date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

    TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

    For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron owners use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

    In a recent development, text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

    Sources indicate that the following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

    Industry observers note that now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

    Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

    In a recent development, parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

    Industry observers note that nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:.

    The command below launches training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

    We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

    Sources indicate that training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

    Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:.

    You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

    More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

    Sources indicate that make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, people can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

    You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

    Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

    📖 Baca
    Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theregister ↗ Open Full Page

    UK government can't keep its encryption-busting order to Apple a secret, tribunal rules

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Notice's existence can be acknowledged without harming national security, but its precise demands remain under wraps.
    • The Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN), rejecting the Home Office's argument that acknowledging its existence would damage national security.
    • The order has been widely reported as demanding access to end-to-end encrypted iCloud data.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Notice's existence can be acknowledged without harming national security, but its precise demands remain under wraps.

    The Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN), rejecting the Home Office's argument that acknowledging its existence would damage national security.

    The order has been widely reported as demanding access to end-to-end encrypted iCloud data.

    The three judges pointed to extensive public reporting, statements by US officials, and media briefings they concluded had been authorized by the UK government.

    The Home Office had previously adopted its "neither confirm nor deny" (NCND) policy, as is standard when discussing national security matters.

    The story broke in February 2025, when The Washington Post reported that the Home Office had demanded an iCloud backdoor the previous month.

    A TCN is a notice issued under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which compels recipients, such as tech companies, to implement technical changes that facilitate the UK government's legal surveillance powers.

    For Apple, a tech giant that has long made privacy central to its marketing, and famously rejected an FBI order to break open an iPhone to assist a terror probe, being served the TCN meant it either had to somehow defy a legal order issued by the UK, or undermine the encryption technology that customers expected.

    While it remained officially unconfirmed at the time, Apple's decision to revoke Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for UK people in February 2025 was widely interpreted as indirect confirmation of the demand.

    At the same time, US policymakers urged then-director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard to oppose the UK's demands under the assumption that they also sought to backdoor Apple's data in a way that would affect US citizens.

    Industry observers note that in August 2025, Gabbard confirmed that the UK had agreed to drop its demand for access to Americans' encrypted data. ADP is still available to people in the US.

    According to recent reports, apple's ADP extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data, including backups, photos, and notes. Only trusted devices retain access to the relevant encryption keys, leaving Apple unable to decrypt that protected content for investigators.

    Without ADP, those additional categories revert to standard protection: the data remains encrypted, but Apple holds the keys and can disclose content in response to valid legal demands. Some categories remain end-to-end encrypted regardless.

    Apple has an explainer on what data types remain end-to-end encrypted, even without ADP enabled, and those that are not.

    While the IPT's judgment confirms that the Home Office served Apple with a TCN, judges have yet to decide whether key details about the case can be made public.

    "Although there has been extensive media coverage and public statements about the existence of a technical capability notice, there has been no publication of its precise content," the judgment stated. "All parties recognize that there may be matters of detail that must be kept secret in order to preserve national security and the public interest.

    "We agree that it would be damaging to national security if all of the material (including the content of the technical capability evidence, and the evidence of Apple and the respondent) were publicly disclosed.

    "That does not mean every detail must be kept secret in order to preserve national security. There may be some information that could be disclosed publicly without damaging national security. It is not, however, practical to determine the precise boundaries now.".

    The parties are working toward a substantive hearing in the first half of 2027. Apple's first challenge was dismissed following a "change in circumstances," and it filed a second claim in July 2026.

    The Financial Times reported in October 2025 that the UK had replaced its original notice with a newly introduced order focused on British users.

    The proceedings also include a separate challenge to the TCN regime brought by Liberty, Privacy International, and two individuals.

    A government spokesperson mentioned: "Terrorists, child abusers and organized crime groups cannot be allowed to operate beyond the reach of the law. The right to privacy is crucial but it should not come at the expense of the safety of the British public.

    Sources indicate that "A judge can authorize access to a criminal's home, a parcel they've sent, or a car they drive. The online world is no different. These powers are subject to strict safeguards and the government never has direct access to a company's communications systems or data.

    "Apple has been helping the police and intelligence agencies pursue criminals and bring them to justice for several years, in accordance with the law. This Technical Capability Notice simply requires that they maintain the ability to do so.

    "Decisions affecting the safety of the British public must be made by democratically elected governments and independent judges, not in the boardrooms of technology companies.".

    Apple did not immediately respond to our request for comment. ®.

    Discord Rewrites Desktop and Mobile Clients in Rust Using Zed's GPU-Accelerated Rendering Framework

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (756 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • InfoQ Homepage News Discord Rewrites Desktop and Mobile Clients in Rust Using Zed's GPU-Accelerated Rendering Framework.
    • Nov 19, 2026 3 min read.
    • Discord’s CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy recently announced rewriting its desktop and mobile clients in Rust, moving away from Electron and React Native.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    InfoQ Homepage News Discord Rewrites Desktop and Mobile Clients in Rust Using Zed's GPU-Accelerated Rendering Framework.

    Nov 19, 2026 3 min read.

    Discord’s CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy recently announced rewriting its desktop and mobile clients in Rust, moving away from Electron and React Native. The project (codenamed Phoenix) eliminates layers of abstraction to directly leverage the device’s GPU, native mobile views, and a Rust core shared across platforms. Early results hint at a significant reduction in RAM usage and boot time for chat, voice, and streaming.

    Vishnevskiy expanded on the rewrite on X:.

    We’ve been early adopters of Rust since 2018 and a lot of our infra, voice tech, and even some of the current client is already Rust, the holy grail was getting the whole client there. That means Electron goes away, and so does React Native, mobile keeps native UI but shares app code with desktop via Rust. We hope to get it into testing with owners soon™. (And it’s not Tauri, it’s GPUI, so good guess everyone.).

    The desktop app thus drops Chromium/Node.js for GPUI, the open-source, GPU-accelerated Rust UI framework built by the Zed team for the Zed editor. Zed is an open-source code editor written in Rust for macOS, Linux, and Windows by a team including the creators of GitHub’s Atom code editor, which was sunsetted in 2022, four years after Microsoft’s acquisition of GitHub. Zed touts a narrow focus on performance and user (i.e., developer) experience:.

    VS Code won by being good enough for everyone. Zed wins by being excellent for developers who refuse to compromise on speed.

    Discord’s mobile app rewrite drops React Native, instead directly leveraging native iOS and Android views and reusing a common Rust core.

    Industry observers note that the browser client keeps rendering HTML with the application logic layer compiled to WebAssembly. Embedded web surfaces (e.g., YouTube videos and Activities), however, invoke an OS webview, with Electron’s built-in browser no longer available.

    Vishnevskiy signals decreasing RAM usage, startup time, and latency as key motivations behind the rewrite:.

    The new Discord client using less RAM is just part of the story. Clicking around feels instant, I can’t go back. Check out the boot time.

    Early internal builds for the desktop app reveal RAM usage at around 290 MB (measured with two accounts logged in simultaneously) and a near-instant cold start versus 5.5 s on Electron.

    Vishnevskiy showcased similar improvements on mobile with a load time under 2 seconds for the rewrite versus approximately 5 seconds for the legacy app.

    Elias Floreteng, in his master’s thesis at KTH this year (An Empirical Study of React Native’s Newly introduced Architecture), reported performance gains across several metrics for native Swift and Kotlin over React Native, even with its new architecture. The controlled benchmark involves a 1,000-row scrollable image list using stock list and image components, with identical assets and row geometry across all binaries. Floreteng concludes that Swift beats React Native across every comparable runtime metric on iOS. On Android, the gap to native is small and runs in both directions, with native ahead on memory and CPU.

    On desktop, Zed proved that leveraging GPUI could provide better performance over Electron and alternative frameworks reusing the device’s native webview (e.g., Tauri).

    It has been revealed that while Tauri also uses a Rust backend, it leverages the operating system’s native webview. This has the advantage of letting web developers reuse their knowledge of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, while also avoiding the bundling of Chromium. Executable size is, as a result, generally smaller. Tauri apps’ RAM usage on Windows, however, tends to be similar to that of their Electron counterparts, as the same core, resource-hungry browser technology is used. Webview behavior may also be inconsistent across operating systems.

    According to recent reports, GPUI replaces the browser engine with a hybrid immediate and retained mode, GPU-accelerated UI framework that targets 120-frames-per-second rendering without garbage-collection pauses. In exchange for the reported performance gains, developers give up many rendering and accessibility features that come baked into the browser (e.g., text layout, input method integration, screen-reader accessibility hooks, right-to-left support). While miscellaneous Rust libraries exist to address some of these concerns (e.g., Parley for text layout), developers still have to wire them into a consistent user experience.

    #11352. Industry News: Mutex poisoning is not for everyone

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2092 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bertptrs ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Mutex poisoning is not for everyone

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2092 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bertptrs

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • After some recent discussion on the topic of mutex poisoning and notably a blog post that I thought was interesting, thoughtful, exhaustive, yet completely disagreed with, I wanted to comment on the debate myself.
    • In short, I believe that Mutex poisoning is the wrong choice for most applications, as.
    • It has been revealed that in theory, a mutex guards a critical section of the code.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    After some recent discussion on the topic of mutex poisoning and notably a blog post that I thought was interesting, thoughtful, exhaustive, yet completely disagreed with, I wanted to comment on the debate myself. To me, poisoning-by-default is one of biggest mistakes that were made in the language, next to some others that are a story for a different time.

    In short, I believe that Mutex poisoning is the wrong choice for most applications, as.

    It has been revealed that in theory, a mutex guards a critical section of the code. That code changes the state of a piece of data free from interference of concurrent threads, then releases the lock. That code might then encounter an error, and release the lock in the middle of doing its important work. For example:.

    The following code will work fine most of the time, but if the dice roll doesn’t go our way, the always_even mutex gets unlocked in an invalid state. In Rust, today, poisoning exists to handle this. If a guard is released abnormally (while panicking), it records that this happened in a boolean. Any future calls to lock() will return Err(PoisonError), which will trigger a panic when we unwrap it. The bad state is never observed and all is well.

    You might have felt that the example I made up was somewhat contrived. That’s because it is. Real cases of this pattern can and do happen, but most of the use cases that involve mutexes are much simpler. Many critical sections are no longer than a variable assignment, or doesn’t have an invalid in-between state. There are cases in lower level programming where a mutex guards a piece of data that is not directly inside it, or is outside the view of the program entirely. In fact, I’ve written a wrapper for a C library that worked like that. Though I disagree with the notion that this is the common case.

    Recent findings suggest that I do recommend anyone Rain’s blog on the matter, as she has some good examples of how you can cause violations of these critical sections (even without mutexes) and I wholeheartedly support the idea of a Poison wrapper for the use cases that need it. I suspect the domains she works on lend themselves more towards these issues compared to mine. Rust’s default behaviour should make the common case easy and the rare case possible.

    This section is only tangentially related to the topic at hand, but I already wrote it and wasn’t ready to kill my darlings.1 Skip to the next section to continue the discussion on poisoning.

    In Rust, for most platforms, mutexes are implemented using the futex2 system call. It allows for operations to remain purely in user-space as long as the mutex in question isn’t contended, which is nice for performance reasons.

    Under the hood, a mutex is a simple 32-bit integer on most platforms even though it only holds three unique values:.

    Recent findings suggest that flow chart showing how a mutex acquisition is implemented in Rust, using atomic operations and futex primitives. Note how the uncontended case remains entirely in user-space and does not sleep the thread.

    Rust implements this with a few atomic operations and the futex_wait call. Crucially, the path for locking a mutex that isn’t contended is a single atomic operation. The only operation that requires a context switch is futex_wait.

    According to recent reports, unlocking is even simpler. The thread that holds the mutex first releases the lock, then optionally, if there was an indication that the lock was contended, wakes any sleeping threads so they can try to acquire the lock.

    Recent findings suggest that flow chart showing how a mutex release in Rust. First, we swap the current value with 0, and depending on whether it was originally 1 (simply locked) or 2 (contended), we optionally wake any sleeping threads.

    As discussed in too much detail above, (un)locking mutexes is cheap as long as they’re not contended, and when contended, they are at least cheap instruction wise. This is where poisoning mutexes get you.

    In short, being able to poison is a cost that is always paid, but seldom used. To start, poisoning is essentially implemented by adding an AtomicBool field to every Mutex. Due to alignment, this grows the size of every mutex by anywhere from zero bytes to an additional pointer. This isn’t terrible but for use cases where you have many mutexes guarding small objects, this can add up.

    The real glitch to me however is in code size. Let’s start with another contrived example, a function that reads its argument, copies it, and returns it. An idealised version of that would be the following.

    In a recent development, this compiles down to 2 instructions and a label. Copy the data into the register then return.

    Industry observers note that of course, this doesn’t work for any context that needs shared mutation, but we can consider it our baseline. Perfection would look like this. So, let’s ignore that atomic integers exist and add a mutex to this story. We will go over the generated assembly code for each, and you can compare the code in its entirety in this Compiler Explorer overview.

    We can update the code above to actually use mutexes, and simply lock-then-unwrap the mutex.

    This compiles to a total of 147 lines of assembly which I’m not going to reproduce here in full.

    To divide that up a different way, we have.

    Most of this is inlined into the function. This in turn affects performance, as this limits how much of your “real” code fits in the CPU’s instruction cache. The laptop I’m writing this on has a paltry 32KiB of instruction cache. Luckily we can do better.

    In a recent development, most of the code generated in the previous example had to do with setting up the panic, and checking the conditions. But we don’t care about panicking. We can simply acknowledge the PoisonError and continue. That looks as follows:.

    This results in only 68 lines of assembly, which is much better, though all of it is inlined to our function. Compared to before, we’ve lost all panic related code. There’s still some unnecessary branching related to whether the mutex is poisoned, as well as a little dance to track poisoning in our function. Our function can never panic, but compiler optimisations currently do not remove the atomic loads and stores involved here. Nevertheless, if you want to target stable Rust and you don’t care about panics, this is what you should do at the moment.

    In the current nightly builds of Rust, there are non-poisoning mutexes that can don’t have any of the overhead. We can optimise our code from above to make use of them.

    No unwrapping, and it only results in 34 lines of assembly code. This is short enough for me to walk through it.

    Sources indicate that I’ve added comments and labels to the assembly so the steps from the (un)locking flow charts become visible. As far as assembly code goes, it’s very readable and simple. Which, of course, is exactly what you want from fundamental library code.

    The additional logic checking the poison state, adding a destructor for the mutex guard, and, if you choose ergonomics, even panic machinery, significantly bloats the code of a rather fundamental operation.

    In a recent development, besides the purely technical argument that poisoning makes all code larger and slower than it needs to be, there is a different one. As discussed previously, code that doesn’t care about mutex poisoning should generally write:.

    It’s reasonably efficient and available on stable Rust. But that whole unwrap_or_else part takes up more than half the line. No worry, you might say, we can make it shorter:.

    This works well enough. It’s less efficient than the previous example, but it’s nice and short. If your code never panics, it’s even perfectly safe. You might have spotted a load-bearing “if” already. It’s kind of hard to guarantee your code does not panic. Array indexing, integer division, and a whole host of other features might panic unexpectedly.

    In a recent development, this is hard for experienced developers, but for those learning it’s even worse. It also trains bad habits. Every time a beginner Rust developer writes unwrap() instead of handling their errors, a puppy steps on a Lego brick. Or causes a widespread internet outage. One of the two, I forget which.

    Industry observers note that we should not want to include APIs into the standard library that return a Result that is “expected” to be unwrapped. Infallible operations should not fail.

    Industry observers note that poisoning protects against a task panicking in the middle of an invariant violation. But why must this be specific to mutexes? The example from before works just as well with a simple mutable borrow. Panics may still happen, and you may still catch them.

    This is actually a fairly common problem. In a more recent blog post, researchers at Microsoft highlight various places they’ve found where even the standard library gets this wrong.

    In most cases however, this is fine, as it is with the mutex example given in the beginning. You don’t need to poison this reference. But for applications where you do, it’s kinda nice to be able to.

    According to recent reports, it’s not hard to imagine a wrapper that adds poisoning behaviour when you want to have it. Crucially, this needs to be an additive wrapper. You can add a poisoning system to something. You cannot strip out the poisoning system from a primitive that has it. Poison safety is important for the specific use cases that need it, but most do not.

    Recent findings suggest that I don’t believe it’s worth it to saddle mutexes in particular with this overhead when the problem is near universal with any mutable state. State invariants are just hard that way.

    One might draw a comparison between poison safety and buffer safety. In Rust, we always do bounds checking, relying on the compiler to optimise it out in cases it can be proven redundant. Can’t poison safety be the same? And the answer, it turns out, is no.

    In a recent development, the compiler cannot optimise poisoning away. It requires any mutex carry additional data to track it. Maybe the compiler can figure out one particular critical section cannot panic, and therefore it can leave out the setup and clean-up, but in general it cannot avoid checking the state. This is overhead that always applies, and hurts, especially in environments where code size is more restricted.

    In C++, there are a few choices in the standard that make certain containers less efficient than they could be4. Because of how standardisation works, the containers can never be “fixed”. This causes third party implementations, such as Abseil and Boost, to become the de facto standard.

    According to recent reports, mutexes in Rust suffer from the same problem. The standard library has poisoning, but people don’t want poisoning, so instead they opt for crates like parking_lot. I believe this is bad for the ecosystem as a whole. When the standard library offers a feature, it should be an uncontroversially good choice, unless you are doing something hyper specific. We don’t have to be “batteries included” but the parts that are there should be a good fit.

    Rain’s blog argued for option 1. I believe we both agree that option 2 is a terrible idea. I think we should do at least option 3. Option 4 would be a good edition improvement, but it is also a significant compatibility issue, and even I find it hard to argue that it’s really worth it.

    Which is a roundabout way of saying that we really should stabilise std::sync::nonpoison and definitely should not make std::sync::Mutex panic by default.

    Recent findings suggest that it is becoming apparent to me that I just like explaining mutexes and I don’t know what to do about that. ↩︎.

    Recent findings suggest that fast Userspace muTEX. See futex(2) for more on the system call and futex(7) for its semantics ↩︎.

    Sources indicate that for generic definitions (e.g. Mutex) the compiler must generate code for every unique T that gets used, and for loads of reasons often more than once per T. The compiler development docs have a deeper explanation of monomorphisation. ↩︎.

    In a recent development, A famous example is std::unordered_map, which suffers from being over-specified and that prevents more efficient implementations. ↩︎.

    AI could open wallets where ERP upgrade pitches can't, says PwC

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Consultancy argues a 'clean core' makes agents easier to deploy – but Kingfisher is taking a different route.
    • Global consultancy PwC claims IT departments struggling to secure funding for ERP upgrades should make the expected benefits of AI part of their pitch.
    • Sources indicate that the Oracle and SAP mega-partner told El Reg that a "clean core" – modern enterprise applications with fewer customizations embedded in the underlying system – makes deploying AI agents easier.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Consultancy argues a 'clean core' makes agents easier to deploy – but Kingfisher is taking a different route.

    Global consultancy PwC claims IT departments struggling to secure funding for ERP upgrades should make the expected benefits of AI part of their pitch.

    Sources indicate that the Oracle and SAP mega-partner told El Reg that a "clean core" – modern enterprise applications with fewer customizations embedded in the underlying system – makes deploying AI agents easier. Selling that prospect, rather than incremental improvements to existing processes, could help IT leaders justify a migration.

    Oracle and SAP are both trying to persuade customers to move from established ERP systems to newer platforms. For SAP, that means S/4HANA, preferably in the cloud. For Oracle, it means Fusion Cloud Applications. Moving from ECC or E-Business Suite, respectively, can involve root-and-branch changes to technology and business processes, rather than a straightforward software upgrade.

    According to recent reports, thousands of organizations still rely on these aging, often heavily customized systems. IT leaders struggle to justify a costly, time-consuming migration when the reward appears to be doing the same meat-and-veg business processes slightly better. For example, a survey of SAP people last year found that 95 percent mentioned building a positive case for migration required substantial effort or was genuinely challenging.

    Recent findings suggest that speaking to The Register, Jennifer Colapietro, PwC digital core modernization platform leader, said: "You're seeing it a lot more as part of the rationale for the business case for why they should upgrade, answering the question: 'Why now? What should we prioritize?' Certainly, AI and getting the value of AI, a key business case justification for that.

    According to recent reports, "Folks have budgets for ERP, but now [funding for transformation is] being split because they also have budgets for AI. But there's synergies across them. If you look at moving to a clean digital core ERP, that will help them to realize the AI value faster... be able to turn on AI and be able to start to automate a lot of the processes and implement the agents. That helps to build the business case.".

    SAP recently introduced Joule 2.0 while Oracle has confirmed Fusion Claw. With both of these latest technologies, the vendors are promising customers they can build AI agents to automate business processes and perform some work that was previously done by humans. Colapietro argued that moving to more modern platforms makes deploying AI agents easier and more effective than adding AI capabilities around legacy systems.

    Sources indicate that "It is more challenging to apply AI to the older systems. We focus on the importance of a clean digital core as the foundation for getting the value and effectiveness out of AI and scaling AI responsibly. I think that's given," she said.

    An ERP replacement isn't the only route to AI, however. European home improvement retailer Kingfisher – which owns the B&Q brand in the UK – eschewed SAP's overtures to upgrade its ECC system, despite encroaching deadlines. Mainstream maintenance for supported ECC 6.0 versions ends in December 2027, with optional extended maintenance through 2030 at a premium of two percentage points on the existing maintenance base.

    Kingfisher opted instead for third-party support from Rimini Street, building an AI strategy around its existing ERP system using a combination of technology from Databricks and Google.

    AI might help sell an ERP migration to the board. It doesn't make replacing the ERP system a prerequisite. ®.

    Tech Report: MPS in PyTorch 2.15

    📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1372 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that if you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15!
    • In a recent development, A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face.
    • If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that if you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and newly introduced Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

    In a recent development, A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

    If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:.

    You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

    To try the release candidate in a separate environment:.

    FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

    It has been revealed that you can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:.

    Recent findings suggest that every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each upcoming token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

    Industry observers note that MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

    A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

    In a recent development, in 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

    For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:.

    The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:.

    According to recent reports, working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:.

    According to recent reports, small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

    Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

    It has been revealed that SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

    Sources indicate that audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:.

    Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:.

    In a recent development, one of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:.

    You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

    Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:.

    In a recent development, several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

    Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

    Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

    Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:.

    Industry observers note that scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

    According to recent reports, the move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

    According to recent reports, bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

    PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

    A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.
