    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

    Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this newly introduced generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

    A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

    Here's what changed, and what's next:.

    In a recent development, the core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:.

    The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

    Over the past year, we've added several major features:.

    On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

    Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

    Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

    With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too substantial to run on the device with the same session code:.

    Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

    Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

    API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

    AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

    While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:.

    In a recent development, the first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:.

    Industry observers note that and if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

    If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

    Recent findings suggest that community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

    Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

    DreamCoder: coding harness and IDE from the author of Mastering Emacs

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4833 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Masteringemacs

    ⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, it’s been a little bit quiet around these parts; sorry about that.
    • It’s called DreamCoder, an AI coding harness that is very different from the ones you’re probably familiar with already.
    • Recent findings suggest that I installed Claude Code a few days after its first release some time in May 2025.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, it’s been a little bit quiet around these parts; sorry about that. I’ve been really busy for the past fifteen months with a major project that I am finally ready to formally release. So I’d like to talk about that project, and also a potted history of AI and Emacs.

    It’s called DreamCoder, an AI coding harness that is very different from the ones you’re probably familiar with already.

    Recent findings suggest that I installed Claude Code a few days after its first release some time in May 2025. I put some coins in the slot machine and I put it to work building a complex piece of enterprise middleware I’d built several times in my career. Wow.. watching this thing chomp its way through the project with that chaotic, early Sonnet energy. It was far, far from perfect; it required a lot of human steering, input and correction, but the speed advantage was undeniable, and seeing it jump between disparate programming languages, frameworks and theoretical and practical programming from one turn to the next was just such a sight to behold.

    One thing that struck me with Claude Code is that it was the first terminal application I’d used in a long time. I found it an odd choice for a coding agent; then everyone else copied them and made their own terminal coding agents.

    Why on earth do I have to stare at a shoe rack-sized terminal window to do this? Sure there are GUI versions also; but the terminal interface remains the primary modality for most of these tools. Most GUIs, and most harnesses now have them also, are second-class citizens. And they all look the same. A boring sidebar with chat headings and a chat pane is what most of them look like.

    According to recent reports, but a serious coder needs more than that. Even a casual user will bristle when they try to copy and paste multi-line text in a terminal.

    So in May 2025 I decreed that I would build a better harness, and surely now that I have AI this should not take more than 2 or 3 months to build.

    And so, after 15 months of work, and endless UI and backend iterations, culminating in a successful beta test, I am now ready to release DreamCoder, which is I think the acme of what a coding harness should be.

    Before I get into the meat and potatoes of all of that, I want to talk about AI history and Emacs’s role in it.

    Let’s roll back time to the 1950s.

    Emacs and LISP, if you did not know, both have a special place in the annals of AI history.

    Sources indicate that john McCarthy was an AI researcher at MIT, and in the 1950s he set out to create the Advice Taker, a piece of software that envelops a framework for what a basic human should know that he called commonsense reasoning using “mathematical logic”. His postulation was that if we can express with symbolic precision all the aspects of what constitutes humanity like ordinary facts about life, that we can set in motion the rudiments of AI.

    In the 50s there was little in the way of computer software that could do this. To formalize such a system you need a lot of data, rigorously formatted, and a method of manipulating the data. The data and code itself may intertwine recursively, and so an ordinary programming language would not work.

    Recent findings suggest that to help him achieve this, McCarthy created the LISt Processing (LISP) language made up of two facets: M-expressions, a functional language in the vein of Algol; and S-expressions, designed for symbolic data representation, and never intended as a method of writing code. S-expressions were dolled up with parentheses. M-expressions meanwhile used square brackets to visually separate the two. Uniquely, the language specification had an eval feature that would prove that the language is also a universal Turing machine… if only McCarthy had the means to do so. It was theoretical because McCarthy lacked, in time, staff and money, what he needed build this recursive evaluator that can take as input its own world state and evaluate it alongside fresh expressions, a fact made even more apparent by the sheer complexity of his M-expression language and the limited resources he had at the time.

    It has been revealed that steve Russell who worked with him proved him wrong the way most young people do: by just doing it. Russell wrote the first LISP Interpreter with a working eval function, but M-expressions got sidelined; the imperative, procedural nature of programming got squished into S-expressions instead. They had to hand roll the language on paper then punch it into cards and then batch run them. Eliding M-expressions was a simple matter of pragmatism. And so LISP was born. And through several accidents of history, M-expressions never gained traction. M-expressions live on in Wolfram’s Mathematica, but few other places.

    Much later, McCarthy eventually conceded that,.

    “One can even conjecture that LISP owes its survival specifically to the fact that its programs are lists, which everyone, including me, has regarded as a disadvantage.”.

    S-expressions were always intended as the storage format with a bridge language to manipulate them. But by pushing evaluation into the same symbolic representation format as the data, we have what we call LISP today. That is why LISP is so unique. Consider a simple calculator. (+ 2 2) can simultaneously represent an expression that we want to compute, two plus two, or perhaps a ledger of record of a calculation we have already done.

    McCarthy never built the Advice Taker in its purest form. He and his team ran into many philosophical, mathematical and computational walls that kept them occupied for a long time.

    The idea behind the Advice Taker was simple. If you want to go somewhere in your car, you can symbolically express this by building a chain of narrative facts – kinda like a flowchart, but as small snippets of rules and facts, not as one grand design.

    The system would automatically resolve ambiguities, and all the logician had to do was capture the microcosm of the world he wished to represent:.

    It has been revealed that and so on. If you’re a student of Computer Science you’ll see echoes of Prolog here. The intent was simple: if we can symbolically express the world around us, we can advise that symbolic world with real-life facts, and have the automaton that uses this reified symbolic world change with it.

    In a recent development, but the axiomatic complexity of a world model would never survive an encounter with a 3-year-old child. Every axiom you write begets a fresh one — so you can walk to your front door? Well what if the door is locked? Or what if your car is parked on the street and not in your drive way?

    It has been revealed that A rules-based order of the world is a tender, beautiful one; but it is hard to build. It’s a fractal of ever-more specific and pedantic rules that conspire against you, just as you think you have a soluble world, typed and ready.

    Anyone who has ever written Prolog knows exactly what that feels like!

    I have my own personal story to add to this. In the 90s as a teenager I got a summer internship at a business that built banking software. They clearly didn’t know what to do with us teenaged interns, so on our first day they crammed us in a room and split us into teams and told us to build a flow chart for assembling a bike. Team exercise or something. Best one wins. We were told to be as specific and explicit as possible and account for as many conditions as we could think of, and the poor employees who had to mind us did their best to help. I distinctly recall losing because in my flowchart I forgot to open the box the disassembled bike came in.

    McCarthy meanwhile eventually moved on and set up his own AI lab at Stanford, but the idea of the Advice Taker lived on.

    It has been revealed that in the late 70s Stallman and Steele create EMACS (Editing MACroS), also at MIT’s AI Lab, a set of building blocks on top of TECO, a famously inscrutable text editor. TECO did not update the screen by default; you had to toggle that on and hope your edits worked. You typed out terse keyboard commands, crossed your fingers and hoped you got it right, and then you patiently waited for your text manipulation to take effect. Rinse and repeat until you got what you wanted.

    Recent findings suggest that stallman and Steele wanted more: they wanted macros so they could automate tedium of typing all that line noise. This strand of augmentation and later on self-modification is of course a unifying theme in Emacs today. The history of Emacs is long; but its outcome is known to us. I am typing this very article in Richard Stallman’s Emacs.

    McCarthy’s Advice Taker left its mark in a subtle but indelible way. Warren Teitelman built the ADVISE system in his thesis with a cool title that reads like something out of a pulpy 1970s sci-fi novella: PILOT: A Step Toward Man-Computer Symbiosis. Teitelman, he later mentioned, was deeply inspired by McCarthy’s original idea of advising systems.

    Industry observers note that in his thesis, he describes a method of arresting a function call and inserting code before or after it is run. He was tired of editing other people’s LISP code by hand, and wanted a way of modifying their code without touching it directly. He built and rebuilt his system several times over the years, culminating in his ADVISE system in Interlisp, a structured editor and language runtime for manipulating LISP code and data. Interlisp eschewed plain text files; instead, you manipulated the tree at a high level of abstraction with explicit instructions like “move X list to Y position”. You can see my own attempts at merging structured editing with plaintext editing in Combobulate.

    According to recent reports, MIT AI hackers eventually implemented Teitelman’s ADVISE system from his PILOT thesis in their own versions of Emacs. Later, it was canonized in Chalupsky’s own 1992 re-implementation in Emacs Lisp that lives on (M-x find-library advice.el) as one of Emacs’s advice systems to this day.

    What began as an idea for expressing automata using symbolism in an as-yet theoretical language in the 1950s culminated in a system for dynamically altering functions in GNU Emacs in the 1990s. What an unlikely lineage and history.

    Symbolism and AI did not end with advising functions. There were many attempts at symbolic intelligence. Terry Winograd’s SHRDLU; Marvin Minsky’s Frame Systems; and even Emacs’s ELIZA-style M-x doctor all make use of symbolic “AI”.

    None of them brought us closer to the AI that proponents of symbolic AI hoped they would.

    In hindsight that seems obvious.

    Writing a LISP macro just so will not produce artificial intelligence; nor will a carefully crafted web of rules and symbolic algebra suddenly spark intelligence. We know that today, but for a generation of computer scientists it felt like the future we have all read about in science fiction novels: a perfect, logical intelligence. A positronic brain. Robby the Robot; HAL 9000; C-3PO; Data; or the Speedies and Cuties from I, Robot. The unifying theme of these science fiction stories is they are automatons that follow strict rules — they obey Asimov’s three Laws of Robotics.

    Every turn of hardware and software brought them ever closer to one day realizing the vision of an artificial intelligence, captured in neat axioms and LISP S-expressions, and modified in tools like Emacs.

    It is surprising that symbolic AI, the vanguard movement for artificial intelligence, would instead dissipate into the wider body of Computer Science and programming as tools, languages and concepts, but not survive as a viable method of achieving AI.

    In a recent development, perhaps we always knew. Because at some point – even if we never really fully internalized it – we discovered that a ductile system that is shaped by its master’s desires is a tool that survives the ages because it remains eternally useful.

    A cast-iron system made of stern rules cannot spawn general intelligence.

    For all the mathematical purity, beauty even, of the idea of a clockwork mind that is introspectable and malleable and its behavior expressed as S-expressions and interpreted by elegant algorithms and honed macros, we can, through the benefit of hindsight – now that we do have AI through other means – see that it was not to be.

    The argument in favor of ductility is especially poignant when you learn of the Connectionists, which sounds like a bad 1960s band, but was in fact a loose coalition of people who believed firmly that neural networks, not symbolic AI, were the path to success. The Connectionist viewpoint was deeply unpopular in AI academia of that era, and funding for it was scarce.

    In a recent development, frank Rosenblatt invented the Perceptron, a foundational concept in neural networks, in 1957. Before Rosenblatt died in 1971, Marvin Minsky, an authority in the AI movement at MIT and a leading proponent of Symbolism, knifed the idea of Perceptrons and neural networks in a book he co-authored with Seymour Papert. They named the book, which they also dedicated to Rosenblatt, Perceptrons. The book deftly explains the mathematics of Perceptrons but undercuts their possible utility by showing that a single-layer Perceptron cannot represent an XOR gate. It was a deliberately obtuse reading of what neural networks could and could not do. With one additional hidden layer, a network can represent an XOR gate. It was a sneaky thrust of the stiletto: Minsky’s claims were overstated. A fact that was not lost on anybody in the Symbolic or Connectionist camps.

    It’s disputed if the Perceptrons book led to the first AI winter in the 1970s. It certainly did not help. But funding for many AI research paths dried up in the 1970s.

    The Connectionist movement was vindicated in the long run. They lost the battle then, but they won the war, and the fruits of their research eventually gave us AI.

    The ductility we so prize in our software and tools today is antithetical to a strict, symbolic world model spun of axioms and facts that we hoped would one day birth AI. Yet to try and give birth to this world they had to build the most ductile tools of them all: LISP and, from that, also software like Emacs. The ultimate hacker’s tool.

    It is ironic then that a neural network, a crude facsimile of how a brain works, a construct that is by its nature ductile and malleable, won out in the end.

    So I feel a profound sadness that I started out programming DreamCoder in Emacs, the most extensible editor in the world, by hand back in May 2025, only to see DreamCoder write itself… in DreamCoder today.

    I am still sad, but I also know that our industry completely reinvents itself every decade or two. This is my second career upheaval. Most programmers today have not been around long enough to go through it themselves. So I feel for them that this especially massive quake is their first encounter with how unsentimental our industry is.

    But for all the sadness, I wake up every day with a feeling of optimism that I have not felt in a very long time.

    I finally get to build again, no longer weighed down by my decades of knowledge and experience that held my ambition in check. I truly have not felt this liberated since I was a teenager programming in Delphi, blissfully unaware that the things I was busy building were impossible for a self-taught teenager to ever realize. I see this reflection in others: the best programmers I know also love AI. Amateurs also revel in AI’s capabilities, happy that they can finally solve problems they could never afford to pay a programmer to do for them.

    Sources indicate that I must admit that building software has, over the years, gotten a lot more complex, with an ever-larger share of that work being repetitive tedium. This is more so with hobby software – as I do not get paid to do it, so I do not have a moral duty to see it through – where I’d do all the fun bits leaving just the enervating, boring and soul-crushing parts behind. Do you have a projects folder full of sad, abandoned projects like I do?

    Now I can craft in abundance. AI has freed up a lot of toil but I somehow still find myself busy all day doing real work.

    Building a coding harness is perhaps the closest I will get to the optimism all those researchers and scientists must have felt in the 1970s and 1980s. They hoped that with a little bit more work, their logical rules would kindle a fresh intelligence. Fifty years on, and I can simply tell DreamCoder to improve itself and watch as it changes before me. I can ask the AI running inside it to analyze the changes I have made to its tools and prompt and have it adjust them accordingly. It feels like science fiction; the very thing the researchers of yesterday strove to build. Yet we really do live in this reality now.

    Industry observers note that so. DreamCoder. Let me address the 900 lb gnu in the room: DreamCoder is not an Emacs-related application. The reason is unfortunately one of economics and access: I want to build an AI coding harness for everyone. But don’t worry: I have some cool plans for DreamCoder + Emacs, and AI + Emacs more generally going forward. So stay tuned.

    But what about all those other coding harnesses? Well, most of those harnesses all suffer from the same mistakes. It is a problem that is not unique to coding harnesses or the people who make them, but a constraint we all labor under, and one that is not easily replaced by AI:.

    Taste is a scarce, human resource.

    And for all the bounty of AI, it still requires a human to persevere and to see things through. One thing intensive use of AI coding has taught me is that we’re going to need a lot of computer programmers who know what they’re doing going forward. I believe this is so, because let us be honest, most people do not want to program computers, even if that computer can actually do the bulk of the work for them. It requires a steady hand to build reliable software; that has not changed.

    Therefore, if we programmers have to spend a lot of our time interacting with AI, then the tool we do it with should be ‘human-centric’ in its design, and it should take advantage of all the modern features we have at our disposal.

    Back in May 2025 I took a look at all the tooling and remarked “no, thank you.” Today I look at the landscape and I feel pretty much the same.

    Recent findings suggest that and I think I am not the only one who feels that way. Most of these coding harnesses, to me, feel bristly. They shouldn’t be; but they are like that because we are at an notable inflection point where no one really knows what the future looks like. We’re all just… fumbling around a bit. It’s an exciting time to build software, even if we don’t quite know what the world will look like a few years hence.

    One thing I am adamant about is that DreamCoder must be a powerful, frontier-class coding harness. That means it should have all the features you’d expect from that: backgroundable sub agents, MCP servers, cache efficiency, and all that stuff. Check.

    According to recent reports, but that stuff quickly recedes into the background because, you know, it just works. Day to day you will dart between chats and terminals and whatnot, and you need an interface that accommodates that. Emacs is a tiling window manager; so is DreamCoder. DreamCoder’s window manager is a little bit cleverer than most window managers as every pane has a minimum, comfortable and maximum size. The window manager will therefore ensure windows always fit snugly on your screen, and you’ll never end up in a situation where windows are tiny and unreadable. It has a sophisticated constraint satisfaction solver that tries to balance your demand for a newly introduced window (“open a terminal”) with the challenge of keeping your visible panes roughly the same size. If DreamCoder can’t wedge in a new pane, it’ll punt one to the hidden window bar. Just click it to resurface it, or hover it to see what it’s doing; it’s a live view.

    Because of my Emacs roots, I think a good tool must be keyboard-friendly. Because it runs on a browser you get the mouse for free of course. But smacking the tab button over and over is a frustrating user experience in complex webapps, and doubly so a tiling window manager: where exactly are you going to end up when you tab from one window to the next? To combat that, I built an avy-style window and “point of interest” selector for chats. Tap a key and pick from a selection of “embark”-like actions such as clicking links or opening pictures. It’s a work in progress, but I think it works well.

    Recent findings suggest that most high-volume operations like opening and creating panes is done through a Helm-like interface with search-as-you-type. It’s really efficient, of course. And it works with a mouse also; which is sort of the point. The keyboard’s there for those who want it, and the mouse for regular folk who are just getting started. One unique feature of the design, which admittedly I am still exploring privately, is that everything is stored as Javascript objects (on account of running in your browser) so it’s not too much of a leap to build “macros” that prefill most of these dialog windows, leaving behind just the fields you want to edit.

    It has been revealed that but yeah. With DreamCoder I want to take the best of Emacs and its coterie of third-party packages and bring some of that with me. The world is still not ready for an Emacs-shaped future, sadly, so that is why DreamCoder is a standalone application and a web frontend.

    Another thing that drives me wild: I see people with tmux running 10 claude codes (or codex, or…) cycling between them like a duck gallery at a carnival to see if one of them is done working, or if it needs human intervention.

    Recent findings suggest that so there’s two things to unpack here: one is running lots of things in parallel, and the other is observability. You need insight into what is going on: is an AI jammed because it’s awaiting an answer or a tool safety prompt? Perhaps you’ve parked a bunch of chats pending some conversations with coworkers or other work that must finish first.

    In DreamCoder you have workspaces. They’re like virtual desktops (or window configurations in Emacs lingo): a snapshot view of panes as you want em. As you can see from the screenshots, panes expand to fill all the space. So if you want more space, you can: resize them (with the mouse or keyboard); shuffle them to a named workspace; or float them so they sit on top of the other windows.

    But if you’ve got a lot of things happening in multiple workspaces, it’s hard to keep tabs on that. That’s why DreamCoder has a big, honking minimap in the top-right corner. One for each workspace. The minimap is a miniature of your actual layout. Each pane in the map gently pulses when it’s working, and it makes it abundantly clear when it’s blocked. When there’s nothing to do, it’s green.

    Because workspaces and panes are distinct things you interact with, it must be easy to navigate between them.

    Sources indicate that I also wanted full-on, optional Emacs key bindings, but that is… pretty much impossible to properly build. Browsers lock you out of some rather key Emacs button combinations. Sadly that feature is parked until I can solve it on all major browsers without breaking your normal browser keys.

    In a recent development, that’s not to say it doesn’t have Emacs-inspired key bindings. Most global actions are reachable with Alt+x, akin to M-x; local, pane-specific ones with Alt+c. Alt+m activates keyboard mode: you can now type the number of the named pane to jump to it; or WASD to switch the active pane in that cardinal direction.

    Support for open weight models like Qwen, Gemma, Deepseek, GLM, etc. is also very vital to me. They work so well. I’m really surprised, here in late 2026, just how capable small models are at local-only development compared to just one year ago. Qwen 3.8 27B, for example, is fantastically good for its size. You can do a lot of good software development with it if you’re a capable hand yourself. Bigger models equal more auto piloting; but that Qwen model? Wow. So local models work great. In fact I think the future is local for a lot of use cases. Intelligence is fast approaching a cost where it will be too cheap to meter. If you remember the personal computer revolution in the 1980s and 1990s, then there are definitely echoes of that here.

    If you’ve been holding off on local models then I do recommend you reconsider. Small ones like Qwen 3.8 27B (or its cousin, Flash Next) can run well on a high-end gaming rig or Mac, or with a little investment if you do not have that. If you have a dinky old computer and you’re cash starved, then not all hope is lost. Turn to the potato agronomists on twitter: give twitter’s AI, Grok, what you have and what you can reasonably spend and tell it to track down the cutting edge setup for your rig. This is no lie the fastest, easiest way to catch up to the cutting edge of self-hosted inference today. Five minutes.

    Sources indicate that as I’ve been building DreamCoder, I have come to the belief I’m not just building a coding harness. Coding harnesses are an IDE for the future; it will do more than just display a chat window for coding agent work. DreamCoder does more than that already. It’s going the way of Emacs in that it’ll consume a wide range of adjacent workflows and tools. But I have only just gotten started. I am brimming with ideas I’m building in parallel, but they take time because as I said it’s not about the code; it’s just one small facet of building something that works well. But you know that already: it’s always the last mile.

    DreamCoder is the most ambitious, technically complex and advanced software project I have ever built in my life. And that’s just the beginning. I’m not done. I’ve barely started. I will be blogging about this going forward, in addition to my usual Emacs scribblings.

    In fact, the thing I’m at the moment grinding away at is a world-class pentest and cybersecurity suite in DreamCoder. Every single bit of software we have ever written is vulnerable; we have many rough years ahead of us. Just look at the crippling vulnerabilities coming out every day now almost. Even the most security conscious person is going to find themselves on the wrong side for no other reason than we depend on packages that were mature and stable and assumed to be secure. DreamCoder can do its bit to help catch many of most obvious weaknesses, especially as fresh software is minted every day that also needs thorough testing.

    Sources indicate that to round it off, I would like to formally invite you to join me in making DreamCoder better by trying it out. It’s great. It’s not a toy; it’s not a demo; and it’s not a weekend prototype. It’s a frontier coding harness that has most of what you’d expect: MCP, backgroundable sub agents and shell commands, terminal windows, skills, hooks, 99% cache hit, it runs for days, and an interactive UI for all of it. There’s a handy dandy importer for your Pi, OpenCode or Codex configs also to help you get started. A couple of clicks and your model settings are set up in DreamCoder. Ready to go.

    Recent findings suggest that please do e-mail me your thoughts ((rot13 "zvpxrl@znfgrevatrznpf.bet")) on AI, coding harnesses, what you’ve built with it, and what you think more generally about where our world is heading. I’m keen to hear from you.

    • Nov 19, 2026 3 min read.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    InfoQ Homepage News NetWasm 0.10 Speeds Up C# on WebAssembly, Now Faster Than Mono AOT.

    Nov 19, 2026 3 min read.

    Sources indicate that the team behind NetWasm has published a write-up of its 0.10 optimisation work, spanning releases 0.10.1 to 0.10.8. The changes touch exception handling, array bounds checks, WebAssembly SIMD and integer division. On the project’s own benchmark set, NetWasm now comes out ahead of Mono AOT and gets close to desktop .NET on some workloads.

    In a recent development, netWasm is a compiler and runtime that compiles C# programs ahead of time into small, standalone WebAssembly files. It takes the IL that Roslyn produces and emits Wasm, using its own runtime and a CoreLib ported from .NET. The yardstick is the Mono AOT build for WASI, which runs .NET on the same engine. A fresh garbage collector had already put NetWasm in front on allocation-heavy code, but plain loops were still slower: a quicksort of 100,000 integers took 77.2 ms, against 58.0 ms for Mono AOT.

    Much of the early gain came from exception handling in 0.10.1. Wasmtime adds extra register save-and-restore code around any function that can throw or catch, floating-point registers included. Methods with null, bounds or checked-arithmetic checks paid that price on every call. Throws now go through a shared function and the catching handler releases the frames, which cut UI churn from 17.6 to 7.9 ms.

    According to recent reports, version 0.10.2 inlines small straight-line methods in loops, tuple swaps included, and skips checks already performed on the same array and index. The quicksort fell to 54.0 ms. DoomSharp, a C# software renderer for Doom that ships a NetWasm build, served as a second test case. Value-type accessors now compile to plain field loads, and at O3 small branching helpers are inlined inside loops. Together these brought a 120-frame render from 3,595 down to 1,934 ms.

    SIMD arrived in 0.10.7. Vector128, Vector and PackedSimd lower to 128-bit Wasm instructions, and element-wise array loops handle four or more elements per iteration, with a scalar fallback. Hoisting loop-invariant Math calls allowed a solver for Burgers’ equation, a fundamental partial differential equation from fluid mechanics, to vectorise: its first test dropped from 497 ms to 71 ms, against 186 ms for Mono AOT and 93 ms for desktop .NET.

    It has been revealed that version 0.10.8 targets division and range-checked arithmetic. A remainder that follows a division now reuses the quotient and skips repeated zero-divisor and int.MinValue / -1 checks. A trial-division test fell from 1,376 to 765 ms, while Mono AOT needed 862 ms.

    It has been revealed that across the 2,213 cases, 0.10.8 at O3 with NetWasmGC takes 0.41 times Mono AOT’s time as a geometric mean, excluding five cases where Mono’s LLVM removes the work. Against desktop .NET 11 RC3 JIT the ratio is 0.87, down from 2.15 for 0.10.6. By family, the ratio to Mono AOT runs from 0.34 for intrinsics to 0.81 for math. The 120-frame DoomSharp render takes 1,623 ms on NetWasmGC, compared with 2,371 ms for Mono AOT and 1,053 ms for desktop .NET JIT.

    According to recent reports, those figures come from Wasmtime 49.0.3 on an Apple M1 Max, using cases from dotnet/performance plus five NetWasm workloads. The authors also found that identical loops at different addresses could differ by up to 15 per cent, so their A/B tests align every function to 4 KiB.

    The article is open about what is left. Desktop .NET is about 3.1 times faster on vector benchmarks, because it can use host SIMD directly while Wasm is limited to fixed 128-bit operations. Math.Pow is 1.4 times slower than on Mono AOT, and CopyBlock64 is 3.3 times slower. One workload, NewtR, regressed to 1.9 times slower than in 0.10.6, which the authors blame on Wasmtime’s register allocator keeping a value in a stack slot around the loop.

    Recent findings suggest that since the numbers are self-reported and come from one machine and one runtime, results elsewhere may differ. NetWasm can be tried in the online playground, and local setup is covered in the compile and publish guide. Developers can find the documentation is in the official GitHub repository.

    Microsoft suggests Registry hack to work around hotpatch woes

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (355 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theregister

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • App problems in Windows after default hotpatching?
    • Some Windows 11 applications might fail to install or launch after Microsoft's November hotpatch, but not to worry: there's a Registry tweak to work around it.
    • It has been revealed that microsoft has confirmed it isn't administrators' imaginations.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    App problems in Windows after default hotpatching? Who could have foreseen that?

    Some Windows 11 applications might fail to install or launch after Microsoft's November hotpatch, but not to worry: there's a Registry tweak to work around it.

    It has been revealed that microsoft has confirmed it isn't administrators' imaginations. The November hotpatch is causing application errors, including in little-used and obscure apps such as Outlook.

    In a recent development, affected applications may fail during installation, launch, or use, displaying errors such as "ERROR_ALLOTTED_SPACE_EXCEEDED (0xC0000099)." Microsoft's investigation points to applications that load the 32-bit Windows Installer DLL, msi.dll. The problem is more common with 32-bit software, but can also affect 64-bit applications "under certain circumstances.".

    According to recent reports, the workaround involves fiddling with the Registry on affected devices, so is not for the faint of heart and a backup is a good idea before diving in. Microsoft says the key "HotPatchTableSize" in the folder "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Memory Management" needs to be set to "2000" followed by a restart.

    Just the thing to round out the week for administrators.

    Industry observers note that the issue affects the November hotpatch, not the standard monthly cumulative security enhancement. "Devices which installed the November 2026 Windows monthly security update are not expected to be affected by this issue," Microsoft stated.

    In a recent development, windows hotpatches are security updates that don't require a device restart (unless, as in this instance, administrators have to do so to address errors after a hotpatch is installed). Windows 11 hotpatching requires version 24H2 or later, an eligible subscription, and the necessary management and security configuration.

    "Hotpatch update package size is significantly smaller than the standard cumulative updates," Microsoft mentioned, and the goal is to "streamline the installation process and enhance compliance efficiency.".

    Sources indicate that the offending hotpatch, KB5132043, was released on November 10. It followed the October 13 baseline, which was a prerequisite.

    Microsoft made hotpatching the default in Windows Autopatch earlier this year. At the time, we asked: "What could possibly go wrong?".

    It has been revealed that thanks to November's hotpatch, we have our answer. ®.

    ⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that xint is reporting that it has discovered a collection of five critical vulnerabilities in the NGINX web server.
    • Recent findings suggest that xint recommends updating to NGINX 1.31.9, which was just released, and to block the SCTP module on hosts that do not need it until a kernel fix is available.
    • More seriously, it looks like the 'most severe' of the attacks requires sending 128 gigabytes of data; so with luck, we won't see this one be seriously exploited over the internet.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that xint is reporting that it has discovered a collection of five critical vulnerabilities in the NGINX web server. The worst flaw, it says, would allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute commands on an affected nginx server with HTTP/2 enabled. The organization also reports a local-privilege escalation (LPE) kernel vulnerability, which was introduced in the 4.15 kernel, in the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) subsystem. If chained with the NGINX vulnerability, it would allow an attacker to gain root privileges on the host. A kernel patch for this is not yet available.

    Recent findings suggest that xint recommends updating to NGINX 1.31.9, which was just released, and to block the SCTP module on hosts that do not need it until a kernel fix is available. See the mitigations section of their report for more information.

    Anyways, go give your distro security team a hug.

    More seriously, it looks like the 'most severe' of the attacks requires sending 128 gigabytes of data; so with luck, we won't see this one be seriously exploited over the internet.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX.
    • According to recent reports, TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit.
    • Industry observers note that TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

    According to recent reports, TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

    Industry observers note that TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

    The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

    Industry observers note that until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

    Industry observers note that to make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

    In a recent development, torchTPU adds TPU as a upcoming backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:.

    Recent findings suggest that the extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

    In a recent development, transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

    Sources indicate that the model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

    Recent findings suggest that TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

    The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

    Models too massive for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

    Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:.

    TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1.

    The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

    According to recent reports, TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

    The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

    Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

    It has been revealed that we're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

    It has been revealed that the Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

    In a recent development, it's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an glitch on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 complications, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

    If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

    In a recent development, TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

    We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an matter and tell us about it.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that ericsson and Altair Semiconductor have completed what they describe as the first network connection using enhanced Reduced Capability, or eRedCap.
    • Conventional 5G hardware is built to cover demanding workloads, including large downloads and mobile video.
    • Early 5G Reduced Capability, or RedCap, gave device designers a way to use standalone networks without implementing the full set of broadband capabilities.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that ericsson and Altair Semiconductor have completed what they describe as the first network connection using enhanced Reduced Capability, or eRedCap. The November 19 announcement described a test pairing Ericsson’s radio access network software with a device built around Altair’s ALT1550 modem. It is a step toward standalone 5G for wearables, trackers and sensors that do not need a phone’s data rates and cannot easily accommodate a phone-sized battery.

    Conventional 5G hardware is built to cover demanding workloads, including large downloads and mobile video. An asset tracker might send location updates intermittently, while a wearable assistant might transmit a short voice query or receive a response. The performance that makes a broadband device versatile can be an unnecessary design burden for products that move much less data.

    Early 5G Reduced Capability, or RedCap, gave device designers a way to use standalone networks without implementing the full set of broadband capabilities. eRedCap, introduced in 3GPP Release 18, goes further toward the low-data-rate end of that range. Ericsson’s technical overview of RedCap distinguishes the kinds of workloads these technologies can support and describes eRedCap’s potential to lower device cost and energy use. That is a design goal, not a measured battery-life result from the November test.

    Altair already makes LTE-M and NB-IoT chipsets for products such as smart meters and trackers. Its cellular IoT portfolio positions the ALT1550 as a way for customers building around those earlier connectivity options to consider standalone 5G. The test matters because a modem and a radio network have to work together before manufacturers and carriers can validate an actual product. It does not establish that every existing device can move to 5G without a fresh hardware design.

    The modem supplies connectivity rather than inference. An AI device can run some processing locally and use the network when it needs outside information or a model running in the cloud. The modem test did not demonstrate either of those AI workloads, and the companies did not name a wearable ready to ship.

    According to recent reports, that distinction matters when deciding where eRedCap might fit. Glasses that handle wake-word detection locally and send occasional voice requests have different network needs from glasses that continuously upload video for remote interpretation. The former design can make a modest data link useful; the latter needs enough bandwidth and responsiveness to handle a sustained stream. In both cases, the battery also powers the camera, processor, microphones and any display. A simpler modem helps address one part of that budget without solving the rest.

    It has been revealed that altair says the milestone keeps commercial deployments on track for 2027. That is a target, not a launch date or a promise of carrier coverage. The announcement does not identify participating carriers, device makers or markets, nor does it publish measured throughput, latency or energy consumption for the connection. The next evidence to watch is testing on commercial networks and devices that show what these trade-offs mean outside the demonstration.

    Industry observers note that for AI hardware makers, the immediate result is narrower but useful: a modem built for modest data rates has connected to Ericsson’s network software. A wearable with a focused set of AI features may not need a premium radio, but it still needs a network that supports the device and a product design that makes good use of the connectivity.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Windows Search gets a makeover, while Hello lights up dim rooms.
    • Microsoft has delivered its final scheduled non-security preview revision of 2026 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2, with an updated Windows Search experience and a brighter Windows Hello for users who prefer darker rooms.
    • Sources indicate that the optional KB5132057 enhancement arrived on November 19, after this month's Patch Tuesday.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Windows Search gets a makeover, while Hello lights up dim rooms.

    Microsoft has delivered its final scheduled non-security preview revision of 2026 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2, with an updated Windows Search experience and a brighter Windows Hello for users who prefer darker rooms.

    Sources indicate that the optional KB5132057 enhancement arrived on November 19, after this month's Patch Tuesday. Microsoft is skipping December's non-security preview because of reduced holiday operations, though that doesn't cancel the monthly security release. This last preview is quite a doozy.

    The significant-ticket item is the "latest Windows Search Experience." We saw a preview of this last month, and Microsoft has gone well beyond the "just make it work" request of many Windows users. Results appear faster with less clutter, the tool uses memory better, and files can be previewed directly in Windows Search.

    Industry observers note that we're less convinced by inline actions, which let users perform common tasks directly through Windows Search without opening Settings. In our testing, "turn on dark mode" worked, but "switch on dark mode" did not, thus highlighting the limitations of the tool. In addition, we remain unconvinced that Windows Search is the place to run actions.

    That said, anything that makes Windows Search less of a punchline for unkind jokes about performance and accuracy is welcome, as are other features, including an optional screen-brightening feature for Windows Hello facial recognition in dim rooms, and the PowerToys-esque Run dialog, which consumers can enable in Settings.

    Industry observers note that while some of the newly introduced features won't be enabled immediately, Microsoft has included fixes that will be available right away. One addresses an glitch where Windows Fax and Scan could fail to connect to a fax server. Handy for those occasions when email falls over into a heap.

    According to recent reports, there are also fixes for Windows IoT Enterprise LTSC activation failures and the misleading "Something went wrong" message shown on Android devices during cross-device passkey authentication. At the time of writing, Microsoft still lists the problem as something for which "we are working on a resolution to be released in a future Windows revision.".

    Sadly, not everything has been pushed off the naughty step. SQL Server queries using OLE DB providers can still leave connections to external databases open after they've finished. Microsoft is working on that one and "will provide an revision in an upcoming release." ®.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    InfoQ Homepage Presentations RIIIR: Rewrite It In *Idiomatic* Rust (with AI).

    Nicholas Matsakis shares why AI makes Rust the ideal choice for modern production systems, skipping steep adoption hurdles via compiler guardrails. He discusses Symposium - an open-source, agent-oriented toolchain from the Rust Foundation - and demonstrates how the Agent Client Protocol (ACP) standardizes agent-to-tool extensibility across diverse enterprise developer workflows.

    Niko Matsakis is one of the lead designers of the Rust programming language and co-lead of the Rust language design team. He is a Senior Principal Engineer at Amazon and a Project Director on the Rust Foundation Board. He is the creator of Symposium, an open-source platform for agent mods built on the Agent Client Protocol.

    Recent findings suggest that QCon AI is a practitioner-led event focused entirely on the engineering discipline required to scale these workloads safely. It provides direct access to the architectural playbooks and failure metrics that peer organizations use in production.

    Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness.

    Niko Matsakis: My name is Nicholas Matsakis. I am one of the lead designers of the Rust programming language. I've been working on it since 2011. I also am a senior principal engineer at Amazon. I started there about five years ago, in part because Amazon has been adopting tons of Rust, and I wanted to see it firsthand, see how it was going. I'm going to just show my whole cards with you and just tell you all the things I'm going to tell you. Step one, I'm going to try to convince you that Rust and AI is a really great combination, perhaps better than some of the alternatives out there. I have a project I'm curious to get feedback on that I think makes it even better, which I call Symposium, and covers up some of the gaps I see. Next, that actually, if you look at how Symposium works, what you'll find is it reveals something about the way we're presently building all our development tools here, which is that individual vendors, like Anthropic or OpenAI or whatever, everyone's trying to build a complete tool that solves all the problems, and I want to see us do more of an extensibility story where people can plug in and add things and you have a whole bunch of extensions. I think we're only scraping the surface of what is possible, but it's very difficult to do with the way the tools are set up now. Then I'll talk to you about Agent Client Protocol, which is an interesting way to get past that and get to a more extensible model.

    How many have heard of Rust? Rust is all about having a language that can go as low-level as you want, as efficient, give you as much control over the hardware. Low-level enough to be used in a kernel, but be productive. High-level enough that you can write application-level software in it, and it's not too bad. It may not be the minimum line count or what have you, but it's not too bad. Low-level enough for a kernel, I mean that quite literally. We are the only language apart from C, not even C++, that's allowed in the Linux kernel, just C and Rust. Also, we're being used in the Microsoft's kernel and elsewhere. That's been pretty cool. In terms of high-level enough for an application, just to give you some idea, this is a library called ratatui, which is a text user interface library, and they have all kinds of neat little demos.

    Recent findings suggest that you're seeing more and more of this user-facing software where performance may not be the number one criteria, but it works really well in Rust, and then it does scale up to crazy things like this oscilloscope or whatever that is. I've been giving a lot of talks on Rust for the last 15 years. I was at QCon in Brazil, in Sao Paulo in 2019 giving a talk like this. What I would say is it's sometimes a bit of a tough sell, because Rust's whole premise is like this eat your spinach thing. You know where your parents were like, eat it, it's good for you. We're telling you, Rust is going to make your code faster, it's going to make it more efficient, but it is going to take you a month and a half or three months or however long it's going to be to learn how it works and incorporate those new style of development into your workflow.

    People are like, I would like it to go fast, but I want to ship tomorrow, so actually I'm going to stick with TypeScript. I can hire all the people I need. That makes a lot of sense. What I try to tell them is, yes, it is spinach, but it's like Popeyes spinach. You're going to eat it, and then you're going to be stronger, you're going to go faster. It's going to be great. Usually it doesn't win over, but that's changed a lot. What's happened is, if the agent's doing the coding, the agent already learned Rust in its training, its reinforcement learning stages and whatnot. It already passed that stage, so you just get to skip to the Popeyes stage, to the part where you've got this type system that's giving the agent guardrails and helping it stay on track and get programs that are more likely to be correct. You don't have to take it from me. You can take it from Greg Brockman, co-founder and president of OpenAI, who stated Rust is a perfect language for agents, given that if it compiles, it's approximately correct.

    In terms of this range of applications, another thing pulling people in is, like I stated, Rust is low-level enough for a kernel, but usable enough for an application. It covers a wide space. You have things like codex-rs, which used to be in TypeScript, being ported over. That's something that's pulling people in. Then, of course, there's the old standby, which is efficiency. If you're building network services or whatnot, where you're paying per load, or maybe you're building a mobile app or something that's going to take your user's battery, then it becomes a really major consideration. You can save quite a bit of money. That's, of course, what's driving Rust at Amazon. We run things at really large scale. It's been fascinating, though, to watch the shift. When I first got there, it's the same as what I told you, people are thinking, Rust is maybe going to take me some time to learn.

    I'm only going to use it in the critical data paths. S3, EC2, Lambda, those are the first adopters where the real heavy workloads are driving. Then people get used to it, and they started to use it in more and more places. There's an interesting blog post talking about DSQL, which is this serverless SQL database, and their story where they went through that whole trial.     In a recent development, it can see, what did you type? Should I modify it? Should I add stuff? Should I do context augmentation? What should I do to your prompt before I send it to the agent? It can say, here's the tools I would like the agent to have available to it. It can take the responses from the agent and fork off sub-agents, which is also something you can't, as a program, do, and have parallel work happening, can move to other servers, whatever. It's super cool. It's a little scary. I think this is the thing I'm really interested in exploring. For this to work, of course, we have to get ACP-wise used more broadly and so on. Here's me saying, use Zed, or IntelliJ. They're really good. Plus, they use ACP. Everybody wins. I'm expecting that we will see more things like this, whether it's ACP or something else.

    As agentic coding becomes more mainstream, we're going to need to have some standards that let us build on top of it and build more complex workflows. One of the places we're seeing a lot of interest, actually, is in enterprise applications and so on, where they want to build integrations for their employees to offer a better experience than just a CLI.

    You should use Rust for your next project, especially if you're using AI. If you've tried it and bounced, give it another try because it feels different now. Second, when you do it, use Symposium, cargo agents init. Easy. Third, portability sucks, but I hope it will get better.

    According to recent reports, participant 1: For teams that are not familiar with Rust, what's your recommendation on how to start with it? Because with AI, you can really start along with building immediately, and we do, but the fear is that you don't understand the language completely, but then it may end up in production. What's your recommendations for teams that are just starting and they want to ship faster or something like that?

    In a recent development, niko Matsakis: How do you avoid digging yourself into a hole? That is exactly what battery packs are meant to answer, but I'm still trying to make them a real thing. First off, I worry a little less these days because it's so much easier to make changes. Even if you've built stuff, refactoring it is easier. Secondly, what I found really helpful when I'm learning new things is to just really aggressively ask the LLM about its choices. Like it made some choices. You could ask it why. Often, it will give you a good answer. Sometimes it'll say, you're right, that was a bad choice. I'm like, I didn't mean to imply that actually, but ok, go ahead, refactor it. It can go both ways. You don't just have to take the code. You can ask it all about the code and so forth. I think that's the best that I know of. Of course, what I've seen within Amazon, the old advice is still true. Hire someone who knows Rust. That's the surefire way. If you can't do that, then as you get experience, of course, you'll start to have homegrown experts of your own.

    Participant 2: I think a lot of us have noticed when writing skills and however much stuff you put in place to try and ensure that the LLM actually uses it or uses it as intended, and so on, sometimes it will just not do it or ignore it. That kind of skills are too loose, hooks are too hard. How do you make it deterministically actually use this stuff? Have you found through this Symposium project any ways to do that better or make sure it actually does the right thing?

    In a recent development, niko Matsakis: How do we nudge the LLM to be more deterministic? This is exactly why I'm so interested in ACP, actually. I'll give you an example, that retcon thing I revealed you, it began as just a giant LLM script where I told it how to rebase and do stuff. What I found was it worked like 90%. Usually, it would forget some parts of the branch. It just would be like, I'm done. I'm like, no, you're not, you've left off a whole thing. Or it wouldn't check that the test pass and everything else. Now when it's written in Rust, like I'm guaranteed every commit passes the test, every commit is formatted because it's got a deterministic backing. I have been toying with similar things for skills where I had experiments where I would detect with some various heuristics and things that I thought a skill was probably good and give it some extra hints to avoid that problem.

    I've backed off from a lot of that, partly because models get better, but also because I think we need telemetry first. I feel we need deterministic stuff, and I feel we need a way to measure, are we actually helping or not? Because what I noticed is a lot of times it's a little unclear. I want some better infrastructure where I can actually measure, how often is a skill being used? If I do give it some nudges, am I actually making people's lives better? Like I could do A/B tests, stuff like that. I think it's a real concern, and I don't think there's a great answer right now.

    📅 21 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1279 w)

    Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

    📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1279 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
    • In a recent development, this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
    • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

    In a recent development, this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

    Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

    According to recent reports, the Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating Fresh Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

    You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

    Sources indicate that the modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

    Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

    After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

    For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

    You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

    The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

    All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

    Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

    Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

    The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

    Call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

    After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

    The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

    According to recent reports, the table demonstrates which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

    Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

    Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

    In Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

    It has been revealed that the system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

    In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

    The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

    Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

    The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

    The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

    In a recent development, in the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

    For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

    Recent findings suggest that with @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

    The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

    The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

    The table reveals one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

    Recent findings suggest that both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

    key_averages() reveals which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

    You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

    According to recent reports, in Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

    Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!
