    #11336. Tech Report: We Need Smart People Who Give a Shit

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1258 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Violetpixel ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: We Need Smart People Who Give a Shit

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1258 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Violetpixel

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Something I learned a long time ago, something that's been proven to me time and again, is that the world is held together by smart people who give a shit.
    • Sources indicate that when I worked at Stripe I learned a lot about various banking and money movement systems, and it's terrifying how flawed and fragile these systems are.
    • The reason there's a mismatch between the technical reality of the ACH system and how it functions in practice is due to a single factor: smart people who give a shit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Tuesday, November 17th, 2026 @ 7:01 PM PST.

    Something I learned a long time ago, something that's been proven to me time and again, is that the world is held together by smart people who give a shit. This truth always comes into stark focus when I learn how a complex system functions—or, rather, how it barely functions.

    Sources indicate that when I worked at Stripe I learned a lot about various banking and money movement systems, and it's terrifying how flawed and fragile these systems are. ACH is a great example. It's a complex system we rely on every day that is just barely good enough to function. It's old, riddled with flaws, and encumbered with legacy baggage. And yet, despite all of those problems, ACH usually works great and is generally considered to be safe, cheap, and reliable.

    The reason there's a mismatch between the technical reality of the ACH system and how it functions in practice is due to a single factor: smart people who give a shit. Every problem with ACH is fixed, patched, bypassed, overridden, routed around, or manually handled by people who have two things:.

    Sources indicate that those two things feed into each other. You have to care about a complex system to dive deep enough to learn how it works, and when you know a lot about how a complex system works you care more about it, especially if the system is important or critical infrastructure.

    In a recent development, now, you can replace "ACH" above with a myriad of other complex systems—everything from huge infrastructure to nice-to-have apps—and everything I noted remains true, both about the systems themselves and the people who keep them running. The world runs on these systems, and they depend on smart people who give a shit. Take those people away, and the systems collapse.

    And collapse is what we're starting to see. Some recent examples of various failures from just this past week or so: Microsoft 365, Air Traffic Control, United Airlines' systems, the NSA's network, many major banks, Apple's systems, and more. We're told these failures and problems are not related. They're not the result of a cyberattack. They're not the fault of generative AI.

    I guess that depends on how you look at it.

    I don't have inside information about what's going on, but my experience dealing with complex systems tells me there's a common through line to all of these disruptions: there aren't enough smart people who give a shit.

    Capitalism has never been particularly kind to smart people who give a shit (or people in general... but I digress). Capitalism does, however begrudgingly, recognize that smart people who give a shit are required to build and maintain complex systems that serve capitalist goals. Thus, those people have been accommodated and incorporated into the system by virtue of their necessity and, in many cases, their rarity.

    Sources indicate that now, though, generative AI is here. To the people running the show—leadership and management—it seems like they can get the same or better value (and even more output!) from a machine. The machine is cheaper, works longer, doesn't take sick days or vacations, doesn't ask for any benefits, and never pushes back against a bad idea.

    People who don't do the actual work—the people who aren't in the trenches—have a hard time telling the difference between a flawed system held aloft by the drive and determination of smart people who give a shit and slop provided by generative AI. To them it's all just output: words you can read, code that runs, and pixels that look nice to their eye. It's all the same to them, so why does it matter where it comes from?

    Industry observers note that it matters because generative AI isn't smart, and it doesn't give a shit. What seems like intelligence is an illusion propped up by a massive amount of data strip-mined from the commons with weights that nudge the output toward a generally desirable shape. What seems like care, concern, and attention is just generative AI doing what it's designed to do: telling you what you want to hear. The math and logic that power LLMs are as cold, unfeeling, and indifferent as the laws of physics.

    Sources indicate that smart people who give a shit notice things. They connect dots. They notice when things don't feel right. They know when something is about to go off the rails, and they know how to get things back on track. They know how to handle edge cases. They know how to manually handle a unique situation. They know what the right thing to do is, and they know when they need to put in extra effort or time to make something happen. Generative AI falls far short in these areas, but this is the glue that holds complex systems together. More prompting and more output isn't a substitute for this.

    Industry observers note that it's hard for capitalist leadership to internalize any of that, though. It would be such a relief for them, such a burden lifted, to replace all those smart people who give a shit with generative AI. It would be so much easier to win at capitalism if generative AI lived up to the hype, and there's so much pressure for leadership and management to believe that the hype is real.

    Thus, a lot of the smart people who give a shit have been laid off, and the ones that remain are hollowed out. Telling people to stop doing the job they signed up for in favor of babysitting LLMs so they can do that job instead is a great way to make people less smart about the system they used to work on and give less of a shit about it. Every prompt moves them one step further away from the system they used to know inside and out. Every generated output that becomes part of the system means those people understand less about how the system actually works. Those people are robbed of the things that make them smart (the struggle of building and learning) and the things that made them gave a shit (a sense of ownership and close connection with the system).

    It has been revealed that we've moved from a world dependent on complex and fragile systems held together by smart people who give a shit to a world of complex and fragile systems run by generative AI. The people running the generative AI are not as smart, nor do they give as much of a shit. There are, of course, exceptions (which is why a lot of things are still humming along), but we are on a course where the number of smart people who give a shit are decreasing, and that's a big problem. As long as the number continues to go down, more systems will fail.

    Industry observers note that I think what we have here is a hot stove moment for capitalism. When you tell a young kid a stove is hot and they shouldn't touch it, you'll find there are two kinds of kids. For one kind of kid, the warning is the lesson, and they don't touch the stove. For the other kind of kid, the only lesson that works for them is being burned. They have to touch the stove at least once to learn the lesson. Capitalism was told the stove was hot, but their hand is on it right now.

    Unfortunately, we're all getting burned.

    Tech Report: 'Critical' 1970s-era Fujitsu UK police system could remain unsupported for three years

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1024 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Home Office needs more time with the PNC, which began life more than 50 years ago.
    • The UK's Home Office faces running the Police National Computer (PNC) without vendor support for three years or more as it misses another deadline to decommission the ageing crime-fighting system first introduced in 1974.
    • The PNC was first launched in 1974, when Tom Baker began his iconic role playing Doctor Who, and has seen the tenure of 26 UK Home Secretaries, surviving multiple efforts to replace it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Home Office needs more time with the PNC, which began life more than 50 years ago.

    The UK's Home Office faces running the Police National Computer (PNC) without vendor support for three years or more as it misses another deadline to decommission the ageing crime-fighting system first introduced in 1974.

    The PNC was first launched in 1974, when Tom Baker began his iconic role playing Doctor Who, and has seen the tenure of 26 UK Home Secretaries, surviving multiple efforts to replace it.

    Sources indicate that A notice in December 2024 said that the Home Office was "focused on the development and adoption of the Law Enforcement Data Service (LEDS) products to replace existing PNC capability across all police forces and other non-policing PNC consumers, enabling the retirement by March 2026 (the point at which PNC support will expire)." We understand that PNC support refers to the Fujitsu support contract for the mainframe, which is housed in north London. Support for the Software AG database on the mainframe OS (BS2000) ran out at the end of 2024. So the database holding the crucial police data remains out of standard support and potentially will stay that way until 2027.

    The decommissioning date for the PNC had already been pushed back by the need to delay and "reset" the LEDS in 2020. The Home Office launched its successor, National Law Enforcement Data Service, in 2016, and planned to finish the new system by 2020 at a cost of £671 million.

    The Home Office told The Register this week that it needed more time, and it aimed to begin decommissioning the system from March 2027, raising questions over how it would be supported.

    A Home Office spokesperson noted: "We are modernizing policing systems to adapt to evolving challenges, including rolling out the LEDS to replace the Police National Computer.

    "While LEDS is already operational, we are continuing to run the legacy Police National Computer system to support the operational needs of all UK police," they mentioned.

    Officials noted the PNC would remain available throughout the transition and would only be disconnected when police forces have confirmed that they no longer need it.

    Sources indicate that earlier this month, in a written response in the House of Lords, Lord Hanson of Flint, a junior minister, mentioned the PNC might be required until early 2028. Some LEDS services were already live and the program was "targeting completion of the remaining development, adoption and readiness activity in early 2027 as we prepare for our final stages for LEDS deployment before retiring the PNC," he said.

    "Once the transition of all police users to the LEDS has been completed and policing has confirmed that the PNC is no longer required, the system will be disconnected and decommissioned. The decommissioning process is expected to take place between late 2027 and early 2028," he noted.

    Sources indicate that according to the National Audit Office (NAO), the PNC is the most vital national policing information system in the UK. It serves front-line officers from all 45 local police forces, as well as by 127 other organisations that need to access its data. In 2019-20, the police searched or updated the PNC 133 million times.

    The ongoing delay to the decommissioning of the PNC raises questions about how — and whether — it is being adequately supported.

    The PNC is sited at a datacenter in Hendon, North London, and is based on a Fujitsu BS2000/OSD SE700-30 mainframe, but this is technology originally developed by German engineering outfit Siemens inherited by Fujitsu when it acquired the data processing division of that manufacturer.

    It was the subject of controversy in 2021 when an error led to the accidental loss of 413,000 records of police evidence from the system, the result of a scripting error in code designed to weed out records targeted for deletion, although the lost data was eventually recovered.

    In 2022, Fujitsu — the Japanese tech giant at the center of the Post Office Horizon scandal — was awarded a £48 million ($56.6 million) renewed contract for support and maintenance of the PNC after no other companies tendered for the work. The contract was set to expire in March 2026.

    In its 2021 report, NAO remarked the Fujitsu mainframe computer used by the PNC would reach the end of its supported life by 31 December 2021.

    "The Software AG database used by the PNC is only supported on the Fujitsu mainframe until 31 December 2023. The Department has an option to extend the contract for this support for a further 12 months but it has not yet agreed this with the supplier. If [the replacement system] is not ready, the PNC will need to be moved off the mainframe onto a supported operating system from 2025 or run unsupported," the report noted.

    In a recent development, however, at the time, the Home Office told the NAO it had decided to accept the risk of running the PNC without support for the database for 12 months after December 2024. "This would leave the PNC at higher risk of disruption for at least a year, although the Department's view is that the actual risk profile is low because of the mitigation actions put in place," the report stated [PDF].

    It added that moving the PNC to a latest operating system could take three years and Home Office estimated that it will cost at least £30 million, including the cost of rewriting code for the new OS.

    A report from the Public Accounts Committee later in November 2021 said: "The team that maintains the PNC is under-resourced and several staff are nearing retirement… The Department currently aims to run this piece of critical national infrastructure without full manufacturer support for the database after 2024, meaning it will not have that support for at least a year, though the Department plans to provide in-house support instead.".

    Sources indicate that unless the Home Office has come up with another initiative in the meantime, it is set to extend that out-of-support period to around three years. It has been offered the opportunity to provide additional comment. ®.

    Announcing jj-musubi: live sync for Jujutsu

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (860 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Serpentine

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that I’m pleased to announce a upcoming source control tool, jj-musubi, that live-syncs copies of a Jujutsu (jj) repository across multiple machines.
    • jj-musubi makes repos on multiple machines feel like jj workspaces (worktrees if you speak git).
    • It’s intended for use by one person who works across several machines, so it has no security model (or rather, that is the extent of its security model).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that I’m pleased to announce a upcoming source control tool, jj-musubi, that live-syncs copies of a Jujutsu (jj) repository across multiple machines. Every time jj snapshots my work, jj-musubi syncs it to every machine in moments, and also commits, rebases, fetches, and so on.

    This simple capability is surprisingly powerful.

    jj-musubi makes repos on multiple machines feel like jj workspaces (worktrees if you speak git).

    It’s intended for use by one person who works across several machines, so it has no security model (or rather, that is the extent of its security model).

    Sources indicate that jujutsu already treats the working copy as a commit. Running jj status records a snapshot of my edits in that commit, which jj-musubi then syncs to my other machines. I like to have my shell prompt run jj status, so in practice I rarely have to think about snapshots.

    Sources indicate that jj-musubi does not write to the working copy. Each machine has its own working copy and workspaces as usual, so syncs of commits, snapshots, and rewrites can bring in new history while a build is running, without changing the files under it. On a laptop, I can work offline, and my machine will sync when I’m back on the network.

    This has also proven handy when I have agents working on several machines. I can give each agent its own jj workspace on different systems, then run jj diff -r devbox/agent-1@ on the laptop to see what one of them has done so far. If one finds a bug that another needs to fix, they can coordinate and see each other’s work without overhead.

    jj-musubi refers to a collection of copies of a repo as a hive.

    Industry observers note that I often run agents in temporary disposable VMs. jj-musubi supports this by allowing an agent to lease its repo’s membership in the hive: if it doesn’t renew that lease in time, its repo gets forgotten about, so temporary repos or vanished containers can’t just stack up and clutter things.

    Industry observers note that back when I was at Meta, I kicked off the project that became Sapling and Mononoke. Sapling’s Commit Cloud gives engineers there a similar way to move work between machines, and Google engineers have something similar with an internal jj server.

    Since then, I’d missed that everyday convenience for the machines I already use, and felt like I could get it without massive infrastructure or hosting. With jj-musubi, one machine runs a hub, and daemons exchange jj history with it over SSH. That’s almost as lightweight as you can get.

    In a recent development, what’s tricky is getting concurrent work right. That’s already hard in any distributed source control system, and when syncs are live and we plan for disconnected work in an unreliable network, the difficulty goes way up.

    As a user, I shouldn’t have to care about when exactly I can safely close my laptop after finishing an edit; all of my changes should make it through either just before I close it, or right after I reopen. No work should get lost or corrupted in the presence of interrupts, resends, delays, or machines sleeping, and the system should stay reliable even when machines go offline forever.

    I used Lean to prove key properties of jj-musubi’s network protocol, and tests compare the Rust code against that model. An extensive body of other tests run real jj repositories through concurrent edits, interrupted syncs, hub restarts, and a myriad of other nasty situations. Mutation and adversarial testing ensure that when bugs are injected, sensible things happen. The safety guide details all the checks (and the parts I don’t yet cover).

    According to recent reports, it might sound spooky or dangerous to be able to see in-progress work on one machine from another. How can that be safe?

    If you use jj in multiple workspaces, you’re already used to the novelty of being able to check out the same change in two workspaces and modify it. jj simply marks the change as divergent, but it won’t patch either working copy with changes from the other until you decide to, e.g. by calling jj workspace update-stale. In jj, dealing with divergent versions of a change is similar to any other kind of conflicted merge.

    Industry observers note that jj-musubi uses jj’s existing workspace machinery, so everything will feel familiar. The only difference is that when you run jj-musubi, a workspace’s name is prefixed with the name of the machine it lives on.

    Start with e.g. a laptop and another machine that’s always on (let’s call it devbox), with a copy of a jj repo on each. On each machine, download the binary or build it yourself:.

    Sources indicate that run musubi hub on devbox; it will keep your sync data in ~/musubi-hub. In the laptop’s repo, run musubi create --hub devbox. In devbox’s repo, run musubi join.

    Industry observers note that I provide builds for Linux, macOS and Windows, and the quick start walks through setup and the first sync. If you try it and something surprises you, I’d like to hear about it.

    #11332. How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

    📅 21 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2222 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

    📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2222 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
    • Industry observers note that in an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens.
    • The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

    Industry observers note that in an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

    The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

    Industry observers note that one of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

    According to recent reports, the model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

    According to recent reports, we rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

    The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

    For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

    It has been revealed that the first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

    Recent findings suggest that the second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

    The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

    Industry observers note that to see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

    This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

    Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

    Industry observers note that the third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

    In a recent development, and the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

    Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

    Recent findings suggest that they choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

    Industry observers note that they work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

    VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

    It has been revealed that first, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

    Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

    Industry observers note that to find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

    It has been revealed that third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

    An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

    According to recent reports, A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

    That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

    To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

    According to recent reports, the model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

    In a recent development, getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

    The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

    In a recent development, to find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

    VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

    VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

    According to recent reports, specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

    The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

    Breaking: Garage Door Spam

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (385 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Harrison

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In the beginning, my garage door opener worked fine.
    • I continued using it because I trusted that notifications were meaningful...
    • Sources indicate that this is un-fucking-acceptable.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In the beginning, my garage door opener worked fine. When the door opened or closed, I would get a notification. If I'm away from home and the door opens, something weird is going down. The "myQ" app generally worked although it was encrusted with ads:.

    I continued using it because I trusted that notifications were meaningful...

    ...until recently (October 2026):.

    Sources indicate that this is un-fucking-acceptable. As in, absolutely fucking not.

    The manufacturer (Chamberlain) cut off third-party access to its APIs (via myQ) in late 2023. In response, I purchased a pair of ratgdo32 devices to opt out of the bullshit.

    ratgdo is a WiFi control board for your garage door opener that works over your local network using ESP Home or HomeKit.

    The device is a ~$62 board from ratcloud llc running open-source firmware that wires to the opener's existing terminals and speaks LiftMaster's Security+ 2.0 protocol locally.

    These were easy enough to hook up. I won't reproduce the instructions here.

    The bundle included six black wires, an auxiliary harness I didn’t need.

    Sources indicate that my router hands each board a fixed address at 192.168.0.192 and 192.168.0.245. Apple's HomeKit just worked and I'm able to control them with voice commands: “Hey Siri, open Door 1”.

    The devices have their own web interface:.

    When I was growing up, my father wired a mercury switch onto our garage door that lit up a light in the hallway when we'd left the garage door open. This was a valuable signal that helped our family avoid accidentally leaving the door open overnight. Since the ratgdo32 has a JSON status endpoint, I was able to rebuild Dad's solution in software with Slack:.

    The script runs at night checking for an open door:.

    It has been revealed that the repo maintainer made my day when I submitted a tiny pull request: "Simple and useful. Happy to merge this. Thank you.".

    Both boards are now reachable over my Tailscale network, so my monitoring software can load /healthcheck. This required a custom route:.

    After approving the route, my monitoring software can verify the hardware is working.

    Everything runs locally with no cloud, and notifications now say who opened the door which myQ never did.

    To anyone at Chamberlain responsible for myQ, I offer my sincerest Fuck You.

    J-POWER, Hitachi and Macnica revealed on November 19, 2026 that they had agreed to jointly study a physical AI development platform for critical infrastructure, with next-generation transmission-line inspection drones as the first proposed use case.

    At this stage, the agreement covers joint studies and demonstration planning. Physical AI applies artificial intelligence to machines operating in the physical world, such as robots and drones. The companies expect it to support more advanced and autonomous inspection and maintenance in Japan, where critical infrastructure sectors face shortages of skilled workers and aging equipment.

    The proposed platform would train AI in simulation for infrastructure operation, maintenance and control, validate the models and install them on equipment and robots. Field data would then feed further training and validation, creating a simulation-to-reality cycle known as Sim2Real.

    The companies say training and validating models solely in real environments creates constraints in time, cost and safety. The design therefore combines digital twins, which replicate real environments, with a platform intended to manage confidential data securely while supporting continuous AI training, validation and operation.

    Technologies under consideration include NVIDIA’s Omniverse simulation libraries, Cosmos world-model platform and Isaac robotics development platform. Hitachi would combine these with HMAX Data Fabric, which organizes field data and expert knowledge for AI use, and HMAX AI Operations, which monitors AI operating conditions and model-specific risks.

    Industry observers note that an edge environment based on NVIDIA Jetson would support studies of real-time equipment recognition, anomaly detection, autonomous movement and path planning. The companies intend for those inference tasks to run on field equipment, so robots and drones would not need a continuous cloud connection at infrastructure sites.

    In a recent development, the first initiative will examine demonstrations of next-generation transmission-line inspection drones using real J-POWER Group power generation and transmission facilities as testing environments. J-POWER will plan use cases, provide those facilities, and evaluate and verify the study results.

    It has been revealed that hitachi’s Forward Deployed Engineers team will refine and evaluate use cases, study the platform architecture, and build and verify the platform, drawing on power-sector knowledge and expertise in IT, operational technology and AI. Macnica, an authorized NVIDIA distributor, will support the design, construction and operation of the Sim2Real demonstration environment and help examine robotics use cases and applications.

    Industry observers note that results from the initial drone work are intended to guide practical applications in inspection and maintenance automation, advanced autonomous control and disaster-recovery support. The companies also strategy to expand partnerships beyond electricity into other critical infrastructure fields, including railways and industrial plants.

    According to recent reports, implementation on the AI data center that J-POWER and Hitachi are separately studying is also under consideration. The companies’ AI Factory concept spans data collection, learning, validation, inference and continuous improvement.

    It has been revealed that running the platform on that data center is intended to integrate operation of the digital infrastructure supporting AI with power infrastructure. That would deepen coordination between power and communications that the companies call watt-bit collaboration.

    Sources indicate that J-POWER executive officer Shingo Koizumi described the aim of developing the initiative into a landmark model for physical AI in critical infrastructure. The proposed drone demonstrations are the first practical test of that ambition: they must establish whether simulation-trained models can work dependably on operating power assets before the same development process can support the partners’ wider aims.

    Producing Healthy Code with Artificial Intelligence Costs Fewer Tokens

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (746 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • InfoQ Homepage News Producing Healthy Code with Artificial Intelligence Costs Fewer Tokens.
    • Nov 19, 2026 4 min read.
    • Agentic AI can speed up velocity, but the gains vanish within months as code complexity grows.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    InfoQ Homepage News Producing Healthy Code with Artificial Intelligence Costs Fewer Tokens.

    Nov 19, 2026 4 min read.

    Agentic AI can speed up velocity, but the gains vanish within months as code complexity grows. In his presentation on AI-friendly code at GOTO Copenhagen, Adam Tornhill highlighted that healthy code makes AI perform better and costs fewer tokens. Safeguarding means keeping code health high through agentic refactoring, with an MCP supplying code health data, so AI can maintain the code it generates.

    Developing software with agents is significantly harder than writing code manually, Tornhill argued. But with agentic AI, they can complete tasks two to three times faster, he added. It also helps them unblock themselves and reduces coordination needs.

    Tornhill mentioned a study done on 1000+ open-source projects which showed that with AI, velocity went up during the first few weeks, but after two months the velocity gains were fully canceled out due to a massive increase in code complexity:.

    AI operates in a self-harm mode, often writing code it cannot reliably maintain later.

    Sources indicate that code health measures how easy code is to understand, change, and maintain. Research done on human coding (before AI) shows that if you have healthy code, you can be up to 10x faster than someone who works on similar problems in unhealthy code, Tornhill noted. The defect risk is reduced 15 times, and code reviews go twice as rapidly, he added.

    According to recent reports, building a prototype was never the hard problem in software; 95% of the costs for any software project come after the first release. This is where code quality, maintainability, and architecture start to matter, Tornhill said.

    Sources indicate that recent research reveals that large language models perform consistently better in healthy code. AI won’t generate perfect code; if we want to survive in the Agentic age, we need to focus on safeguarding, Tornhill said.

    Industry observers note that the average codebase has a code health of 5.15, where AI-friendly code starts at 9.5. Technical depth is a bottleneck for enterprise adoption of agentic coding; what’s needed is an agentic refactoring, Tornhill argued. Claude can be used to fix code health complications, but only to a certain extent:.

    As a best-case scenario, an agent can fix roughly 50% of the code health issues for lower-health code. Once the code health improves, the AI performance drops sharply, and Claude can only correctly refactor 20% of the code. AI tends to become conservative, doing small changes that don’t really move the needle on code quality.

    According to recent reports, adding an MCP with code health data can lead to a 90%-100% fix rate, Tornhill said. Agentic refactoring turned out to be a predictable and mechanical process at scale, where AI was capable of doing codebase-specific refactorings.

    Healthy code is also financially viable code, with healthy code, you can do things with 40% to 45% fewer tokens, Tornhill mentioned.

    By refactoring code, modularizing it and making it healthy, we can also reduce organizational friction, Tornhill said. Code quality at the module level is a largely solved problem with the automation we now have. Scaling AI friendliness to the design and architectural level is the next substantial challenge, he concluded.

    InfoQ interviewed Adam Tornhill after his talk.

    InfoQ: How can we measure code health?

    Adam Tornhill: Code Health is a multifacetted concept, so we need to combine multiple metrics. We’ve found that it works best when combining measures from three levels of software design:.

    InfoQ: How do you safeguard AI-generated code?

    In a recent development, tornhill: Safeguarding needs to happen at multiple levels, and all safeguards need to be completely automated in an agentic context. Examples of concrete safeguards include linting, code coverage, mutation testing to ensure your tests actually test, and higher-level metrics like Code Health. In practice, these safeguards are exposed to agents as local MCP servers or command-line tools.

    InfoQ: How can we do refactoring at scale with agents?

    Tornhill: The main steps are to establish a baseline, build a safety-net for behavior, and provide a feedback loop to the agents refactoring the code. The whole process is highly iterative.

    Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

    📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3117 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done.
    • Recent findings suggest that we built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome.
    • ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

    Recent findings suggest that we built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

    Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

    We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

    Recent findings suggest that each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

    Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+.

    So we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

    Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

    We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

    We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

    Industry observers note that table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

    According to recent reports, training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

    What does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but tech giant policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

    Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

    In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

    ThinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly new solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

    In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

    Sources indicate that and bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

    If you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 indicates which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

    It has been revealed that the executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

    Industry observers note that after training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

    Table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

    It has been revealed that the headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

    Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

    It has been revealed that the observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

    Sources indicate that overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

    Recent findings suggest that figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

    Pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

    The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

    Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

    Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:.

    In a recent development, table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

    At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

    Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

    Sources indicate that figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

    According to recent reports, the move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

    Recent findings suggest that the dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

    According to recent reports, these results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

    Sources indicate that figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

    According to recent reports, selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

    Every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

    In a recent development, training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

    Sources indicate that for the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each upgrade generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

    According to recent reports, zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

    That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

    Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:.

    No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

    It has been revealed that thinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

    Recent findings suggest that why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++.

    A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

    The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

    We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

    So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

    Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:.

    success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½).

    Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

    In a recent development, we partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:.

    Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

    Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update.

    Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

    When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

    The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

    Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

    Recent findings suggest that when an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

    Sources indicate that in the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

    Two reward paths, one binary verdict.

    It has been revealed that we release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training. The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are:.

    PostgreSQL 19 Released

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1527 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Postgresql

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • November 19, 2026 - The PostgreSQL Global Development Group today announced the release of PostgreSQL 19, the latest version of the world's most advanced open source database.
    • Mission-critical usage of PostgreSQL continues to rapidly rise, and PostgreSQL 19 responds to this by simplifying both administration and development for these workloads at scale.
    • According to recent reports, "For over 30 years, the global open source community has built PostgreSQL into a database that organizations trust with their most critical data," said Jonathan Katz, a member of the PostgreSQL core team.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    November 19, 2026 - The PostgreSQL Global Development Group today announced the release of PostgreSQL 19, the latest version of the world's most advanced open source database.

    Mission-critical usage of PostgreSQL continues to rapidly rise, and PostgreSQL 19 responds to this by simplifying both administration and development for these workloads at scale. This release introduces the REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) command so users can optimize tables for their current workload without disruption to ongoing operations. PostgreSQL 19 gives users better control over plan stability and query performance with the latest pg_plan_advice extension. Developers will find many delightful features in this release, from support for "read-your-writes" consistency on standbys to "get or create" behavior that saves a network round trip.

    According to recent reports, "For over 30 years, the global open source community has built PostgreSQL into a database that organizations trust with their most critical data," said Jonathan Katz, a member of the PostgreSQL core team. "PostgreSQL 19 continues that commitment to reliability, giving customers new ways to manage their workloads without disruption and to build applications that span multiple systems.".

    PostgreSQL, an innovative data management system known for its reliability, robustness, and extensibility, benefits from 30 years of open source development from a global developer community and has become the preferred open source relational database for organizations of all sizes.

    In a recent development, tables that receive many updates and deletes can build up unused space, known as "bloat," which can also significantly impact query performance. The VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER commands were previously used to handle this, but had tradeoffs, including preventing access to the table until the cleanup finished. PostgreSQL 19 introduces the REPACK command, which reclaims this space and can reorder a table's data to match an index, and with REPACK (CONCURRENTLY), can do so without blocking reads or writes. REPACK replaces the VACUUM FULL and CLUSTER commands, both of which remain available for compatibility.

    The PostgreSQL query planner usually picks an efficient strategy for each query, but the plan can change as your data changes, and sometimes the new plan is slower. PostgreSQL 19 adds the pg_plan_advice extension, which allows stabilization of plan choices and the ability to experiment with different looks using the "plan advice" mini-language. The companion pg_stash_advice extension stores advice and automatically applies it to queries based on their query identifier, so you can fix a slow plan without changing your application.

    PostgreSQL 19 also helps autovacuum keep up on busy systems. Autovacuum can now vacuum indexes using parallel workers, controlled by the new autovacuum_max_parallel_workers setting, and uses a new scoring system to decide which tables to process first. Queries that read a table can now automatically mark pages as all-visible in the visibility map during execution, reducing the work that future vacuums need to do. Additionally, vacuumdb --analyze-only now analyzes partitioned tables when no tables are specified.

    Recent findings suggest that this release adds fresh views for monitoring workloads, including pg_stat_lock for per-lock-type statistics, pg_stat_recovery for recovery status, and pg_stat_autovacuum_scores to show how autovacuum prioritizes tables. The new IO option for EXPLAIN ANALYZE and the matching auto_explain setting report asynchronous I/O activity. PostgreSQL 19 also reports the amount of WAL written for full-page images in pg_stat_wal, EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, WAL), and in vacuum and analyze log events.

    Sources indicate that previously, PostgreSQL often required users to restart their server to enable logical replication, which could be disruptive in production workloads. PostgreSQL 19 simplifies logical replication initialization by automatically raising the effective WAL level to logical when you create the first logical replication slot. You can see the WAL level in use with the latest effective_wal_level setting.

    PostgreSQL 19 also adds logical replication of sequence values, which you can publish using FOR ALL SEQUENCES with CREATE PUBLICATION. CREATE PUBLICATION also adds an EXCEPT clause to exclude tables when publishing FOR ALL TABLES, and CREATE SUBSCRIPTION can now get its connection settings from a foreign server, such as one defined with postgres_fdw, using the SERVER clause. Additionally, the new retain_dead_tuples subscription option lets PostgreSQL detect updates that conflict with a concurrent delete, and these conflicts are counted in pg_stat_subscription_stats.

    For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the fresh WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary.

    Sources indicate that postgreSQL 19 also improves queries on foreign tables. With the newly introduced import_stats option, postgres_fdw can import table statistics from the remote server when you run ANALYZE, instead of sampling rows from the remote table, which helps the query planner choose better plans.

    In a recent development, postgreSQL 19 adds INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT, which lets the RETURNING clause return existing rows that conflict with an insert, simplifying the common "get or create" pattern. COPY can now output data as JSON, including as a single JSON array, and the SQL/JSON path language adds string methods such as lower(), upper(), replace(), split_part(), and btrim(). Additionally, the lead(), lag(), first_value(), last_value(), and nth_value() window functions can now skip NULL values using IGNORE NULLS. The random() function can now also generate random dates and timestamps within a range.

    This release also makes many workloads faster without changes to your application. PostgreSQL 19 improves the performance of foreign key checks, which in testing made bulk inserts nearly 2x faster, and adds more query planner optimizations, such as converting NOT IN clauses to more efficient anti-joins when NULL values are not present, and performing eager aggregation before joins to reduce the number of rows to process. PostgreSQL 19 also builds on the asynchronous I/O subsystem added in PostgreSQL 18. When io_method is set to worker (the default), PostgreSQL now automatically adjusts the number of I/O workers between the fresh io_min_workers and io_max_workers settings, which replace the io_workers setting. There are also scalability improvements when using LISTEN and NOTIFY to exchange notifications in multi-channel workloads.

    Finally, the latest password_expiration_warning_threshold setting warns users when their password is about to expire.

    In a recent development, postgreSQL 19 adds server-side support for Server Name Indication (SNI), letting a single PostgreSQL server present a different TLS certificate based on the hostname a client connects to. You can map hostnames to their certificates and keys in the new pg_hosts.conf file. PostgreSQL 19 also now complications a warning after a successful md5 password authentication, which you can turn off with the md5_password_warnings setting. md5 password authentication was deprecated in PostgreSQL 18 and will be removed in a future release. If you require password-based authentication, use SCRAM authentication. This release also removes support for RADIUS authentication.

    According to recent reports, just-in-time compilation (JIT) is now disabled by default, as the cost estimates PostgreSQL used to decide when to use it proved unreliable. If you run many large analytical queries, you may want to enable JIT. When PostgreSQL is built with LZ4 support, the default TOAST compression method is now lz4.

    Many other new features and improvements have been added to PostgreSQL 19 that may also be helpful for your use cases. Please see the release notes for a complete list of new and changed features.

    PostgreSQL is the world's most advanced open source database, with a global community of thousands of people, contributors, companies and organizations. Since its beginnings at the University of California, Berkeley over 40 years ago, PostgreSQL has continued with an unmatched pace of development. PostgreSQL's mature feature set not only matches top proprietary database systems, but exceeds them in advanced database features, extensibility, security, and stability.

    For explanations of the above features and others, please see the following resources:.

    There are several ways you can download PostgreSQL 19, including:.

    Other tools and extensions are available on the PostgreSQL Extension Network.

    PostgreSQL 19 comes with HTML documentation as well as man pages, and you can also browse the documentation online in both HTML and PDF formats.

    Industry observers note that postgreSQL uses the PostgreSQL License, a BSD-like "permissive" license. This OSI-certified license is widely appreciated as flexible and business-friendly, since it does not restrict the use of PostgreSQL with commercial and proprietary applications. Together with multi-manufacturer support and public ownership of the code, our license makes PostgreSQL very popular with vendors wanting to embed a database in their own products without fear of fees, vendor lock-in, or changes in licensing terms.

    In a recent development, postgres, PostgreSQL, and the Elephant Logo (Slonik) are all registered trademarks of the PostgreSQL Community Association. If you wish to use these marks, you must comply with the trademark policy.

    In a recent development, postgreSQL enjoys the support of numerous companies, who sponsor developers, provide hosting resources, and give us financial support. See our sponsors page for some of these project supporters.

    There is also a large community of companies offering PostgreSQL Support, from individual consultants to multinational companies.

    If you wish to make a financial contribution to the PostgreSQL Global Development Group or one of the recognized community non-profit organizations, please visit our donations page.

    DeepMind Institute Maps Four Routes From AGI to Superintelligence

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (994 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite
