    💡 Key Takeaways
    • DeepMind Institute published an essay on November 19, 2026, outlining four ways AI could move from human-level artificial general intelligence (AGI) to artificial general superintelligence (ASI), while stressing that continued rapid progress is possible but far from assured.
    • The four routes are continued scaling of models and data, technological paradigm shifts, coordination among large agent populations, and recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems contribute to improving later systems.
    • The essay uses AGI for systems with roughly human-level capability across almost all cognitive tasks.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    DeepMind Institute published an essay on November 19, 2026, outlining four ways AI could move from human-level artificial general intelligence (AGI) to artificial general superintelligence (ASI), while stressing that continued rapid progress is possible but far from assured.

    The four routes are continued scaling of models and data, technological paradigm shifts, coordination among large agent populations, and recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems contribute to improving later systems. Each presents different technical bottlenecks and measurement problems.

    The essay uses AGI for systems with roughly human-level capability across almost all cognitive tasks. ASI must reliably outperform large groups of human experts on work that could take those groups years, using fewer resources and less time, across virtually all tasks of human interest. Narrow superhuman performance in chess, Go or protein-structure prediction does not qualify.

    Recent findings suggest that the essay builds on From AGI to ASI, a technical report Google DeepMind dates to June 12, 2026, and on subsequent institute discussions. The report’s arXiv text illustrates the ASI bar as reliably outperforming tens of thousands of well-coordinated experts working on one problem for ten years with technology and cultural artifacts available in 2010. The earlier report introduced the same four-pathway framework.

    Industry observers note that ASI would still sit well below theoretical intelligence limits. The essay identifies physical, logical and complexity constraints that would prevent arbitrarily precise predictions of real-world systems, including climates, immune systems and human societies. Human-level AI is therefore one point on a continuum, with a large and largely uncharted range between it and those limits.

    The essay estimates that global effective compute, which combines hardware improvements, AI-hardware investment and algorithmic efficiency, has grown at least tenfold per year. Extrapolating that rate for a decade yields a factor of 10 billion. For each AI agent presently runnable, the scenario implies more same-quality agents than the human population, provided those trends hold.

    The essay’s cost example applies roughly 4x lower compute demand per year from hardware and inference-efficiency gains. At that rate, a workload costing $1 billion in compute tokens would cost $1,000 after ten years. The resulting standardization and automation of cognitive work is described as “cognitive industrialization,” analogous to the commoditization of routine physical labor. Even without dramatic frontier advances, that shift could reshape knowledge work and the wider economy.

    The essay cautions that scale by itself could still fall short of full AGI if some cognitive tasks require human assistance. With broadly human-level systems available, faster and more numerous agents could help bridge the gap to a weak form of ASI, aided by digital systems’ processing speed, memory, movement across computing hardware, nearly lossless copying of code and memory state, and high-bandwidth sharing of experience.

    It has been revealed that continued scaling faces possible exhaustion of high-quality training data, diminishing returns as each capability step requires multiplied compute and model size, and physical or economic limits involving power generation, grids, chip fabrication and hardware interconnects. Scaling laws fitted to current architectures, data and evaluations cannot confidently predict how much scale AGI or ASI would require.

    Paradigm shifts address gaps in continual learning, some forms of world modeling, decision-making and sample efficiency, meaning how much training data a system needs to reach a given capability. Current systems may also be unable to invent genuinely new concepts and abstractions, rather than merely recombining existing ones. Researchers are divided over whether incremental changes to the prevailing transformer paradigm can close those gaps or deeper shifts will be required.

    The essay claims agent coordination offers a collective route, but multi-agent scaling laws are missing. Coordination inefficiencies, misinformation, manipulation and collusion can weaken large groups, requiring institutional and organizational defenses. Recursive self-improvement adds feedback loops through code and hardware designs, reusable data produced during deployment, or specialization within agent groups. Poor feedback can stall or degrade these loops, with faster progress expected where outputs can be checked automatically, such as mathematical proofs.

    These pathways can compound. The essay argues that if one stalls, economic and geopolitical competition can shift effort toward the others, so restricting only training compute would not necessarily stop overall progress. Suppressing one input while others advance could also create a capability “overhang,” followed by steeper gains when the constraint is relaxed or circumvented.

    Recent findings suggest that the proposed response is to model, measure, forecast and repeat through interdisciplinary work spanning frontier labs and national and global institutions. Some necessary metrics require frontier-model access, sizable evaluation compute and new benchmarking and modeling methods.

    According to recent reports, whether those pathways will produce ASI, and on what timetable, remains unresolved. The nearer-term challenge is building evaluations that can distinguish greater agent speed and numbers from genuinely latest capabilities, while giving public institutions enough access and computing capacity to track pathways that may reinforce one another.

    Jonas Reeve is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI, focusing on cognitive AI, artificial general intelligence (AGI), and the theoretical foundations of machine intelligence. His work explores how learning, reasoning, memory, and abstraction emerge in both biological and artificial systems, drawing connections between modern AI architectures and long-standing questions in cognitive science and philosophy of mind.

    According to recent reports, with a conceptual and reflective approach, Jonas examines frameworks such as reasoning models, agentic systems, emergent cognition, and alignment theory, aiming to clarify what progress toward AGI actually means—and what it does not. Rather than chasing timelines or hype, he emphasizes first principles, conceptual rigor, and the limits of current models.

    Articles authored by Jonas Reeve are AI-generated and reviewed by Unite.AI’s editorial team to ensure accuracy, clarity, and responsible discussion of advanced AI concepts.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that in a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

    According to recent reports, the torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

    The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

    In a recent development, to look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

    It has been revealed that at the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We strategy to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

    Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

    On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:.

    No need for torchrun: the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

    According to recent reports, A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:.

    Industry observers note that each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

    At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

    Everything the Space demonstrates comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

    Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:.

    The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

    Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • InfoQ Homepage News .NET 11 : ASP.NET Core: Union Type Support, OpenAPI 3.2 by Default and Blazor AI Components.
    • Nov 19, 2026 3 min read.
    • Industry observers note that last week, Microsoft shipped ASP.NET Core in .NET 11 as part of the wider .NET 11 release.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    InfoQ Homepage News .NET 11 : ASP.NET Core: Union Type Support, OpenAPI 3.2 by Default and Blazor AI Components.

    Nov 19, 2026 3 min read.

    Industry observers note that last week, Microsoft shipped ASP.NET Core in .NET 11 as part of the wider .NET 11 release. The update spans Minimal APIs, OpenAPI, SignalR, Blazor, authentication, and the Kestrel server. As stated in the announcement, .NET 11 is a Standard Term Support release with two years of support.

    Industry observers note that on the API side, developers can now use C# 15 union types in JSON request and response bodies across Minimal APIs and MVC. The release notes limit the feature to JSON bodies, so route, query, header, and form values cannot bind to a union.

    Minimal API validation also runs asynchronous validators, which keeps threads free while a rule waits on a database lookup or a remote call. The framework can now localize validation messages and display names itself, and endpoints can skip the remaining middleware pipeline through a newly introduced [ShortCircuit] attribute.

    It has been revealed that developers who generate OpenAPI documents now get version 3.2 unless they select an earlier one for tooling that has not caught up. As described in the release notes, the framework depends on Microsoft.OpenApi 3.3.1 for this, and the notes label that upgrade a breaking change.

    With 3.2, endpoints that stream server-sent events are documented with a schema for each event's payload, and the generator emits an anyOf schema for unions. Generated documents can also describe endpoints that use the HTTP QUERY method, and APIs that carry the [Obsolete] attribute show up as deprecated.

    Industry observers note that signalR adds authentication refresh, so a long-lived connection no longer has to close when its access token expires. As reported, server developers enable it per hub, while the .NET client refreshes automatically by default and the TypeScript client can do the same. Blazor passes the refreshed identity on to Interactive Server components while the circuit stays connected.

    Blazor receives the longest list of changes, and many of them target static server-side rendering. With the upcoming CacheView component, developers can cache the rendered markup of a component subtree, and the child components do not run when a cached copy is served. Blazor now ships client-side validation for static SSR forms, enabled by default.

    In a recent development, developers can also carry data between requests with TempData or session values. According to the release notes, the Blazor Web App template drops its app.UseAntiforgery() call, because a middleware for CSRF protection is now added by default.

    It has been revealed that for Interactive Server apps, an opt-in package pauses the circuit of a hidden browser tab after a delay, two minutes by default, to free server memory. Lists built with Virtualize may now mix items of different heights, and Microsoft raised the default OverscanCount from 3 to 15. Page and sort state in QuickGrid now lives in the URL query string, with sortable headers and pager controls rendered as links instead of buttons.

    The release notes flag this as a CSS breaking change, because custom styles written for the buttons also have to target the links. The release also includes Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.AI, a set of components for chat and agent interfaces. According to the announcement, Microsoft treats that package as experimental and will keep it in prerelease throughout .NET 11.

    Industry observers note that on the security and server side, an experimental package adds Device Bound Session Credentials, a protocol that ties session refresh to a private key held by the browser. Response compression and request decompression gain Zstandard support, which is on by default.

    Kestrel's HTTP/1.1 parser no longer throws exceptions on malformed requests, a change that is reported to raise throughput by up to 20 to 40 percent under heavy invalid traffic. The shared framework libraries of ASP.NET Core are now compiled with runtime-async, described in the release notes as an internal change with no public API impact.

    Industry observers note that two older APIs are on the way out. The Microsoft.AspNetCore.Grpc.Swagger package is now deprecated, and Kestrel's TlsClientHelloBytesCallback option is obsolete in favor of the new UseTlsClientHelloListener extension.

    Other changes in this release are native OpenTelemetry tracing attributes, client-side cancellation of SignalR hub invocations, scrolling to a specific item in Virtualize and QuickGrid, passkey display names inferred from the authenticator, and TimeProvider support in ASP.NET Core Identity.

    For interested readers and developers, the full release notes are available in the What's new in ASP.NET Core in .NET 11 article on Microsoft Learn.

    In a recent development, the San Francisco manufacturer, founded in 2022, develops crop-intelligence products for growers of high-value specialty crops. The acquisition brings that plant-level data capability into Deere’s precision-agriculture portfolio. Tim Marquis, Deere’s director of farm systems innovation, described the objective as connecting crop intelligence with equipment that can execute fieldwork precisely throughout the growing season.

    Orchard AI’s cameras travel through orchards and vineyards on farm vehicles, collecting data on individual trees, vines and plants across the season. Deere notes the system analyzes hundreds of images per tree on each pass, producing yield estimates, fruit counts, fruit size and color data, and canopy measurements. Its FruitScope software makes that information available for farm-management decisions.

    Orchard AI’s product documentation says FruitScope Vision cameras can mount on tractors, all-terrain vehicles and other farm vehicles already in use, operate at 1 to 12 mph, and return scan results the next morning. The hardware is designed for operations ranging from 100 acres to more than 10,000 acres. FruitScope OS provides per-tree maps covering fruit count, size, color, disease and canopy conditions, with harvest-planning and crop-load-management tools on phones and computers.

    Orchard AI describes Canary AI as software that reasons over farm data to answer questions and recommend what to do next. Its listed crops include apples, wine and table grapes, blueberries, cherries, almonds, pistachios and citrus. The organization offers a per-acre, per-year subscription covering the camera hardware, unlimited scans, FruitScope OS, Canary AI, training and support, with no separate hardware purchase. That model gives Deere a subscription software offering built around repeated crop scans, in addition to the sensing equipment itself.

    Deere framed the technology around the cost of poor timing: a missed spray application or mistimed harvest can affect fruit quality, yield and a season’s profitability, while weather, labor constraints and changing crop conditions narrow decision windows. The workflows identified for the combined technology include pruning, thinning, applying crop treatments where needed and determining which blocks are ready for harvest.

    It has been revealed that one proposed workflow uses higher bloom counts to generate a prescription for where to spray. The recommendation could be delivered to a mobile device for in-field application or to an in-cab G5 display. Deere presented these examples as possibilities, not as a commitment to specific product availability. The proposed connection would move crop data beyond a dashboard and into instructions for work in specific blocks.

    Tyler Klick of Redwood Empire Vineyard Management, an early user of Orchard AI’s technology, said the scans provided useful precision-farming insights into vineyard conditions, and that CEO Charlie Wu’s team had listened to customer needs and put them into action.

    In a recent development, justin Rose, president of Deere’s Worldwide Agriculture & Turf Division for Small Ag & Turf, noted the firm wants to use its scale to help Orchard AI reach more growers. “A major part of what makes Orchard AI successful is its speed of innovation and the close relationships it has built directly with customers,” he said, adding that Deere wants to preserve those strengths.

    Recent findings suggest that for Deere, the strategic value is the potential to make plant-level intelligence an input to fieldwork rather than another standalone dashboard. Turning Orchard AI’s maps into routine equipment workflows, while retaining the grower relationships that shaped the product, is the central integration question raised by the acquisition.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    LFM3 is our newly introduced generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

    LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.

    LFM2 highlighted that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

    LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:.

    The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

    Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

    The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders:.

    Sources indicate that each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

    Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

    To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:.

    For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

    Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

    To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:.

    See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

    Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a upcoming in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

    To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:.

    Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:.

    Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:.

    See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

    According to recent reports, reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

    To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:.

    Then ask a question about a photo by voice:.

    See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

    Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

    To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:.

    Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:.

    Recent findings suggest that for brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

    In a recent development, LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

    Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

    According to recent reports, we adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

    California Attorney General Rob Bonta served NVIDIA with an investigative subpoena on November 19, 2026, seeking information on whether advanced chips or confidential information reached China and whether the firm misled investors and the public about the risk. The state will use the responses to evaluate possible violations of California law.

    The California Department of Justice is examining actions by both NVIDIA and former CEO Jensen Huang. Bonta’s announcement describes an evidence-gathering investigation, not a completed legal finding or a filed enforcement action.

    Recent findings suggest that those questions create two distinct lines of inquiry. One concerns whether advanced chips or confidential information may have reached China. The other concerns whether NVIDIA accurately described that risk to investors and the public, bringing possible technology transfers and securities disclosures into the same state investigation.

    California’s securities antifraud statute makes it unlawful to offer, sell, buy, or offer to buy a security in the state through a written or oral communication containing an untrue material fact. It also covers omissions of material facts needed to keep statements, in their circumstances, from being misleading. Bonta summarized the principle: “Companies cannot mislead their investors.”.

    It has been revealed that in a quarterly report signed August 26, 2026, NVIDIA disclosed that U.S. government licenses granted beginning in February 2026 allowed small amounts of H200 products to be shipped to specific China-based customers. Chinese government restrictions prevented the organization from selling all products covered by those licenses.

    NVIDIA reported a $0.4 billion charge for H200 excess inventory and purchase obligations in the first half of fiscal 2027 as demand diminished, after which it made only a fraction of the permitted shipments. Those shipments represented less than 1% of Data Center revenue in the quarter ended July 26, 2026. The licenses required inspection in the United States before shipment to customers, with the products subject to a 25% tariff upon importation into the United States.

    That licensed H200 program does not define the boundaries of California’s inquiry, which refers more broadly to advanced chips and confidential information. The filing nevertheless documents the controlled-sales framework and the practical limits of NVIDIA’s oversight after a sale.

    NVIDIA mentioned it has assisted and will continue assisting authorities regarding attempted diversion, but lacks physical control over its products after sale and must rely on customers’ and partners’ compliance programs. Reports of diverted controlled products, even unsubstantiated or untrue reports, and compliance failures by customers or partners could damage its business, relationships, and reputation.

    Recent findings suggest that the subpoena follows NVIDIA’s November 12, 2026 leadership announcement, in which Huang resigned as president, CEO, and director, effective immediately. Colette Kress became interim CEO while remaining executive vice president and CFO, and the board began a search for a permanent successor. The board stated it expected operations, customer commitments, and the product roadmap to continue without interruption under Kress and the leadership team.

    Industry observers note that for Kress’s interim team, the subpoena connects possible transfers of chips and confidential information with the accuracy of NVIDIA’s public risk disclosures. The company’s filing places tightly conditioned H200 licenses alongside its limited control after sale, making customer and partner compliance programs consequential to the facts California will examine.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (882 w)

    QCon San Francisco 2026: Use AI to Multiply Your Team as a Staff Engineer

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (882 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Use AI to Multiply Your Team as a Staff Engineer.
    • Nov 19, 2026 4 min read.
    • In a recent development, at QCon San Francisco 2026, Jordan Cutler, Senior Staff Engineer and Web Platform Tech Lead at Pinterest, presented how the role of a staff engineer changes when every engineer has access to the same AI tools.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Use AI to Multiply Your Team as a Staff Engineer.

    Nov 19, 2026 4 min read.

    In a recent development, at QCon San Francisco 2026, Jordan Cutler, Senior Staff Engineer and Web Platform Tech Lead at Pinterest, presented how the role of a staff engineer changes when every engineer has access to the same AI tools. The session argued that most "AI for engineers" content focuses on individual productivity, while the real question for staff engineers is where their leverage comes from now. According to Cutler, AI did not change what a staff engineer is for, but it changed where the leverage is.

    The talk opened with a reflection on Cutler's previous conference talk, where he showed how AI could turn a four-hour task into four minutes. At that point he was shipping roughly as much as his whole team, which he described as multiplying himself rather than his team. That framed the central question of the session: what does a 10x engineer look like when everyone has AI?

    To illustrate why this matters, Cutler shared internal Pinterest data on merged pull requests per engineer per week between Q1 2025 and Q3 2026. The top 10% of engineers went from 6.7 to 11.3 merged PRs per week, a 68% increase, while the bottom half went from 1.0 to 1.15, an increase of 14%. Everyone has AI, but not everyone uses it the same way, and the gap keeps growing. The presentation organized the response to that gap into three moves: multiply yourself, multiply your team, and multiply the system.

    The first move, multiply yourself, is about going first. Cutler explained that he tries new tools before his team does, and that part of that work is hitting dead ends so others don't have to. He mentioned examples such as an agent harness that could not be steered mid-task and a remote agent runner that required too many follow-ups. Sharing those findings early means the team does not lose a week on the same experiments. Running many agents also revealed a new problem: he kept giving the same corrections in every session, such as avoiding em-dashes, adding a diagram to the PR description, and keeping pull requests small.

    The second move, multiply your team, started from a limitation: the folder made him faster, but only he had it. With new people joining the team and a new area to ramp up on, Cutler found himself repeating the same comments in code review, such as asking why a value is null instead of fixing the cause, testing like a user would, and keeping PRs small. The talk emphasized that the value of encoding that judgment grows with every teammate who adopts it, compared to the flat curve of a single engineer working alone.

    The third move, multiply the system, is about moving up a level. Cutler used the history of container shipping as an analogy: ports got better at loading cargo by hand, but the standard box changed the economics entirely, from $5.86 a ton to 16 cents a ton. At Pinterest, migrations were the cargo, one kind of change spread across hundreds of files and dozens of teams. Instead of running each migration by hand, the team built a system where a staff engineer points to a plan and an example, an engineer puts it on a schedule, and an agent running in a sandbox splits the work into PRs team by team. A class component migration ran three to five times faster than by hand, in the background while teams worked on other things.

    The talk also covered what went wrong. One scheduled job looped and opened 16 PRs in two minutes, increasing CI wait times from under 30 seconds to 14 minutes. The lesson was not to wait for the perfect guardrail, but to ship a small one. Cutler encouraged attendees to find their own "any" problem: a first responder for any incident, a draft fix for any bug ticket, or an agent that triages any flaky test. Today, 40 engineers have scheduler jobs of their own.

    The results were significant. Using the same AI tools as other web teams, Cutler's team now ships about four times as much per engineer, without counting his own PRs.

    In a recent development, the presentation concluded with practical steps: write down what you repeat, put it where people already work, and build for every case instead of one. Some parts of the job cannot be written down, like an honest conversation with a teammate who is struggling, and those remain the staff engineer's responsibility. As Cutler put it, a 10x engineer isn't ten times faster, they are the reason ten other people are. As AI agents become part of everyday development workflows, the role of senior engineers may increasingly shift from personal output toward encoding judgment into the tools, defaults, and systems that entire organizations use.

    • Industry observers note that language models can do a lot.
    • Industry observers note that say a customer calls your support line.
    • In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

    Industry observers note that say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they mentioned (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

    In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

    Today we're announcing two packages:.

    Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

    Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's upcoming speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

    According to recent reports, it's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:.

    The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:.

    The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

    Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

    Industry observers note that parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

    Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

    All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

    According to recent reports, qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:.

    Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

    Recent findings suggest that to add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

    To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:.

    According to recent reports, each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

    Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

    When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who remarked what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:.

    The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

    The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

    We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:.

    Recent findings suggest that parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

    It has been revealed that these numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

    Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

    Recent findings suggest that anyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

    It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

    What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

    Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

    Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:.

    urgent is a Double. team is a Choice containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

    It has been revealed that if you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

    For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

    Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

    The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:.

    Recent findings suggest that the session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

    Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

    Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

    AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:.

    You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

    According to recent reports, raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

    In a recent development, language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

    In a recent development, each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

    AnyDecisionModel has six backends:.

    Industry observers note that the next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

    Recent findings suggest that like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

    Industry observers note that both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

    Add the packages to your Package.swift:.

    For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

    Sources indicate that each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

    In a recent development, try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Complications and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

    Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

    NTT and SSC Space Explore a Global Laser Network for Satellite Data

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (819 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that NTT and SSC Space have signed a memorandum of understanding to study how optical ground stations in different countries could work as one network.
    • The two companies bring different pieces of the system.
    • A satellite can collect more data in a pass than it has time to transmit to Earth.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that NTT and SSC Space have signed a memorandum of understanding to study how optical ground stations in different countries could work as one network. The companies will look at whether a satellite can send data by laser to stations run on different systems and how those stations can pass the data into terrestrial networks. The agreement, signed November 11, is a study of interoperability and commercial requirements, not the launch of a joint service.

    The two companies bring different pieces of the system. NTT supplies optical networking and network control expertise. SSC Space operates satellite ground infrastructure and brings experience coordinating ground-station operations. The first phase covers market needs, technical compatibility, geographic coverage and links to terrestrial networks.

    A satellite can collect more data in a pass than it has time to transmit to Earth. Optical links can move more data during a contact window, but they need precise pointing and a clear enough path through the atmosphere. A spacecraft with a fast laser downlink can still miss its chance to transmit if the receiving telescope is under heavy cloud. That matters especially in low Earth orbit, where a spacecraft moves in and out of view of a given station.

    Sources indicate that one answer is to spread stations across regions with different weather. If a suitable station is in view and clear, an operator can route a contact there instead of waiting for another pass over the cloudy site. NASA’s Laser Communications Relay Demonstration illustrates the approach: its optical relay connected to ground stations in California and Hawaii, both chosen for high altitude and low cloud cover. The experiments found that some thin high clouds were tolerable, but still reinforced the case for having more than one place to receive a signal.

    SSC Space’s existing optical program gives the project a starting point. Its initial sites in Australia and Chile are at existing radio-frequency facilities, with access to terrestrial fiber and the option to support both radio and optical links. SSC Space lists up to 10 gigabits per second for each station. That figure describes the stations’ stated capability, not the expected performance of the proposed joint service.

    Recent findings suggest that NTT has also been working on what happens once a station receives the signal. In a separate agreement with Cailabs, it said it would study connecting selected ground stations to nearby data centers through its All-Photonics Network and coordinating both ground station and terrestrial network resources. Unlike NTT’s separate lunar work with ispace, which includes power transmission, the SSC Space agreement addresses receiving data from spacecraft and getting it onto networks on Earth.

    Sources indicate that for owners of satellite imagery, an crucial measure is the time between an image being captured and its arrival in software that can use it. A higher peak downlink rate helps when the link is available. A reliable choice of stations matters when a satellite has newly introduced imagery but the planned receiver cannot see it through the clouds.

    According to recent reports, NASA’s work using satellite data and machine learning to help forecast flash floods is one example of why timely delivery matters. That project does not use the proposed NTT–SSC Space network, and neither tech giant confirmed an AI system as part of the agreement. The connection is upstream: the sooner a ground network can deliver useful observations, the sooner forecasting and analysis tools can process them.

    The companies have not named a first mission, service start date or service availability target. The test of the proposal is whether an operator can use more than one station without building a separate integration for each site, and whether that flexibility reliably shortens the wait for data when a planned contact falls through.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Bloomberg reported on November 19, 2026 that a recent Apple job listing described an in-house AI agent capable of operating a Mac, in an account carried by TechCrunch.

    The vacancy was for a senior engineering manager to oversee the effort. The report described development as remaining in its early stages and mentioned Apple had eyed introducing the service as soon as the end of 2027, a reported possibility rather than an declared release commitment.

    One reproduced passage makes the scope explicit: “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step.” That mandate combines web browsing, application control, system commands, software development and service integrations, with tool selection itself assigned to the agent.

    The listing also describes agents moving fluidly between tools to complete multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code and APIs. Private operation and the polish associated with Apple’s products are part of the stated ambition. These are hiring-language objectives, not demonstrated product capabilities.

    The report places the prospective Apple agent alongside computer-work services already launched by Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as Meta’s recently introduced Muse agent line. Apple’s approach would bring that competition onto the Mac, where access to local applications, files and system permissions shapes what an agent can do.

    The report also remarked the upcoming macOS 27.3 will display warnings discouraging users from granting full access to third-party agents. That gives the project a second dimension: Apple is exploring broader computer automation while preparing additional friction around sweeping permissions for outside software.

    Sources indicate that apple said in an October 2, 2026 developer notice that some developers use Full Disk Access in ways that could expose files, mail, messages and browsing history without users’ full knowledge and understanding. The permission largely sidesteps normal privacy controls so backup apps can function properly on a Mac; for communication apps, that access can also compromise the privacy of people communicating with the user.

    The notice said Apple will introduce additional controls so granting this level of access requires very explicit user action. It connected the decision to substantially growing risks as AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, with the aim of ensuring owners understand those risks before making decisions about their data and privacy.

    Together, the reported hiring effort and Apple’s permission changes define the central design problem. An agent that moves among browsers, apps, code and services needs meaningful authority to act, while Apple is telling developers that broad access must require explicit action and informed understanding. The practical scope of any Apple-built computer agent will depend on how the tech giant balances those two requirements.

    • The BPF verifier has historically worked by tracing every possible path of execution through a program, checking, at each instruction, that various safety properties hold.

    The BPF verifier has historically worked by tracing every possible path of execution through a program, checking, at each instruction, that various safety properties hold. This works, but it can result in an exponential increase in the number of states that need checking in programs with complicated control-flow. Alexei Starovoitov, one of the kernel's core BPF maintainers, has shared a patch set that substantially reworks how the verifier tracks states, in order to reduce the size of that exponential explosion.

    • Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

    The model is released in two official variants:.

    There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

    Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

    Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

    You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

    Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super notable for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

    Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That remarked, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

    According to recent reports, for community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

    In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

    We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

    Recent findings suggest that mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

    For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

    Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

    Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

    Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

    In a recent development, on coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

    Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

    Recent findings suggest that cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

    Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing highlighted promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

    Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

    It has been revealed that the Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    InfoQ Homepage Presentations AI-Assisted Software Delivery: From Code to Production.

    The panelists explore how engineering teams adapt delivery architectures, pipelines, security, and governance for AI-assisted development. They share practical strategies for verifying AI-generated code, solving testing and deployment bottlenecks, maintaining human oversight, and measuring AI’s true impact on software velocity, quality, reliability, and operational cost.

    Garima Bajpai is the Founder of the DevOps Community of Practice in Canada. Martin Reynolds is a Field CTO at Harness. Patrick Debois is an AI Product Engineer and AI Native Dev Advisor. Gunnar Grosch is a Developer Advocate at Sinch. Renato Losio is an InfoQ Staff Editor, Cloud Expert, and AWS Data Hero.

    InfoQ Live is a virtual event designed for you, the modern software practitioner. Learn from extraordinary speakers driving change and innovation.
