    Design for Understandability

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 28 min read (5640 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jschuster

    ⏱️ ~28 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that this is a talk I gave at Google’s internal Code Health Summit in November of 2025.
    • In a world where LLMs generate much of our code, understanding that code is more crucial than ever.
    • Industry observers note that there’s a better way to go about this.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that this is a talk I gave at Google’s internal Code Health Summit in November of 2025. I’m sharing it here in the hopes that it sparks further learning and discussion.

    In a world where LLMs generate much of our code, understanding that code is more crucial than ever. But with a system as large and complex as Google’s codebase, SWEs can easily fall into a pattern of learned helplessness where the best you can do is tweak the code and pray that it passes the tests. Without understanding, LLMs are little more than complexity-generating machines running at top speed.

    Industry observers note that there’s a better way to go about this. Just as our industry has learned to design software for testability, we can also design it for understandability. We can use ideas like design by contract, class invariants, modularity, and more to create systems that we can understand one piece at a time, rather than piling more onto the significant ball of mud and hoping it doesn’t all collapse.

    According to recent reports, is it easy? No. But is it worthwhile? Absolutely. These ideas aren’t new, but they’re not nearly as widely taught or well understood as they deserve to be, and mastering them leads to a world where we can have more confidence in our code and increase velocity at the same time.

    It has been revealed that hi everyone, thanks for having me! Let’s get started.

    I’d like to start this talk with a question: If LLMs can code, then what is left for human SWEs?

    The tech industry is rapidly looking to large language models to write all of our code. But you might say: isn’t writing code our job as software engineers? Where does this leave the responsibility of SWEs? What is the essential human element that SWEs add on top of LLMs?

    Every one of you is going to have a different answer to this question, and that’s fine. But here’s my take.

    That necessary human element is judgment. Judgment of whether the code is maintainable. Judgment of whether it is healthy.

    Recent findings suggest that LLMs can follow patterns and generate code that looks like what it was trained on. Sometimes they can produce useful tips and critiques for a piece of code. But that critical piece of judgment, of deciding whether some code is suitable for the task it was designed for, is still up to you, the human.

    Because here’s the thing: LLMs today are still a sloppy intern. Sometimes the code they produce is good, but sometimes it’s completely off-track and needs correcting. You wouldn’t incorporate a sloppy intern’s code into your system without a close review first, so you shouldn’t do so for an LLM’s code either.

    YOU are responsible for the quality of your code, regardless of whether you had an LLM generate it for you or wrote it the old-fashioned way with fingers on a keyboard.

    According to recent reports, so where does that leave us? If LLMs are going to write a lot of the code for us, then we’re looking at a future where we humans are going to spend less time writing code, and more time reading code and understanding it, in order to make sure it passes our quality bar.

    This means it’s more important than ever to get better at understanding code, and to speed up that reading and understanding process.

    Now: if you want to get better at something, it’s helpful to set an aspirational goal for yourself. Something that’s above your current skill level, and drives you to get better and better every day.

    Here’s the goal I propose: we should be able to predict the behavior of every line of code, without running a single test.

    Let me say that again: We should be able to predict the behavior of every line of code, without running a single test.

    It has been revealed that now, I know you may be thinking: “Understand every line of code? Without testing? Are you serious?! There’s way too much complexity and legacy code for me to ever be able to do that!”.

    In a recent development, you might think so. And if we take our hands off the wheel and relinquish all control, you might be right. But I’m here to tell you there’s a better way.

    We can design our code to be understandable.

    According to recent reports, consider that a decade or two ago, we used to think that writing multiple tests for every public method in an API would have been infeasible. It wasn’t because we didn’t want to, or that we weren’t trying. It was because we hadn’t designed our code to make testing possible at that level. But gradually, across the software industry, we changed our practices to design for testability. Today, designing our code for testability is so ingrained into our culture that doing anything else is practically unthinkable. We can do the same for understandability, so that our code enables us to understand it better.

    Our own Code Health guide makes a strong case for understandability. It indicates “For code to be sustainable, it must be understood. Change cannot be made unless a developer knows what the system right now provides, and what needs to change to adapt to latest circumstances. As a result, key components of code health include good documentation, easy to understand error messages, and clear, simple code”.

    Recent findings suggest that not only is designing for understandability important, but it’s a learnable skill. It’s not some magical ability that you either have or you don’t. There are specific, concrete actions you can take to improve the understandability of your code.

    In a recent development, I’m going to introduce you to a few of those today. Think of it as a “starter kit” for designing for understandability. We’ll also talk more about a general theme that runs through all of these practices, so that at a certain point you can find even more ways to design your code for understandability.

    Recent findings suggest that the ideas I’m going to show you today are not fresh. But they’re not taught as well as they should be, when they’re taught at all, and most of us have only a rough understanding of how to apply them. My goal today is to sharpen that understanding just a little bit, and make it just a little more practical, so we can kickstart a process of making our code more understandable over time.

    So let’s get started on each of these Design for Understandability practices.

    The first one is Design by Contract.

    To motivate the idea, let’s ask the question: when calling a method, what behavior should you rely on?

    Let’s say we have this binary search method, but its documentation is not terribly helpful (you’ve probably seen something like this before).

    Recent findings suggest that binary search is reasonably well understood, but as a caller of the method, we have some questions we want to ask about this specific implementation. Such as:.

    The documentation doesn’t answer these questions. So what can we do?

    First, we could guess. But we’ll probably be wrong.

    Second, we could read the code. But that might take a long time, especially if the particular behavior we care about is buried several levels deep.

    It has been revealed that third, we could test the code on some examples and see what happens. But just because it works a certain way on some examples doesn’t necessarily mean it works that way for all such inputs. Furthermore, even if it works that way now, there’s no guarantee that it will continue to work that way in the future.

    It has been revealed that the point is that without a clear statement of what this code is intended to do, there’s no distinction between implementation and intent. The SWE who wants to use this code has to guess at which behavior the method commits to, versus which behavior is an implementation detail that might change over time.

    This is where contracts come in.

    There are many ways to define a contract, but for the sake of this talk I’m going to define it as a formal-ish description of the observable behavior that each participant in an interaction commits to.

    In the real world, a basic contract is something like “If I cook dinner, then you will wash the dishes”.

    In programming, an example might be: “If the caller provides a non-negative integer n, then the square-root function returns the square root of n”.

    Let’s see how contracts can help us with our binary-search example.

    It has been revealed that here’s a possible contract for this function. It indicates, “If the list is sorted, binarySearch returns the index of the first occurrence of t in the list, or -1 if not found. Behavior is undefined for unsorted lists.”.

    We can see that this contract answers the questions we asked about it:.

    The power of a contract is that it defines a clear boundary between the author’s intent and the implementation. The caller doesn’t have to guess at the behavior anymore: they can just read the contract, and if a specific detail of the behavior isn’t there, they will know that it’s unspecified.

    It has been revealed that in reality, this isn’t always perfect. Whether intentionally or accidentally, we still tend to end up with code that relies on implementation details rather than specified behavior. But contracts at least give us a way to minimize this behavior.

    Now that we understand what a contract looks like, let’s talk about how contracts can help us reason about and understand our code better.

    In a recent development, suppose you just wrote a method. I’m going to draw that method as a little circle here.

    You want to know if it’s correct.

    I’m going to use a purple circle to stand for methods we’ve read the code for.

    Now, our method doesn’t live in isolation: it calls some other code.

    In a recent development, so, you think “Okay, well, I need to understand what those do. I’m going to read the code for those methods.”.

    According to recent reports, well, those methods call other methods, and we start thinking about this, and figure out how we’re going to reason about those. And at this point you can maybe see where I’m going.

    Recent findings suggest that oh no. Now we have lots and lots of code we have to read across our entire code base.

    Industry observers note that why do we need all this reasoning just to reason about one single method? That’s all we’re trying to do! How did we get so out of control?

    So, let’s back up and try again, using Design by Contract this time.

    Industry observers note that you still have to read your own code. We can’t get around this part; that’s the change we just made.

    Sources indicate that and we haven’t changed the code. It still calls those other methods.

    But now, the trick is that we can read just the contract on those called methods, not the code.

    And that’s it! We can stop here. We don’t need to worry about all of that other code. The contracts tell us all we need to know about calling these other two methods.

    Recent findings suggest that the rest of that code still exists, but we don’t have to think about it. The contract abstracts away all that other behavior that doesn’t matter to us as the caller of these two methods.

    So that is the power that contracts give to us to reason about our code.

    Finally, I’ll wrap up this section with a few tips for writing contracts:.

    Recent findings suggest that first, document the behavior that you’re willing to commit to. This is usually the same as what you want your callers to rely on. For example, you probably want to document the return value of your method. But the exact human-readable text in your error messages? Not so much.

    Second, describe your error handling in your contracts. A contract does not and should not be just about the happy path. If your method might go wrong in some way, tell the caller under what conditions it might go wrong, and how you’re going to signal that to the caller, whether it be through a special return value, or an exception, or something else.

    Finally, keep in mind that the more callers your method has, the harder it is to change the contract. If it’s a private method used only by your team? Sure, that’s probably an easy case to change both the contract and change the callers to match. If it’s a public method on a popular framework used by hundreds of other projects? Then renegotiating the contract is a much more expensive effort, so you should evaluate the costs and benefits carefully before deciding to do that.

    So that was the first element in our Design for Understandability starter kit.

    The next one is data invariants.

    Let me explain this idea with a little story.

    Early in the COVID-19 pandemic, when my wife and I started working from home, we missed having free soda at work. So we got in the habit of keeping cans of Diet Coke in the fridge.

    Sources indicate that but there was a problem: we were great at taking cans out of the fridge, but not so great about putting new ones back in. So if you’re working hard and looking forward to taking a break with a nice cold beverage, it was a big disappointment to open a Coke-less fridge and resort to drinking room-temperature soda from the pantry instead.

    Recent findings suggest that the problem was that we hadn’t set any rules on how we retrieve Diet Coke and how we replenish the fridge. Without any rules governing access to the fridge, we eventually got into an unwanted state: in this case, an empty fridge.

    This happens in code, too. For example, let’s say you have this proto to represent a customer’s order [Note: “proto” is Google jargon for a Protocol Buffers message, similar to a JSON object]. If you receive this proto, how much do you trust that the total actually indicates the total amount on the items?

    In a recent development, probably not much, right? This proto could have come from any part of your code, so it’s easy to imagine that someone forgot to set that field appropriately.

    Recent findings suggest that protos give you completely uncontrolled access to the underlying representation of your data. Protos are great for transferring data back and forth across the network, but they’re poorly suited to situations where you want to rule out certain states.

    Sources indicate that to solve these kinds of problems, we can use data invariants. A data invariant is a statement about a piece of data that is always true.

    Recent findings suggest that data invariants are a principled way to enforce these kinds of valid states in your data. If you use them well, you can avoid a lot of bugs in your code.

    Let’s see how we can use invariants to solve the Diet Coke problem, and similar problems you might come across in your own code.

    First, identify the invariant you want to maintain.

    Recent findings suggest that ask yourself: What’s the property you want to rely on for this piece of data? Where are the places in the code where you explicitly validate and return an error if invalid? Alternatively, where do you make the assumption that it’s invalid, but you’re not actually sure?

    In this case, the invariant we want is “the fridge always contains a Diet Coke”.

    Second, you need to document the invariant.

    Sources indicate that it’s notable to note this is a separate step. It’s one thing to have an invariant in your own head. It’s another thing to write it down so that you communicate it to everyone else who might touch this code. Not to mention that if you come back to this code months or years later, you yourself might have forgotten which exact invariant you meant to maintain.

    Write it down where people will see it: probably close to the relevant data members, or maybe in a class-level comment at the top.

    Third, establish the invariant at creation time. Usually this will be done in a constructor or factory method. In this case, we’re constructing the fridge with a few drinks already added.

    Fourth, every time you change your the data, make sure you maintain the invariant.

    According to recent reports, this is the part my wife and I didn’t do for our fridge. What we should have done is established a rule where if you take a Diet Coke, you put another one back in the fridge to make sure there’s another for the next person.

    Recent findings suggest that you can maintain the invariant many ways – that part is up to you. The key thing is that you always maintain it. Without that, you have to think to yourself “Wait, are there going to be Diet Cokes in the fridge? Did I already take them out earlier? Let me go back and check all my callers to see if they did that already”. With an invariant, though, you just know: If I have a Fridge object, then it definitely has Diet Cokes, regardless of the sequence of operations that led to this point.

    Finally, one last step, and this might be the hardest one: you need to maintain the invariant as the code evolves. It’s relatively easy to maintain the invariant for a single version of code. But over the weeks, months, and years, complexity will creep in, newly introduced requirements will force you to change the code, and you might accidentally break the invariant or forget you even had one.

    Industry observers note that establish the culture on your team that maintaining invariants is just a thing you do. If you have a mental checklist of things you look for in code review, make sure that maintaining the invariants is on that checklist.

    Sources indicate that so how do data invariants help us design for understandability? Let’s first consider what we have to do when we don’t have an invariant.

    In a recent development, recall this representation of all the methods in your codebase, calling each other in various ways. Suppose you have a proto-based version of the fridge, and you want to know if it has any Diet Cokes in it. Because it’s a proto, you don’t have a way of knowing what state it’s in.

    So, you need to check all the callers of the current method.

    And you do the check, crawling across the codebase, and you find that there’s one particular case where you didn’t enforce it.

    In a recent development, of course you can fix these challenges one at a time as they crop up, but all that searching sounds like a lot of work, right? What do you think are the chances you’re always going to find that one particular buggy spot? What are the chances that new methods added to this web of code are going to maintain that condition?

    In contrast, let’s try the version with our Fridge class and its invariant.

    Industry observers note that in this case, the class has an invariant: the Fridge always has at least one Diet Coke, no matter what operations have been done previously or where we came from. By maintaining that invariant, we’ve removed the need to check what every single caller does.

    This is what data invariants do for you: they let you focus on the state you’re in now, and not how you got there.

    That wraps up the section on data invariants.

    The final practice I want to discuss today is isolating side effects and dependencies on global state.

    Recent findings suggest that to motivate this idea with an example. Let’s say there’s a supermarket point-of-sales system with this method to compute sales tax. Now ask yourself: what are the inputs and outputs for this method?

    Seems pretty obvious, right? It takes in a customer’s grocery order and returns the sales tax as an integer.

    But that’s not the whole story. If you dig into the implementation of this method, you’ll find that it reads in a set of sales tax rates from a separate file. That’s effectively a newly introduced input channel! The code depends on that data to compute the tax just as much as it depends on the content of the grocery order itself.

    According to recent reports, and if you look further, you’ll find that the method also records the computed tax in the store’s account database for bookkeeping purposes. That’s a new output, but it’s nowhere to be found in the type signature!

    So functions have two kinds of input and output: the ones that are visible in the type signature, like the order and the computed sales tax, and the ones that are hidden, like the tax rates file and the entry in the accounting database.

    According to recent reports, the hidden outputs are more commonly known as side effects. Side effects generally come in two flavors: mutation, so modifying something like a global variable or one of your input arguments, and outputs outside of your process. That would be things like database writes, remote procedure calls, printing to the console, etc.

    Sources indicate that I don’t know a common term for the hidden inputs, but I would call these dependencies on global state. Again, there are two flavors: dependency on the state of some global variable, or a dependency on the state of the system your program is running in. That’s things like permissions to access the database, the existence of a given file on the file system, and even the ability to read the system clock.

    Industry observers note that so why are these hidden inputs and outputs a problem? They make code hard to test, hard to reuse, and hard to reason about.

    In a recent development, hard to test because you have to make sure you have all the necessary dependencies are set up before you can even run the method in your test. And then once you do run the method, side effects often force the test to rely more on interaction verification than state verification, which can be brittle.

    According to recent reports, hard to reuse because the code now makes assumptions about what kinds of resources you have available to you. If you need to reuse some method in another part of the codebase, but the input data needs to come from a different source, or you need to store the results in a different place, those side effects and global states are going to create a tight coupling between your computation code and the specific sources and destinations for that computation, which will make your life harder.

    Sources indicate that hard to reason about because, by definition, these inputs and outputs are hidden! If you don’t even know that your method is making these kinds of assumptions on the system that it’s running in, then you’re going to make some faulty conclusions about how your code will behave.

    Sources indicate that now I’m not saying all side effects or global state are bad. And I’m not saying we should all immediately switch to a pure functional programming language like Haskell.

    Recent findings suggest that effects have to happen somewhere. Without side effects, computation is just the process of making a metal box hot for a little while(and even that heat is a side effect! although not usually one we care about).

    But by default, we tend to sprinkle them everywhere throughout the code. Need some input? Just read the file at whatever point you happen to be at in the code. Need to store your result? Go ahead and do it 4 layers deep into your business logic.

    Without a principled approach to side effects and global state, we’re constantly running into the kinds of problems we just described.

    There’s a better way, which is to isolate the side effects and the dependencies on global state. Much of our code is just logic on top of the data (once we get it) and creating upcoming data based on that. Divide your code into the computational parts on one hand, and the parts that deal with side effects and global state on the other.

    There are a few common patterns for this.

    Recent findings suggest that one of them is Command/Query Separation. It’s a pattern where each method is either a command, which performs some side effect, or a query, which is a pure function that returns its output as the return value. But you maintain a strict separation so that no function does both of those things.

    Recent findings suggest that another pattern is called “Functional Core, Imperative Shell”. This is a pattern at the architectural level. You focus the inner modules of your system on the business logic and computation, not performing side effects – this is the “functional core”. The outer modules coordinate the effects of your system with that computation, so that the complexity of the side effects is isolated to just that outer layer, and the majority of your system is simpler due to the functional purity.

    As with the other two practices, side effects and global state have a big impact on how we think about code.

    For example, you might be working on a method and need to delete a file. Your assumption is that it should be okay, you think no one is using it.

    Sources indicate that but then it turns out, some other part of the codebase was relying on it, and you just broke them. The code was so far away and unrelated that you didn’t even think to check there.

    On the other hand, if you isolate your side effects and global state such that they only happen in a known region of the code, then you can have confidence that you really aren’t going to break anyone else.

    So, those are the three starter practices for Design for Understandability: Design by Contract, Data Invariants, and Isolating Side Effects and Dependencies on Global State.

    Now, I’ve presented these as independent practices, but in fact they’re not so distinct. There’s a unifying theme to them. That theme is local reasoning.

    What do I mean by local reasoning?

    Local reasoning means you can come to conclusions about some chunk of code by looking only at that chunk of code, plus just a small amount of the neighboring code, like the specifications or contracts of the components that you directly interact with.

    In a recent development, this is as opposed to global reasoning. That’s the kind of reasoning where to answer even a simple question, you have to read a large chunk of the codebase, because the answer could be in any method, at any level of the call stack.

    The benefit of local reasoning is that it puts a hard boundary on how far you have to look in order to figure something out about your system: there’s always a limit to how far you have to search.

    So let’s talk about how each of the practices we talked about enables local reasoning. You may have noticed we covered this already, but let’s review.

    According to recent reports, design by Contract defines the expected behavior for a caller and a called method. That means that to understand what behavior a caller can rely on, or what behavior a called method is obligated to implement, the only place we need to look is the defined interface for that called method. Without that, we would revert to global reasoning to find all the parts of the code that might depend on some aspect of this method’s behavior.

    Data invariants often go hand in hand with contracts, but they usually say something about an entire object rather than a single method on that object.

    If you have a piece of data and you want to know something about its validity, like “does this fridge have any diet cokes?”, an invariant is what lets you immediately conclude yes, without looking at the callers that produced that data.

    Industry observers note that finally, by isolating side effects and global state, you minimize the number of places in your code where a change in one part of the code can cause a problem in a completely unrelated part. So it lets you say things like “this is the only part of the code that’s allowed to touch this file, so I know for sure that it’s safe to delete”.

    Another way of looking at local reasoning is to say that it minimizes the amount of context we need in order to reason about the system.

    Industry observers note that with global reasoning, you might need to know about any arbitrary part of your codebase, because the part that breaks your assumptions could be anywhere. You need to have the whole system loaded into your head in order to understand it.

    Local reasoning keeps the amount of stuff you need loaded into your head to a reasonable size.

    And guess what else benefits from small contexts: LLMs!

    Recent findings suggest that A key portion of making an LLM useful for your work is giving an LLM the right context to give good suggestions. But contexts costs tokens, and your tokens are limited. So LLMs give us another great motivation to use local reasoning and minimize our context.

    In a recent development, in other words, if you want your LLMs to be useful to you, then design your systems for understandability. Keep the necessary context small to make it easier for both you and your LLM to work with your code.

    According to recent reports, at the beginning of this talk, I compared “Design for Understandability” to “Design for Testability”. I’d like to revisit that for a moment.

    Before designing for testability was the norm, the default testing approach was application-level testing. Our code wasn’t set up for practices like dependency injection, so there was no way to run your code without setting up a huge set of dependencies as well. It wasn’t until we started designing and building our systems with testability in mind that we were able to make unit testing practical.

    That’s how it is with understandability and local reasoning, as well. If you don’t design for it ahead of time, it’s somewhere between hard and impossible to use local reasoning. But if you design for it along the way, you can make it work.

    If you’ve never heard of unit testing, then application-level testing seems obvious, and straightforward. But it’s not sufficient for modern software engineering. The same is true for global reasoning. I say it’s time we made designing for understandability a required part of our work, just like we did for testability.

    So you may be thinking: that all sounds good, and these practices sound good on paper, but is designing for understandability feasible in practice? You’re probably not working in a brand-new greenfield project. You’re probably working on old code, with lots of old warts and complexity, and the situation may seem hopeless. Can you really do this?

    Recent findings suggest that I’m here to say yes, this is feasible, if you take it one small step at a time. I’ll share some tips for getting started.

    Sources indicate that first off, take little bits at a time. Don’t try to boil the ocean. Don’t say “We’re going to take two weeks off from our normal work, make all of our code perfectly understandable, and then we’re done!”. That’s not going to work; you’re going to have a bad time.

    Instead, try applying some of these practices to just new methods that you write. You might have some old code out there that’s hard to change. So be it. Start with just the new methods and build some momentum.

    Recent findings suggest that teach your teammates, as well. Maybe share this talk, or find other ways to help your teammates design for understandability.

    It has been revealed that and finally, you might consider group programming sessions where you all get together and discuss: what does designing for understandability mean in your context? The Monarch team at Google did this with their Design by Contract practice and it worked well for them.

    Here are some further resources to learn more about Design for Understandability. I’m not going to go into them in detail, but please feel free to go revisit the slides after the talk and check these out.

    [Public links reproduced here for the blog post:].

    In a recent development, in conclusion: design your code for understandability. Whenever you’re working on some code and realize that you’re falling back to global reasoning, pause for a moment. Ask yourself: can I do this with local reasoning instead? Would a contract or an invariant help here? Or what if I moved the side effects and global state somewhere else? Or, maybe you’ll think of some other practice that fits here – you probably know a lot of local-reasoning practices, even if you didn’t have the terminology to call it that until today.

    Sources indicate that it’s time to make design for understandability just as much a part of software engineering as designing for testability is today. Understandability is not just helpful – it’s crucial, especially with Google-size systems. And not just that, but making your code understandable is doable if you design for it along the way.

    Trust me: you’ll be glad you did.

    The move took the benchmark’s weekly loss to 8.5%, its worst weekly performance since March 2020, when COVID-19 was spreading globally, Reuters mentioned.

    Japan’s Nikkei lost 5%, bringing its weekly decline to 7.7%. South Korea’s KOSPI fell 5.2% and ended the week down 8%. Taiwan shares were down 6.2% on the day and 17.5% for the week, which Reuters mentioned was their largest weekly decline since 1990.

    Reuters identified three existing pressures on AI stocks: Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia, momentum behind the anti-data-center movement following Democrats’ sweep of the US midterm elections, and concerns about rising debt loads across the sector.

    Goldman Sachs analysts remarked no single headline drove the retreat. Asset managers and hedge funds were net sellers of macro products while buying selected consumer and financial stocks, and poor liquidity exacerbated the price movements. That account points to broad repositioning as a key mechanism behind the steep index declines.

    Recent findings suggest that euro Stoxx 50 futures were down 1.7% at 6,017 at the time of the report. S&P 500 futures fell 0.5% and Nasdaq futures declined 1% during Asian trading, indicating that selling pressure was extending beyond the region’s cash markets.

    Recent findings suggest that reuters reported that the dollar index was steady at 103.86 and heading for a fourth consecutive weekly gain after reaching its highest level since April 2025 during the same week. The 10-year US Treasury yield fell for a fifth straight session to 5%, while the two-year yield touched a 10-day low of 4.7216% as investors moved into government bonds.

    The contrast between Anthropic’s strong debut and the broader retreat separates demand for an individual listing from confidence in the sector as a whole. For private AI companies and their backers, that distinction is consequential: public investors embraced a single offering while reducing exposure to the wider sector, with data-center opposition and debt concerns still unresolved.

    Latest Update: Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

    📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1307 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.
    • According to recent reports, today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research.
    • The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

    According to recent reports, today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

    The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

    Industry observers note that participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

    The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

    But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

    Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

    Recent findings suggest that the demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

    In a recent development, the pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many upcoming science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

    Sources indicate that figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

    Industry observers note that when organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

    According to recent reports, publicly available genomic data has proved crucial in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.

    Recent findings suggest that this is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

    Making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an key first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

    A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

    Recent findings suggest that to explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:.

    The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

    Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026.

    The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

    Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

    Recent findings suggest that beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

    Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

    Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge.

    According to recent reports, the CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

    Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or firm building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

    Sources indicate that we also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

    Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that the Department of Health and Social Care and Department for Education announced joint national guidance on November 20, 2026, covering artificial intelligence (AI) use in children’s and adult social care. They described it as the first cross-sector guidance of its kind and cited a local pilot reporting a 63% reduction in administrative time.

    The guidance gives leaders, practitioners and sector organisations a common national framework, including local authorities and providers making adoption decisions. Alongside practical advice, it addresses governance, accountability, data protection and professional oversight, with the aim of making adoption more consistent and increasing confidence across the sector.

    Potential uses include transcribing and summarising case notes, translating information, searching complex case histories and identifying gaps in support. The objective is to reduce administrative work so staff can spend more time supporting people and families, while making services easier to understand and access.

    It has been revealed that the pilot cited in the announcement took place within Swindon Borough Council’s adult social care work and used an AI tool to support social workers. The government reports that a typical Care Act assessment conversation shortened from 1.5 hours to 30 minutes, while assessment write-ups fell from four hours to 1.5 hours. Staff with visual impairments and those for whom English is not their first language saw particular benefits from the tool.

    It has been revealed that at Peterborough council, staff built a bespoke assistant called Hey Geraldine using the knowledge of an experienced occupational therapist, giving colleagues immediate access to guidance. Its reported totals were more than 1,200 questions answered and around 15 minutes saved per interaction.

    Children and Families Minister Josh MacAlister said technology cannot substitute for a social worker’s knowledge and skill, presenting administrative relief as a way to preserve time for listening to children, working with families and securing the support and protection they need.

    Isabelle Trowler, Chief Social Worker at the Department for Education, remarked the guidance recognises AI’s potential while keeping practitioners and their professional judgement central. “Organisations must take responsibility for governing, implementing and supporting its use,” she said.

    The government reports that four in five care providers now use digital social care records, helping almost 90% of people who draw on care. The digitisation effort is intended to cut paper records, repeated conversations, errors and inaccuracies.

    The wider aim is for all care providers to be fully digitised by the end of the current Parliament. For local authorities and providers, the practical task is to turn the national principles into informed adoption decisions: the local projects offer measures of administrative benefit, while organisational accountability and practitioners’ professional judgement remain central to responsible use.

    • Rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort.

    Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.

    Sources indicate that we've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018. Newly introduced contributions have come in under Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception since January 19, 2019. Code contributed before that date was under LLVM's earlier licenses (UIUC/NCSA, plus MIT for some runtime libraries), so we needed permission from its authors to move it over. [...].

    Rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort. Any contributors with code contributed before January 19, 2019 who have not signed a relicensing agreement and do not want their contributions made available under Apache-2.0 with the LLVM-exception can still reach out to the project to ensure their code has the appropriate SPDX license identifier.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Reuters reported on November 20, 2026 that a filing lodged on behalf of developer Zerra DC counted nearly 600 public submissions on its proposed Western Downs Digital Park in Queensland: 595 opposed the Anthropic-anchored AI campus or sought a delay until specified environmental requirements were met, two supported it and one was neutral.

    Objectors principally cited water use, electricity demand and prices, noise, road damage from construction traffic and housing pressure. About one-third of submissions came from people living within 200 km of the site, roughly 250 km west of Brisbane. The filing is an initial response to public consultation rather than a binding planning decision, and it identifies the challenges surrounding Anthropic’s proposed first Australian facility.

    According to recent reports, only five objections had arrived in the month before Anthropic was named as tenant on September 15, 2026; the rest were submitted before public notification closed on November 11, 2026. The filing acknowledged that a significant number raised reasonable matters about water, power, noise, roads, housing and project scale.

    Industry observers note that A Zerra spokesperson said the developer took the submissions seriously and was expanding community engagement, adding that the responses “reinforce that people want a greater say in how the project develops.” The developer also planned to report changes sought by the public. Anthropic declined to comment.

    In a recent development, zerra’s project page describes up to 1.44 GW of proposed IT capacity across four stages, anchored by a long-term Anthropic lease commitment, and lists the development application as under assessment. Final design, staging and development remain subject to planning and regulatory approvals. At that scale, the consultation concerns an entire energy and computing precinct, including grid, water, road and accommodation infrastructure alongside the data halls.

    In a recent development, the proponent’s federal environmental referral places the site about 15 km southeast of Kogan and 37 km northwest of Dalby. It covers approximately 801.3 hectares across six freehold lots and road reserves, with a maximum permanent disturbance footprint of 178.7 hectares. Looks include four data center buildings, substations and switching stations, battery-backed power conditioning, water and wastewater systems, and road upgrades.

    Industry observers note that the referral identifies potential effects from vegetation clearing, habitat disturbance, noise, dust, lighting, stormwater generation, vehicle movements and accidental spills. Proposed mitigation includes environmental management looks, pre-clearance surveys, erosion and sediment controls, and rehabilitation of temporary disturbance areas. Those measures remain proposals within the approval process, while the consultation response documents the community concerns Zerra now needs to address.

    Recent findings suggest that on the project website, Zerra says the data centers would use 100% air-cooled heat rejection rather than evaporative cooling, leaving operational water demand primarily associated with workers and essential site services. No town-water connection or planned extraction from local groundwater aquifers is proposed. Construction water would primarily come from processed coal-seam-gas water, subject to agreements and approvals, with trucked supplies from outside the region as backup.

    Industry observers note that the site’s current modeling for the first building estimates total operational demand at approximately 21 kiloliters (kL) per day, split between about 8 kL recycled on site and about 13 kL of remaining raw-water demand, primarily treated rainwater from an approximately 35,000-square-meter roof catchment. It compares the remaining amount with the daily water use of about 30 typical Queensland households. Those figures apply only to the first building; demand will increase as later stages are developed.

    For power, the campus would connect directly to the high-voltage transmission network at Braemar instead of the local distribution network supplying surrounding homes and businesses. Zerra notes it would fund the dedicated connection and project-specific network upgrades, and use battery-backed conditioning to smooth rapid changes in demand and present a more stable load to the grid.

    The housing plan includes purpose-built on-site accommodation for approximately 1,500 construction workers and an initial operational workforce of about 470. Zerra intends to move operational workers into community housing as additional supply becomes available, consistent with the council’s long-term residential housing plans.

    An economic assessment commissioned for the project estimates, assuming full delivery and operation, an average of about 1,500 direct on-site construction jobs annually, 1,400 direct operational roles and 2,100 indirect operational jobs. Those figures are full-build projections dependent on phasing, timing, occupancy and operating requirements, rather than current employment.

    In a recent development, council assessment now gives those commitments a concrete test: whether the water strategy scales beyond the first building, whether project-funded grid works and battery systems address power concerns, and whether traffic, housing and environmental effects can be managed through each stage. Anthropic’s lease supplies an anchor customer; the submission record shows that community acceptance and regulatory approval remain separate hurdles for the buildout.

    Archer from hackajob confirmed a $10 million fundraise on November 20, 2026, led by Volition Capital with support from AVP, to expand AI products for job candidates and recruiting teams.

    Sources indicate that the manufacturer is responding to a hiring market affected by AI-generated applications, fraudulent candidates and demand for niche skills. Its argument is that one-sided tools encourage candidates to submit mass applications and recruiters to send mass messages, leaving both sides with few genuinely latest connections.

    In a recent development, archer’s product documentation describes a two-sided matching process. Candidates set out the work, pay, location and conditions they want, then receive a shortlist of suitable roles with an explanation of each match. Recruiters specify the requirements for a role and receive qualified candidates in their applicant tracking systems, alongside context that a CV does not contain.

    Industry observers note that the tech giant reports that more than 700,000 candidates signed up to work with Archer in the 12 months before the announcement, more than hackajob’s combined sign-ups during the previous five years. Archer was making 10,000 introductions a week. About half involved people its customers had not previously seen, and introduced candidates were five times more likely to convert to an interview than each customer’s own baseline.

    In a recent development, archer also reports that annual recurring revenue grew fivefold in 2026, while customer cost per hire was 67% lower than hiring through staffing agencies. Google, Sierra and Barclays are among the companies whose talent-acquisition teams use the system. Archer charges per role rather than per hire, so the cost per hire falls as more hires are generated from a role.

    Industry observers note that the business is also moving beyond hackajob’s original technology-recruitment focus after a decade in that market. Archer now supports enterprise sales and front-office finance roles, as well as positions connected to data-center build-outs.

    It has been revealed that recruiters calibrate each role in plain English, supplying the job description, essential requirements, dealbreakers and broader criteria for success. Archer first filters on right to work, salary, location and required office days, then grades candidates against that brief. It confirms a person’s interest, location and pay before making an introduction.

    Recent findings suggest that the company says its own network contains 1.5 million vetted, identity-verified candidates, while a broader headhunting pool covers 25 million professionals in the US and UK. Archer Approves checks that each person has one profile, examines behavioral signals and government identification, and has blocked more than 30,000 fake candidates.

    It has been revealed that for employers, a read-only job feed goes into Archer, and candidates arrive through the existing applicant-tracking-system application flow, tagged as Archer. The firm states this avoids algorithmic hiring decisions because the candidate chooses to apply; recruiters take over at the screening stage and make every hiring decision.

    In a recent development, the firm looks to direct the funding to both sides of the marketplace. A candidate-agent launch is scheduled for January, while Archer OS, the product for talent-acquisition teams, is due for general release in the first quarter of 2027. Archer is also planned to work inside Slack, Teams and the AI tools recruiters already use, extending sourcing and qualification into existing workflows.

    The immediate test for the newly introduced capital is whether Archer can turn that candidate growth into broader adoption of its two-sided service, while expanding beyond technical recruitment and preserving recruiter control over hiring decisions.

    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Infoq ↗ Open Full Page

    AWS Releases a Free Local Emulator of AWS Built Entirely by Agents

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1238 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • InfoQ Homepage News AWS Releases a Free Local Emulator of AWS Built Entirely by Agents.
    • Nov 20, 2026 6 min read.
    • AWS has released AWS Emulator, a free local implementation of more than 200 of its services dedicated to the public domain under CC0, and states that "thousands of autonomous AI agents wrote every line of code" in it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    InfoQ Homepage News AWS Releases a Free Local Emulator of AWS Built Entirely by Agents.

    Nov 20, 2026 6 min read.

    AWS has released AWS Emulator, a free local implementation of more than 200 of its services dedicated to the public domain under CC0, and states that "thousands of autonomous AI agents wrote every line of code" in it. As InfoQ reported at launch, it ships as a single Rust binary generated from AWS's 438 public API models and listens on port 9297. The week since has brought the first independent fidelity numbers and a divided practitioner reaction.

    Pointing an existing SDK, CLI, or coding agent at the emulator is a matter of environment variables, after which the launch post by Daniel Abib indicates, "your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do":.

    It has been revealed that the same shell serves an agent. In the post, Kiro is asked to create and read back a DynamoDB table and problems the ordinary CLI calls against the local endpoint:.

    Matt Wood, AWS's chief AI and technology officer, argues that the loop matters because of what an agent does while a check is slow: "A coding agent can build a lot of software around an incorrect assumption." He also names the failure mode an emulator introduces:.

    An agent learns from the environment it experiences. If the emulator accepts behavior that AWS rejects, training can reinforce a mistake. An agent might also discover a shortcut that succeeds only because of an emulator defect.

    The fidelity scores exist to expose that gap: each release publishes per service how many tests pass out of how many were verified against real AWS, with the failing tests public too, and Abib asks readers to "read a score as a snapshot of a product that's improving.".

    Senior principal engineer Matthew Goldberg traces the project to a three-line prompt given to Kiro, "the simplest prompt that I could think of without any expectation that this would work":.

    Recent findings suggest that kiro came back after 15 minutes with a passable first version of an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS). I refined my prompt and had Kiro build me the rest of AWS over the weekend. And it did. It obviously had gaps, but it was compelling enough that my team started using it to test our software that Monday.

    Sources indicate that the production version is built by three agent teams: "One team manages a test suite; one team finds concerns in the emulator; and one team fixes those issues." Each fix must pass a gate that compiles the change and runs agent reviews for coding standards, security, and fidelity regression. "Our team hasn't written or reviewed any of the code," Goldberg writes, and describes what the gate carries:.

    If any of those checks fail, the change is sent back to the agent for rework; if they all pass, it is merged to mainline. We've seen thousands of concerns fixed every day as hundreds of agents concurrently work on the codebase. Without this merge gate, we wouldn't trust what our agents are building.

    Swami Sivasubramanian, in a guest post on Werner Vogels' blog, recalls rebuilding a replication engine with Kiro that had taken his team four months by hand:.

    It has been revealed that I supervised the agent for four nights before I saw that it had no way to check its results. Once it had a spec and a test environment, the rebuild took about two hours.

    In his telling, the engineer's job becomes "to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when that work is correct.".

    Industry observers note that the first measurements from outside AWS come from Kento Ikeda, an AWS Community Builder, who ran version 1.0.322 in GitHub Actions the day after launch. DynamoDB, S3 and SQS passed roughly 60 to 70 percent of their fidelity tests at service level and 80 to 100 percent on the operations its code called, while CloudFormation sat near 20 percent. The emulator matched AWS's error wording, but a new DynamoDB table stayed in CREATING for three seconds and rejected writes until then. "Being generated from API models only means the shape of requests and responses matches AWS," he writes, and places the tool between mocks and a real sandbox as a third layer rather than a replacement for either.

    The launch post draws its hardest line at security:.

    Recent findings suggest that don't use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn't evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production.

    Recent findings suggest that unimplemented operations return HTTP 501, telemetry is on by default, throttling, outages and regional differences are not simulated, and the repository does not accept pull requests. On Hacker News, one reader quoted the line on the security page that the emulator "never denies a request signed with its own key" and asked why IAM was left out:.

    I think because the agents were only building on the public API surface, it's hard to build this part. But they should've tried and let the agents read whatever policy engines AWS has. Or maybe it's a way to prevent someone from trivially running aws-emulator as AWSaaS?

    In a recent development, the thread's first question was whether this was "just an exercise or a real product they are going to ship and maintain," answered by a commenter identifying as AWS staff with "It's a real product that we initiative to maintain." Another counted "29,684 commits in a repository less than a month old" and mentioned it "does not instill confidence." On r/aws, the most-upvoted comment turned Amazon's own line around, calling agents that fix code "without human review" a terrible idea for a tool used to test before production. The reply was that the API specifications already exist and the SDKs are generated from them, so a server derived from a fixed contract is where agents can iterate until the tests pass.

    Industry observers note that the timing matters to the people in those threads. LocalStack's free Hobby plan now requires an account and prohibits commercial use, with paid seats from $39 a month, and several commenters had already moved to Floci. One of them put the AWS release in that context:.

    But in the wake of Localstack's changes, the landscape has been full of slopware and low trust anyway. I don't think this is worse, for now at least.

    It has been revealed that AWS's version costs nothing and can be forked by either project. Sivasubramanian indicates AWS "will share more about this work at re:Invent" in December.

    #11280. Before You Scale AI Agents, Ask What They Don’t Know

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1252 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Unite ↗ Open Full Page

    Before You Scale AI Agents, Ask What They Don’t Know

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1252 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Picture this: A CFO is getting ready for a meeting with a major institutional investor.
    • Recent findings suggest that the tool confidently states that the investor owns 2.5 million shares.
    • Industry observers note that but there’s a catch: The AI pulled the figure from a Form 13F filing, which reports holdings as of the previous quarter-end.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Picture this: A CFO is getting ready for a meeting with a major institutional investor. To help with prep, the investor relations (IR) team asks an AI tool to pull some background—the date of the last meeting with that firm, priorities expressed, number of shares held, and so on.

    Recent findings suggest that the tool confidently states that the investor owns 2.5 million shares. No one bats an eye, and the CFO continues preparing for this key conversation, full speed ahead.

    Industry observers note that but there’s a catch: The AI pulled the figure from a Form 13F filing, which reports holdings as of the previous quarter-end. The information was accurate back when it was reported… but now, it’s months old. In the meantime, the investor has quietly sold 2 million shares, reducing their position significantly. The meeting agenda (and potentially the meeting itself!) no longer seems relevant.

    What went wrong? In this scenario, the AI didn’t hallucinate or fabricate a number. It retrieved legitimate information but failed to qualify it or explain the limitations.

    While in this case, the consequences might be an awkward conversation or missed opportunity, in other situations, a similarly definitive answer that lacks critical context can carry even greater risks.

    It has been revealed that foundational models are getting better and better. So, why does it seem like confident-but-wrong answers are popping up more and more—something businesses across industries are grappling with?

    For starters, generative AI (GenAI) has become completely pervasive. According to McKinsey’s The State of AI in 2026 report, nearly 9 in 10 business professionals say their organizations regularly use AI in at least one business function.

    And as organizations move beyond experimentation—increasingly relying on AI for everyday business tasks and decisions— they’re also encountering the limitations of what these tools know and understand.

    A recent industry survey shows what’s often at the root of it: In the past six months alone, nearly 6 in 10 businesses (57%) traced a confident-but-wrong AI agent answer to missing or incomplete business context.

    With all the data available to AI, this may come as a surprise. But there’s an important distinction to be made: Context isn’t the same thing as data.

    Context can encompass institutional knowledge, exceptions to the rules, relationships, processes and expectations around how work gets done—nuances that are often unique to each company.

    In a recent development, in my work with investor relations teams, I see just how important these distinctions can be. Consider a few seemingly straightforward examples:.

    Given all this, it’s no surprise that the same underlying model can deliver very different results at different companies, depending on the context and specialized knowledge available to it.

    Sources indicate that purpose-built, industry-specific (or “vertical”) AI can help bridge some of these gaps, recognizing the specialized knowledge, workflows and nuances of a given sector. But even the most sophisticated technology can’t capture everything an organization knows, which is why humans have a part to play too.

    But humans don’t stick around forever. Consider what happens when an experienced investor relations officer (IRO) leaves their company after, say, five years. They’ve likely spent their time identifying and targeting prospective investors, analyzing shareholder activity, cultivating relationships, preparing for earnings, prepping execs… and a whole lot more.

    Recent findings suggest that the company retains the earnings scripts, presentations, and other files. But the institutional knowledge behind them? Much of that walks out the door too, especially when you consider that nearly eight in 10 IROs (78%) don’t have a successor identified for their roles.

    Sources indicate that that’s why organizations need to put in the work to preserve knowledge and understanding in a way that AI systems can use. Simply connecting an AI agent to a shared drive often isn’t enough.

    Having a way to systematically capture key knowledge and workflows—like the reasoning behind key decisions, the history of relationships, and other mission-critical information that never made it into a formal document—is important to businesses across industries.

    According to recent reports, and powering such a knowledge base requires people: both for recording information and applying judgment around it. AI can help organize knowledge, but it’s employees who provide the key context that technology often misses.

    Recent findings suggest that we’ve discussed what happens when AI gets an answer wrong. But sometimes, an AI agent can retrieve information that’s right—it’s accurate, current and relevant—and still create problems by sharing it under the wrong circumstances.

    In highly regulated industries, those missteps are especially costly.

    Industry observers note that in investor relations, for instance, sharing material nonpublic information (MNPI), such as unreleased financial results, with an analyst or investor can violate the U.S. SEC’s Regulation Fair Disclosure (Reg FD)—potentially resulting in financial penalties and reputational damage.

    Other industries like healthcare, financial services, and legal services face similar regulatory risks, highlighting the need for guardrails when AI agents are privy to sensitive information.

    This also highlights why humans remain crucial—an essential part of reviewing and approving what gets communicated. Companies may consider making the level of human review proportionate to the stakes, with different types of AI workflows operating with different levels of autonomy.

    According to recent reports, we’ve probably all encountered situations, in work or life in general, where we don’t know what we don’t know. Sometimes the ramifications aren’t consequential; other times they’re more serious.

    With such massive datasets available to AI today, AI models know a lot more… but still need to “speak up” when holes exist. So, as businesses use AI to tackle more strategic priorities and workflows, it’s vital to ask these questions before scaling:.

    I want to be clear: I’m bullish on AI. I use it daily in my role, see the current and future benefits, and think that—in many ways—we’re just scratching the surface of AI’s potential. I have no doubt that companies that avoid AI, and those that fail to implement it in an organized, effective way, run a real risk of falling behind.

    But adopting AI doesn’t mean giving a general-purpose model access to enterprise data and letting it operate willy-nilly.

    Right now, and as far as I can see, fully autonomous AI isn’t appropriate for every business task or decision. Organizations need to understand where AI can operate independently, where it needs additional context, and where human judgment is non-negotiable.

    Sources indicate that so, before asking what an AI agent knows, ask what it doesn’t. The answers shape how you deploy it, what you trust it to do, and how you set it up for success.

    Dror Nadler is Chief Product Officer at Q4 Inc., where he leads product strategy and innovation, helping investor relations teams harness AI, data and technology to work more effectively. He brings more than 25 years of experience in enterprise technology, SaaS and financial services, with previous leadership roles at Intralinks, Cellrox, Rapid7 and EMC. Throughout his career, Dror has focused on developing and scaling technology products, driving innovation and accelerating business growth. He holds an executive MBA from Boston University, a master’s degree in information technology from Harvard University, and a law degree from Reichman University.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1425 w)
