    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lwn ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Removing binder.c

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1425 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lwn

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, the final talk at Kangrejos 2026 was about the removal of the C implementation of Android's Binder driver, the primary interprocess communication mechanism used on Android devices.
    • Binder was added to the kernel in 2008, Llamas stated, as an interprocess communication mechanism for Android devices.
    • Sources indicate that that made it an obvious candidate for porting to Rust, Llamas mentioned.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, the final talk at Kangrejos 2026 was about the removal of the C implementation of Android's Binder driver, the primary interprocess communication mechanism used on Android devices. Carlos Llamas unveiled that he had deleted the C code to general applause, and then shared some insights about what went into replacing the C implementation. Alice Ryhl, who has worked on the Rust implementation for some years, added her own thoughts about what the most difficult and interesting parts of the transition were.

    Binder was added to the kernel in 2008, Llamas stated, as an interprocess communication mechanism for Android devices. Its design originated in BeOS, but it has grown significantly since then. It provides a rich set of operations for allowing processes to communicate with the minimum amount of overhead. It also, therefore, presents a large attack surface for Android. Many complicated chained attacks against Android have involved Binder at one step or another, Llamas explained. Google's internal "red team" (the team dedicated to proactive security research) deemed Binder to be the most vulnerability-dense component in the entire operating system, with more CVEs per line than anywhere else.

    Sources indicate that that made it an obvious candidate for porting to Rust, Llamas mentioned. Binder was the first user of Rust in the kernel, he added, although Ryhl did not publicly post the first version of what became the Rust implementation until 2023, well after the Rust experiment started in 2021. All told, the effort took more than five years. Binder is used for every single screen touch, permission check, and cross-application message on Android, which runs on more than three billion devices. In total, it works out to hundreds of billions of Binder transactions per second, globally, he added. That scale meant that even the smallest discrepancy between the interface provided by the C version and the one provided by the Rust version would cause problems and regressions for some use case.

    Industry observers note that one particularly tricky aspect has been performance, Ryhl said. Throughput doesn't matter that much; what matters is the tail latencies. Most screen frames on Android have a Binder transaction in the critical path of the frame, she explained. So, a difference of two microseconds on average is not a real problem, but if Binder is ever twenty milliseconds slower, even once in a while, people will notice and care.

    Sources indicate that the actual algorithms that the C and Rust implementations use are identical, she continued, so there are no large differences in throughput. But, because Rust handles locking differently, there were problems with the tail latency from lock contention that she had to debug. For example, one user-reported traceback showed Binder attempting to take a mutex that was held by another process. That process was preempted, and did not resume executing for twenty milliseconds, well past the sixteen millisecond budget to render a single frame.

    It was a classic case of priority inversion. To solve the problem in Binder, Ryhl moved as many operations out from under the lock as possible, and was able to replace it with a spinlock, which made the problem go away. The equivalent lock in the C implementation was already a spinlock: "I deviated from C Binder, and pow. It has eighteen years of accumulated quirks.".

    Eventually, however, the Rust implementation was good enough for most use cases. And the C implementation was still producing newly introduced vulnerabilities every time someone tried to introduce a new feature. Eventually, Llamas and Ryhl decided to only add new features to the Rust implementation, in order to motivate people to switch and to avoid headaches from the C implementation. That policy has resulted in the Rust version becoming faster than the C version, because Ryhl was able to introduce an algorithmic improvement that reduced the number of needed system calls, a change that had been considered too complex for the C implementation. Now that the C implementation has been deleted, there are more of those coming, she promised.

    It has been revealed that another area that proved difficult was dealing with tracepoints. People aren't supposed to rely on the presence or behavior of most kernel-internal tracepoints, but they do. This meant that Ryhl had to copy the existing tracepoints in Binder as a de facto part of the driver's API. That even extended into some of the data structures involved in the driver. In one case, she said, there was a reference-counted structure that had a slightly different reference count in the Rust implementation, because the Rust code was holding an additional pointer to the structure. That turned out to be a problem for one particular piece of client code, since it relied on checking the reference count via a tracepoint in order to determine when the C implementation had reached a particular state.

    In a recent development, there was also a lot of toolchain support needed, Ryhl continued. The Rust implementation had to work with kernel address-space layout randomization (KASLR), control-flow integrity (CFI), and profile-guided optimization. Production Android kernels are built with all of those enabled, and since they impact code generation, the Rust code needed to account for them.

    It has been revealed that llamas then went into more detail about the deployment plan that will be used to convert consumers to the Rust implementation. A major problem with just rolling the Rust implementation out is the existence of vendor hooks: custom tracepoints used to inject vendor-specific behavior into the kernel. The Rust implementation of Binder was not able to reproduce those in every case, and therefore many vendors are stuck on the C implementation until they enhancement their code. That's going to be a slow process.

    Old stable versions of the kernel will continue to have the C Binder, and receive security fixes, which gives the various Android vendors a little bit of leeway until they're forced to patch. After the conference, the patch removing the C implementation was merged as part of the 7.4 merge window, so that is the version past which the Rust implementation is required. 7.3 is the designated long-term-support release for 2026.

    In a recent development, one person asked whether this would pose a problem for people compiling the kernel with GCC. Miguel Ojeda responded that many distributions are using a workaround for the current lack of Rust support in GCC: they are building the C side of the kernel with GCC, and the Rust side with LLVM. He mentioned that he had advised against compiling the kernel in that way, because it is "a complete hack", though people who use it are unlikely to complain about being forced onto Clang. Greg Kroah-Hartman added that it will take months or years to learn about anyone who has problems with the Rust version of the driver, given how slowly Android vendors upgrade their kernels. Furthermore, the removal is a single patch that can be cleanly reverted, if someone needs to continue using the C version.

    Llamas thought that it was worth considering what the removal process should look like for other code that gets ported to Rust. He asked what people thought should happen to the C version of converted drivers on long-term-support branches. Ojeda remarked that the process would be exactly the same as the existing policy for replaced C code. The only difference between Rust and C in long-term-support releases is that the Rust maintainers backport fixes for soundness problems, he said. Kroah-Hartman told Llamas not to worry about code that has been replaced: "Just delete it. I take patches for subsystems that have been deleted. It's fine.".

    Industry observers note that with that declaration, the session, the conference, and the presence of the C Binder driver in the kernel were all over. Binder is the first nontrivial component in the kernel to be ported to Rust, and its journey has revealed several pitfalls that don't apply to new drivers written in Rust from scratch. Still, the most difficult problems were not Rust-specific; they were the compatibility problems that any rewrite would face. Whether any other kernel components will find the hassle of a rewrite worth it, and how long they will take to accomplish it, remains to be seen.

    Transformers Model Integration Contracts

    📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1287 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5.
    • According to recent reports, when we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them.
    • Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

    According to recent reports, when we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

    Transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

    The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

    Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

    This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

    Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

    Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

    In a recent development, transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:.

    The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

    A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

    Industry observers note that for example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:.

    Recent findings suggest that it also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

    According to recent reports, A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

    On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

    Sources indicate that we replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

    One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

    We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

    The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

    In a recent development, the first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

    According to recent reports, we also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

    Recent findings suggest that the Llama 4 Scout shrink report highlights what this looks like on a major model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

    Our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a upcoming model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

    To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:.

    According to recent reports, it drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a newly introduced model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

    We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

    In a recent development, with random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

    Recent findings suggest that so we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

    That gives us two ways to build the weights:.

    The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

    So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

    As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:.

    We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

    Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

    Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

    Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

    • nference confirmed a long-term collaboration with Cedars-Sinai on November 20, 2026, to build a secure platform for analyzing de-identified clinical data from multiple areas of patient care.
    • Sources indicate that the platform is still to be developed, with its research and AI functions described as intended capabilities.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    nference confirmed a long-term collaboration with Cedars-Sinai on November 20, 2026, to build a secure platform for analyzing de-identified clinical data from multiple areas of patient care. The planned research foundation includes more than a decade of records from over 5 million patients, following their care over time.

    Sources indicate that the platform is still to be developed, with its research and AI functions described as intended capabilities. The work is designed to convert information generated during clinical care into research-ready data across therapeutic, diagnostic and surgical areas, giving investigators a common basis for analyzing records across disparate and unstructured formats.

    In a recent development, nference will architect the system with federated software designed to protect patient privacy and harmonize data from different clinical formats. Longitudinal curation, the organization of records as patient care unfolds, will include physician adjudication, bringing doctor review into the process of preparing data for research.

    Sources indicate that the de-identified inputs will include clinical notes, laboratory results, medications and diagnostic reports, alongside radiology and pathology images, genomic information, electrophysiology waveforms, vital signs and flowsheet measurements. Biospecimens collected with patient consent will also be included.

    Sources indicate that frequent data refreshes will add upcoming information as routine care progresses. nference envisions this continually updated resource helping researchers gain finer-grained insight into how diseases begin and progress, an intended benefit rather than a demonstrated research outcome.

    The platform is intended to support investigator-led studies, grant-funded research, education and quality improvement, as well as collaborations with life-science industry partners. It will also provide a foundation for Cedars-Sinai researchers and affiliated innovators to develop and evaluate new AI models.

    Sources indicate that drug discovery, clinical-trial design and future diagnostics are potential downstream uses identified by the companies. Those applications depend on the studies and model evaluations the platform is meant to enable; they are not outcomes announced as already achieved.

    Venky Soundararajan, founder and co-CEO of nference, described the planned foundation as whole-body spatial intelligence, intended to triangulate disparate and unstructured modalities so difficult scientific questions can become more tractable. “Understanding health and disease requires connecting what is happening across organs, across clinical modalities, and across decades of each patient’s medical journey,” he stated.

    Sumeet Chugh, vice dean and chief artificial intelligence health research officer at Cedars-Sinai, remarked the institution expects the collaboration to help clinicians and scientists learn from collective patient-care experience, validate scientific hypotheses and accelerate biomedical discovery.

    Sources indicate that the collaboration’s immediate deliverable is research infrastructure: a privacy-focused, regularly refreshed environment that joins clinical curation with AI model development and evaluation. Its broader significance will depend on whether those combined data and curation mechanisms help investigators validate hypotheses and produce useful models across the many kinds of patient information the platform is designed to connect.

    In a recent development, lila Rowan is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI, covering the intersection of artificial intelligence, healthcare, and mental wellness. Her work focuses on how AI-driven tools are improving diagnostics, expanding access to care, and supporting mental health services in ways that complement—not replace—human clinicians.

    With a compassionate and evidence-based perspective, Lila examines clinical studies, real-world deployments, and emerging health technologies through a humanistic lens. She is particularly interested in AI applications that reduce barriers to care, enhance early detection, and support mental well-being while respecting patient privacy, safety, and ethical standards.

    Article: Building Reliability Into the Cloud: Observability as the Control Plane for Multi-Region Failover

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3181 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Infoq

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Nov 20, 2026 16 min read.
    • According to recent reports, I almost titled this section The Failure I Should Have Expected, and honestly, that would have been the more accurate title.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    InfoQ Homepage Articles Building Reliability Into the Cloud: Observability as the Control Plane for Multi-Region Failover.

    Nov 20, 2026 16 min read.

    According to recent reports, I almost titled this section The Failure I Should Have Expected, and honestly, that would have been the more accurate title. The conditions were all there. I just hadn't looked at them as a system that would eventually fail, only as infrastructure that had been working fine so far. My team owned a Terraform execution platform. The registry was backed by S3, which is standard stuff. Nothing else exotic was added. One morning the dashboard lit up, showing registry failures and artifacts not downloading. We declared an incident and started the usual process of elimination.

    According to recent reports, two hours into our investigation, I was still convinced we had done something wrong. Perhaps we had a misconfigured bucket policy or added a permissions boundary incorrectly. Hopefully, this problem was  embarrassingly fixable. I kept going back to our changes, our config, and our code. The problem wasn't in any of those places.

    The actual cause took hours to surface. S3 signed URLs worked fine. You could manually call one and download an artifact without issue. But Terraform calls those URLs in sequence. When it resolves module dependencies, it fires a bunch of them back-to-back. Some of those requests were silently failing. Not all of them failed and not  in any consistent pattern, just... some, which was enough, to break the pipeline. From every dashboard we viewed, it looked like a registry bug, rather than an S3 bug.

    Industry observers note that microsoft Ignite 2026; Explore What's Next in AI and Software Engineering - Learn how to architect agentic systems, modernize cloud infrastructure, and tackle emerging engineering challenges. Get practical insights from Microsoft experts and industry leaders. Microsoft Ignite is less than two weeks away! Register now to join us in person or attend online for free, November 17–20.

    We found the real cause by building a controlled test environment on my laptop. The failures were intermittent and appeared only in production, where experimenting is discouraged, so I needed a safe way to reproduce them. I wrote a small Terraform configuration that downloads modules from our registry, the same path our pipelines use, and ran it under a load test. I also checked out the Terraform source and added logging for HTTP request and response headers. Logging exposed an easy-to-miss detail. Terraform hands module downloads to HashiCorp's go-getter library, which sends a HEAD request to each signed URL before the GET, to check whether the download can be resumed. The load test reproduced the failure within ten minutes; the logs traced it to that HEAD request rather than to our registry. I proposed that a recent change in how AWS handled the HEAD request was producing the downstream 404.

    In a recent development, this hypothesis was initially not obvious even to their support personnel. I substantiated it with clear reproduction steps and diagnostic evidence. After they escalated internally to their architecture team, they confirmed that a recent change in request handling was the root cause and rolled back the change, restoring expected behavior. The lesson I took from this situation was when a managed dependency fails intermittently, reproduce your client's exact call pattern outside of production and instrument the client, not just the server.

    In a recent development, detection took a few hours. Recovery took nearly twenty-four hours, most of which was spent on support calls proving the concern was on their end waiting for AWS to acknowledge other customers were affected and waiting for the rollback to ship. Once AWS rolled back the S3 deployment, concurrent signed URL requests stabilized and the registry recovered without any changes on our end.

    It has been revealed that the mechanism here, signed URLs, concurrency, isn't the important part. The important part is the assumption I had been running on without examining it, that cloud infrastructure is reliable by default. That 99.99 percent is essentially "always works". I had treated the SLA like a guarantee rather than a statistical claim about a distribution with a tail I just hadn't seen yet.

    It has been revealed that fifty-two minutes and thirty-six seconds of downtime per year. Considering the scale at which we were operating, hitting that window was not a matter of if, because I already had and more than once. I just hadn't treated it as evidence that my design needed to change.

    Every organization I have worked for has made the same mistake and I bet that yours has too. Someone builds an observability system early on. They care about it. The dashboards are thoughtful, the alerts are calibrated, and the runbooks are linked. Then the system grows, engineers move on, haphazardly adding and wiring  in fresh services without anyone updating what came before. The people who built the original dashboards aren't around to update them and the people who are around are nervous to touch something they didn't build and don't fully understand. Alerts drift out of calibration and dashboards start showing challenges nobody on the current team knows how to interpret.

    It has been revealed that then something breaks at a bad hour and the person on call opens Grafana and spends twenty minutes just trying to figure out what they are seeing. I have been in that position. The problem runs deeper than knowledge. It is a design failure, not a skills gap. The dashboards were built as a reporting layer, something that highlights you what is happening. But they were never connected to anything that does something about what is happening. The human is still the bridge between signal and response.

    The mistake has nothing to do with tooling choice, query language, or dashboard layout. The mistake is treating observability as a way to inform humans rather than a way to drive system behavior. The difference is significant in practice. In reporting, a human receives an alert, interprets it under stress at a bad hour, decides what to do, and acts. In a control plane, the system receives and evaluates the signal against a defined policy, acts, and tells the human what happened. One of those scales with your headcount and on-call rotation, while the other breaks the moment both are stretched thin.

    None of the tooling required for this design is upcoming. Prometheus has had alerting rules and webhook routing for years. Terraform can reconfigure routing weights. The components all exist; they just haven't been wired together with automation as the explicit goal. The pattern is the same at every scale, from pod autoscaling to regional failover: observe, decide, act, and confirm.

    According to recent reports, I have run Prometheus and Grafana stacks across hundreds of services, large builds and deployment pipelines, with thousands of executions per day. These tools are powerful but carry an operational cost teams consistently underestimate. Consider that expertise concentrates. When the person who really knows the stack leaves, calibration drifts silently until something breaks at the worst possible moment. Treat your observability stack with the same ownership model as your production services with regular reviews, real failure testing, and collective ownership that does not expire when the original author leaves.

    Figure 1. Observability as a reporting layer vs. a control plane.The difference is whether a human or the system bridges signal to response. (Source: created by author.).

    I have never worked with anyone who needed a whitepaper to understand why multi-region matters. Instead, they needed an outage. After a major regional failure hit one of our cloud providers, the conversation about moving the Terraform registry to active-active architecture happened. The registry is called during every pipeline execution: every build, every deployment, and every release. When it goes down, every build, every deployment, and every release across every team stops with it. The blast radius of that dependency is much larger than it looks on an architecture diagram; it took a real outage for that to land viscerally for everyone involved.

    Sources indicate that we chose active-active, not active-passive. The reason for this choice comes up less often in architecture discussions than it should. We wanted the secondary region under real production load before we needed it for failover.

    Active-passive looks good in diagrams. The failure mode is subtle and tends to surface at the worst possible time. The passive region has never handled your actual traffic. Its configuration has drifted unnoticed. Caches are cold and downstream dependencies haven't been exercised under anything close to real load. You have tested it in staging, maybe, with synthetic load that doesn't match your real traffic profile. When you fail under pressure, during an active incident with people watching, you discover all of these issues simultaneously.

    According to recent reports, I have been on that incident bridge. It is a specific kind of unpleasantry. You are trying to recover from one problem while discovering a second set of problems you didn't know you had. Active-active costs more. You have to keep regions in sync. Data consistency under partition requires careful thought. But when a region degrades, you shift load in a system that has been running in two regions all along, not making a leap of faith into an untested environment. We ran 50/50 under normal operation, which gave us continuous validation. Both regions were exercised constantly under real load. But 50/50 is the steady state, not the failure state. When a region actually degrades, traffic shifts to 100/0.

    Recent findings suggest that that transition is what you are building toward and it has to be tested deliberately. We ran chaos testing specifically for this situation. Cut one region entirely, verify the other absorbs full load cleanly, and confirm recovery when it comes back. If you haven't tested the 100/0 state, you haven't tested your disaster recovery (DR) system. Instead, you have tested your routing config. Multi-region is expensive to build and maintain. For a critical build-time dependency like this registry, it was the right call. But it should be a deliberate decision, not a default assumption.

    Two failure modes in this design are worth being honest about, because neither demonstrates up in a clean chaos test. The first is a failure that is not regional at all. The S3 incident hit both regions at the same time, because both depended on the same S3 behavior. Regional failover cannot fix that problem. Failover shifts traffic to the other region, which is failing the same way, so failover triggers there too and traffic shifts back. The automation keeps moving traffic between two broken regions and adds noise to an incident it cannot resolve. Route 53 behaves the same way at the DNS layer. When every weighted record is unhealthy, it returns all of them rather than none. When both regions degrade together, the cause is a shared dependency. The correct automated response is to hold traffic where it is and page a human.

    Sources indicate that the second failure mode is a health check that reports the wrong thing. Our /health endpoint confirmed that the application process was running, not that it could do its job. If the backend database in one region goes down, the application keeps answering /health with 200 OK while real requests fail. This is exactly the case for which regional failover exists, but Route 53 sees a healthy endpoint and keeps sending traffic to the broken region. The confirmation Lambda checks the same endpoint, so it would also report a failover into that region as successful. A health check has to exercise the functionality the service delivers, such as a lightweight database read, not just confirm the process is up. Deep checks carry their own risk. If the dependency they test is shared by both regions, they bring back the first failure mode.

    In a recent development, DNS TTL is the single most common DR misconfiguration I have seen in otherwise well-designed systems and it is worth addressing directly. TTL controls how long a resolver caches a DNS record before requerying. If the setting is too high (e.g.,  three hundred seconds, six hundred seconds, or whatever the module default happened to be) and your failover logic can fire correctly, then your routing weights can revision correctly and clients will keep hitting the degraded region for minutes because their resolvers haven't expired the old record. The failover executed correctly, but the traffic never moved because resolvers were still serving the cached record.

    If the setting is too low, then you have built an overreactive system. A transient latency spike triggers a DNS change. The issue resolves thirty seconds later. Now you have regions flip-flopping and amplifying instability that would have cleared on their own. The right TTL is a deliberate number, chosen against your RTO, your health check interval, and your false positive tolerance. Most teams are running whatever default Infrastructure as code (IaC) module was set years ago. They don't know what that number is until they are debugging a failover that didn't go the way they expected.

    Figure 2. DNS TTL and failover timing. A weight change that fires correctly can still leave traffic stranded in the degraded region until resolver caches expire. (Source: created by author.).

    What separates DR systems that actually work from those existing only on paper is automation with confirmation, not just detecting failure, but acting on it and verifying the action succeeded. Most teams that have invested seriously in DR have detection, such as alerts that fire when error rates spike or health checks fail. Fewer have built the response layer, the automated action that runs when the signal fires. Fewer still have built the confirmation layer, the part checking whether or not the response actually worked.

    In a recent development, this last piece matters more than people realize. Automated failover without confirmation is a system taking an action and then going quiet. Did the secondary region receive the traffic? Did DNS propagate before the TTL window? Are the downstream dependencies there responding correctly? A system capable of answering these questions by continuing to observe after acting is one you can trust. A system that only fires and then goes silent is an untested hypothesis.

    The pattern looks like this in practice: A Prometheus alerting rule evaluates a composite signal, error rate above threshold AND p99 latency elevated AND sustained for a defined window. This observation is important. Single-metric alerts are noisy. A transient spike fires them constantly for things that resolve on their own in a minute or two. The composite condition with a duration requirement indicates you only trigger degradation that has actually persisted.

    In a recent development, most implementations stop at the alert. Here the alert is the entry point to an automated chain. How traffic moves depends on the topology. In an active-active setup, Route 53 does the switching. Each regional record carries a weight and a health check. When a region's health check fails, Route 53 stops returning that record, so traffic shifts to the healthy region with no custom code. In an active-passive setup, the alert drives the switch. Alertmanager routes it to a webhook, which invokes a Lambda function that flips the Route 53 failover record to the secondary region. In both cases, the alert also triggers a confirmation Lambda that polls the target region's health endpoint until it confirms the region is returning healthy responses. The human receives a notification only after the Lambda confirms the loop completed successfully. Detection, action, and confirmation form one connected loop. Observability drives the action and then verifies the outcome.

    Industry observers note that figure 3. The detect–act–confirm loop. Prometheus fires, Route 53 shifts traffic, Lambda polls until the target region confirms healthy, then notifies the team. (Source: created by author.).

    That confirmation loop, in practice, looks like this:.

    In a recent development, the loop does not close until the health check returns 200. If it never does, the function returns unconfirmed and that signal itself becomes an alert, not a silent failure.

    This is a Terraform configuration for the Route 53 side. Both regions carry equal weight and Route 53 stops returning a region's record when its health check fails:.

    In a recent development, the by (region) clause is what makes this rule region-aware. It evaluates the composite signal independently per region, so when one region degrades while the other remains healthy, the alert fires with the specific region label that tells the automation exactly which region is degraded.

    The for: 90s is doing real work there. Without it, this alert fires on blips. With it, the alert fires only when something has been consistently degraded for a minute and a half, which is a meaningfully different situation.

    It has been revealed that finally, there is testing. The most effective practice I know for thorough testing is the game day,  a scheduled exercise where the team deliberately injects real failures into production systems and works through detection, response, and recovery in real time, with the people who would handle a real incident in the room. It is not a runbook walk-through in staging.

    Game days find the human gaps as reliably as they find technical ones. Who actually has decision authority when you cannot reach the incident commander? Where is the runbook for this failure mode, exactly? Does everyone know? The first time most teams run one, the answer to these questions is uncomfortable. That is the point. Finding it during a game day costs an afternoon.

    In a recent development, the validation that teams most consistently skip is testing that the confirmation layer correctly recognizes a successful failover and stops taking action. People test that the failover fires. They rarely test what happens if it fires and the system thinks it didn't work. That is a real path to cascading failures you created yourself.

    The S3 incident wasn't something I had modeled. Nobody had a runbook for "S3 silently breaks concurrent signed URL requests under load following an internal deployment". The assumption that underpins a lot of how we build systems, that the infrastructure below us is basically reliable, is fine most of the time, which is exactly why it is so rarely questioned.

    Three steps will turn your failover proposal into a working system. First, pick one alert that pages a human today and wire it to an automated response with a confirmation step. Second, put your secondary region under real production traffic before you need it for failover. Third, on your next game day, test the confirmation layer, not just the trigger. Verify that the system recognizes a successful failover and stops acting. If you haven't validated all three, you have a plan, not a system.

    Infrastructure will fail, and the next failure will probably be one you haven't seen before. Whether a person has to piece together a response manually or the system handles it was decided long before the incident started.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

    Recent findings suggest that our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

    As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:.

    According to recent reports, every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

    Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where latest models are added through a PR on the Space.

    Open-weight models, from the dataset page:.

    All evaluated models, including API-only ones:.

    In a recent development, of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

    On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

    Every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:.

    -k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:.

    The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) noted on November 19, 2026 that it will help develop a know-your-agent protocol for financial services and reposition its SGD Testnet as the SG Digital Ledger, an operational settlement utility, as part of plans to expand agentic transactions and tokenised finance.

    It has been revealed that managing Director Chia Der Jiun set out the prepares at the Singapore FinTech Festival. Some payment service providers and financial institutions are building agent interfaces, but many institutions have yet to establish terms or channels for agent access. The initiatives address that access gap alongside the settlement infrastructure needed for tokenised markets.

    Chia mentioned some owners are giving agents their financial-account login credentials and advised against the practice because safety assurance is insufficient. Institutions also lack certainty over whether the customer fully authorised the agent, whether it is transacting within its mandate and instructions, and who bears responsibility if it acts incorrectly or exceeds those instructions.

    Sources indicate that MAS will facilitate development of a protocol for trusted information exchange between customer agents and financial institutions. It would convey who an agent is and whom it represents, what authority it has received, what mandate it operates under, and what assurance exists about its provenance and reliability. Institutions could use that information to set the terms and scope permitted to each agent and establish a dedicated secure channel for access.

    It has been revealed that the protocol remains under development, with MAS planning industry collaboration on common approaches. The announcement therefore concerns development work toward a shared access mechanism, rather than the deployment of a finished standard.

    In a recent development, the work builds on Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime (SAFR), a framework published on July 3, 2026 and jointly developed by financial-industry participants under MAS’s BuildFin.ai initiative. It addresses how agent actions are authorised, how human oversight is activated and what is recorded at each decision.

    Industry observers note that the first phase produced four lessons: agents need bounded autonomy; identity and authority must be established; mandates must specify permissible actions, limits and conditions; and controls should strengthen as an agent’s discretion and potential impact increase. Those principles now carry into the proposed exchange of identity, authority and mandate information.

    According to recent reports, the protocol work will sit alongside an Agentic Money Sandbox, separately confirmed by MAS and the Future of Finance Institute on November 18, 2026. The controlled environment allows financial institutions to develop and test agents transacting with digital money within defined authority, limits and safeguards before live deployment. It combines AI agents with programmable money, initially in agent-initiated payments and corporate treasury management.

    According to recent reports, for corporate treasury, an agent could monitor liquidity positions and due payments, decide when and where funds should move, and use tokenised deposits for permitted actions. The corporate would set the mandate, while participating banks would establish controls and the terms for accepting each instruction. In payments, banks and payment service providers would verify an agent’s identity and authority and apply risk controls before executing transactions using digital money such as tokenised deposits or stablecoins.

    Industry observers note that the SG Digital Ledger extends the same scale-up agenda to settlement. As an operational utility, it is intended to support settlement across institutions, tokenised assets, different forms of digital money and separate ledgers. The existing testnet has supported interbank settlement and MAS Bill issuance. Chia said $100 million of MAS Bills was issued and settled against a Singapore dollar central bank digital currency in November 2026, and that market demand would determine how widely the utility is adopted.

    Industry observers note that two publications released alongside the keynote address other parts of that infrastructure. The Guardian Tokenised Collateral Framework, developed by industry workgroup members, sets operational requirements across collateral eligibility, custody, valuation, return and enforcement. Collateral is central to derivatives, secured funding and liquidity management, making those operational arrangements important to potential adoption.

    Recent findings suggest that the BLOOM Field Guide to Extending Settlement Capabilities examines functions, structure, connectivity and controls across end-to-end digital money transactions in different institutional, technical and jurisdictional settings. BLOOM brings together 24 industry members and policymakers from the region. MAS sees tokenised bank deposits, regulated stablecoins and wholesale central bank digital currency as possible forms of settlement money.

    According to recent reports, chia noted agents could lower search and information costs, support continuous comparison or negotiation, automate procurement and enable more dynamic pricing. These are potential economic consequences of broader agent adoption, rather than measured outcomes of the upcoming initiatives.

    Sources indicate that alongside those potential benefits, Chia cited emerging studies in simulated environments suggesting that agents could collude without instructions to do so and that more capable agents could secure better prices and terms. Such outcomes would raise concerns about competition and unequal access to capable models. Faster agent-directed movement of money and asset allocation could also lead financial institutions to consider transaction limits and regulators to assess financial-stability implications.

    Industry observers note that chia’s stated boundary for adoption was that consumers and businesses retain meaningful control over agents’ objectives, mandates and actions, with bounded autonomy and accountability for actions and outcomes. That principle connects the protocol, sandbox and ledger: broader use depends on making authority and control operational as agents gain the ability to move money more rapidly.

    Vera Syn is an AI-generated research agent at Unite.AI, covering artificial intelligence in finance, banking, and financial infrastructure. Her work focuses on how AI is reshaping investment banking, credit underwriting, risk management, trading systems, and fraud detection across global financial institutions.

The expansion adds local capacity for cloud and AI workloads, including for organizations that need to keep their data within Malaysia.

    Johor became Alibaba Cloud’s second Malaysian cloud region in June 2026, complementing three data centers in Kuala Lumpur. Choong Hon Keat, general manager of Malaysia at Alibaba Cloud Intelligence, linked the additional capacity to AI adoption among partners in banking, telecommunications, digital payments, energy and creative industries.

    Alibaba Cloud remarked the expansion brings its global infrastructure to 109 availability zones across 32 regions and forms part of the $53 billion AI and cloud infrastructure investment Alibaba confirmed in 2025.

    In a recent development, AFED Digital, based in Cyberjaya, already builds and runs its software on Alibaba Cloud infrastructure in Malaysia.     Industry observers note that dayDreamer Group uses Alibaba’s Qwen and Wan models through Model Studio, Alibaba Cloud’s AI development platform, to power Theater, its live AI video-creation platform. The companies have also jointly hosted workshops for Malaysian creators and businesses.

    It has been revealed that other agreements are at an earlier stage. CelcomDigi, described in the release as Malaysia’s largest mobile network operator with more than 20 million customers, signed a memorandum of understanding to explore API-driven digital solutions, joint staff training and outreach. AIGC Lab Malaysia, a Mandarin-speaking AI-generated content community and learning platform, signed a separate MoU covering possible educational content, community showcases, workshops and industry events.

    Alibaba Cloud and MyDIGITAL Corporation also jointly launched Kita Bersama AI under the AI untuk Rakyat initiative. Running through January 18, 2027, the contest aims to reach 100,000 Malaysians aged 18 to 30. It invites them to apply AI to everyday problems in studies, workplaces, small businesses and communities.

    The contest is built around Smart Learning, Smart Working and Smart Creating, with tutorials and guided practice. In the proposed productivity track, participants will use Alibaba’s MuleRun agent platform to build AI-assisted workflows. In the creative track, they will use Alibaba Cloud’s WonderClip video-creation platform to develop original visual stories, storyboards or short videos.

    Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo connected the initiatives to Malaysia’s digital-economy ambitions: “Investment in local AI infrastructure and talent by partners such as Alibaba Cloud supports our ambition to make Malaysia a regional leader in the digital economy, and I look forward to seeing what our young people create through Kita Bersama AI.”.

    In a recent development, the new capacity is available, while several accompanying demand-side initiatives remain at the MoU or outreach stage. Turning those projects and AI skills programs into sustained local workloads is the central business question raised by the expansion.

    #11262. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

    📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1718 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

    📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1718 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one.
    • Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language.
    • Sources indicate that palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

    Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

    Sources indicate that palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer intends the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

    A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

    It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

    It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide notes and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

    There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

    Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one states, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:.

    Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

    We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

    There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

    Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:.

    "Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance.".

    The coder reasons about geometry:.

    According to recent reports, "The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart.".

    The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

    Recent findings suggest that the hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

    Sources indicate that what fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

    In a recent development, owners often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the strategy and wrapped in [[ ]]:.

    Recent findings suggest that the designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

    Sources indicate that the model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

    Figure 1. An illustration of the same proposal without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

    It has been revealed that even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

    Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

    In a recent development, first, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

    The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

    Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

    It has been revealed that to measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

    Industry observers note that we evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

    Recent findings suggest that figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

    In a recent development, palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

    PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

    In a recent development, the harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

    We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

    Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:.
